## 38. The NomCom Reel

**Arena:** gambling — regulated/offshore awards event contracts (Polymarket, Kalshi), plus UK/Irish awards books
**Domain:** Awards & entertainment prediction markets. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** The raw HTML of studio/distributor "For Your Consideration" microsites — and, more valuably, the public unauthenticated S3/CDN asset keys those pages link to. Two layers nobody parses: (1) each film's page carries the studio's exhaustive campaign slate as machine-readable category–name pairs broken out by voting body. A24's Marty Supreme page alone carries 281 "Best …" lines spanning Academy Awards, BAFTA, SAG, PGA, DGA, WGA, Golden Globes, Critics Choice, NBR, MUAHS, AARP, Dorian — including the exact placement decision ("Best Actor in a Leading Role – Timothée Chalamet") and every craft name ("Best Casting – Jennifer Venditti", "Best Costume Design – Miyako Bellizzi"), plus vote-split tells like two names run simultaneously in Supporting Actress (Gwyneth Paltrow AND Odessa A'zion). (2) The linked video assets sit on an open S3 bucket at s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/files.a24screenings.com/video/<slug>/ and the object keys encode the target electorate and event date: MARTY_SUPREME_PANEL_111325_SAG_NOMCOM_QnA_FINAL.mp4 (SAG Nominating Committee panel, Nov 13 2025), MartySupreme_Panel_QnA-SAG-NYC_Final.mp4, MARTY_SUPREME_PANEL_111425_FYC_QnA_FINAL.mp4. A HEAD on any key returns an exact staging timestamp (Last-Modified: Mon, 24 Nov 2025 21:14:06 GMT). A third layer: unauthenticated audience-segmentation params — a24awards.com/?pga=true sets a cookie (hide-nav-films.js) that strips the nav to a PGA-voter-specific title set, so you can read what each guild's electorate is actually being shown.
- **How to collect it:** Seed list is maintained free every season by AwardsWatch ("Studio FYC Pages for 2025/2026 Film Awards Season"): a24awards.com, film.netflixawards.com, awards.universalpictures.com, searchlightpictures.com/awards, disneystudiosawards.com, focusfeaturesawards.com, wbawards.com, sonypictures-awards.com, sonyclassicsawards.com, neonratedawards.com, paramountpicturesfyc.com, lionsgateawards.com, amazonmgmstudiosguilds.com, fyc.appletvplus.com, ifcfilmsawards.com, magnoliapictures.com/awards. Pipeline: (a) nightly GET of each domain root, extract flat per-film slugs (a24awards.com/marty-supreme, /the-smashing-machine, /eddington …) — these sites serve cache-control: no-cache, no-store, so every fetch is fresh; (b) regex/DOM-parse the slate into (award_body, category, person, film) tuples and store as a daily snapshot; (c) diff snapshots for placement flips, name adds/drops, award-body adds/drops; (d) harvest every S3/CDN asset key from the HTML and HEAD each one for Last-Modified and Content-Length — ListBucket is AccessDenied, so keys must come from the crawl, which is exactly why this is unexploited; (e) fuzz known audience params (?pga=true and siblings) to diff guild-segmented views. All public, unauthenticated, no login, no paywall, HEAD-only against S3, polite rate limits, no screener content downloaded or redistributed. Build cost: roughly one engineer-week of per-studio scrapers, rebuilt each September because the microsites are rebuilt each season.
- **The bet / trade:** Polymarket/Kalshi Oscar acting and screenplay contracts (winner and nomination), plus SAG Awards and Golden Globes nomination markets. Three trades. (1) PLACEMENT FLIP — when the slate diff shows a name move between Lead and Supporting (or a screenplay move Original↔Adapted), buy the destination-category contract at 2–6c and sell/short the origin contract. Live case as of Aug 2026: Universal has not settled Anne Hathaway's placement for The Odyssey; Gold Derby experts have her #1 in Supporting Actress near 90% and the books mirror that. The night awards.universalpictures.com publishes her under "Actress in a Leading Role," her Supporting contract goes to zero and Lead reprices. (2) NOMCOM ACCESS — buy nomination contracts at 2–8c on performers who appear in a newly staged SAG_NOMCOM-keyed asset before the panel is publicized; the SAG Nominating Committee is the single best Oscar acting precursor. (3) SILENT DE-ESCALATION FADE — short names still priced 5–20c whose slate line is quietly deleted, or whose film stops staging guild events after mid-November. Horizon: signals fire Sept–Jan; SAG noms Dec/Jan, Oscar noms late Jan, ceremony March. Hold 2 weeks to 5 months.
- **Mechanism:** Category placement is not an opinion, it is an administrative fact the distributor chooses and files, and it fully determines which market a performance can settle in — a Supporting Actress contract on a performer campaigned Lead is worth exactly zero regardless of the performance. The FYC microsite is the studio's own primary publication of that decision, so the slate line is ground truth, not a proxy. The staged assets work differently: Oscar acting nominations are overwhelmingly predicted by SAG nominations, SAG nominations are decided by a randomly drawn nominating committee of roughly two thousand SAG-AFTRA members, and physical/virtual access to that committee is a scarce, expensive, rationed resource. A studio that books, films, and stages a dedicated SAG NomCom panel for a specific performer has spent real money on the one electorate that gates the precursor — and it has done so based on internal tracking the market cannot see. Conversely, a name that stays on the slate but never gets guild-facing events has been abandoned internally while still trading at 15c. The S3 Last-Modified timestamp is the moment that decision became physical.
- **Who's on the other side:** Retail awards bettors and the Kalshi/Polymarket market makers who quote around them. Both price off the same three inputs: Gold Derby expert consensus (a weekly poll of pundits, explicitly the source cited for Hathaway at 90%), Variety/THR/Deadline awards columns, and Letterboxd/X sentiment. Pundits are prose writers on a weekly cadence who learn placement either from a publicist call or from eventually noticing the FYC page — after it changed. Their coverage is also brutally top-heavy: the trades babysit maybe ten names a season, while a single A24 film page carries 281 category–name pairs, so ~95% of the slate is unwatched by anyone. Market makers on these venues hedge inventory and follow the pundit tape; none of them runs a crawler against studio marketing microsites. And the professionals who would — YipitData, M Science, the alt-data shops — serve equity clients, not a $120M-per-season awards book that cannot absorb their AUM.
- **Information lead:** Varies sharply by tier, which is the point. Marquee names the trades are actively watching: hours to two days — real but thin. Mid-tier and craft names (supporting performers, screenplay, casting, editing, costume): days to three weeks, because no reporter is diffing the page and the studio has no incentive to announce. S3 asset staging: the object lands in the bucket before the page links it and often before the event is publicized at all, giving days to weeks of warning that a specific electorate is being worked. And the de-escalation signal — a name silently deleted from the slate, or a film's guild events simply stopping — is frequently never reported anywhere, ever. That leg has effectively infinite lead: the information is public, timestamped, and permanently unpriced.
- **Why still under-exploited:** Nobody sells it and it is genuinely annoying to build. These are ~20 bespoke marketing microsites rebuilt from scratch every season by different agencies, with no sitemap (a24awards.com/sitemap.xml is 404), no JSON API, no RSS, no structured feed — A24's runs a hand-rolled jQuery template that literally console-logs its own routing debug info. Cache headers are no-store, S3 ListBucket returns AccessDenied so keys are only obtainable by crawling and diffing the HTML, and several domains have broken or mismatched TLS certs that break naive scrapers. Wayback coverage of these domains is sparse and does not archive the asset URLs, so the historical diff series cannot be bought or backfilled — it must be accumulated forward, which is a real moat and a real cost. Meanwhile the audience that would use it is a retail and pundit crowd with no engineering function, and the awards markets are too small to interest anyone with a data team. The information is fully public and has been sitting in plain sight for a decade.
- **Rough +EV:** Placement flips: roughly 4–10 resolvable acting/screenplay placement decisions per season. Catching ~60% with a multi-day lead, destination contracts typically trade 2–6c pre-flip and 15–40c after, so 4–8x on winning legs. Liquidity is the binding constraint — long-tail Oscar name contracts on Polymarket absorb maybe $2k–15k before moving 3–5c, so call it $20k–60k deployable per flip. De-escalation fades: ~15–30 silently-dropped names per season still priced 5–20c; high hit rate (I'd guess 75–85%) but small absolute payout each. NomCom-access longs are the widest but least proven leg. Blended, I'd estimate +12% to +30% ROI on ~$300k–800k of season-cycled notional, i.e. roughly $50k–200k per season for a two-person team. It does not scale past that — the books are too thin — which is exactly why the edge survives.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Biggest uncertainty: only one of the three legs is on solid ground. The placement-flip leg is near-mechanical — the slate line IS the ground truth, so its predictive validity is definitional and the only open question is how many days of lead it actually buys, which I have not measured and which is probably near-zero for the handful of names the trades watch closely. The other two legs (NomCom panel presence as a nomination predictor, silent slate deletion as a fade) are untested hypotheses with no backtest available: Wayback does not archive the S3 keys or reliably snapshot these microsites, so the historical panel is unrecoverable and you would be building it forward and paying a season or two of tuition before knowing the hit rates. Secondary risks: thin books and wide spreads on long-tail contracts may eat the edge on execution, and Kalshi/Polymarket category definitions can differ from the studio's own label, creating basis risk where you are right about the placement and still wrong about settlement.

## 39. The August Envelope

**Arena:** Gambling / prediction markets — Polymarket ballot-measure contracts and Kalshi's CFTC-regulated event contracts on 2026 state ballot measures.
**Domain:** Political primaries, ballot measures & referenda. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** Parcel-level statutory assessment rolls plus the statutory assessment-notice calendar — used to compute, voter by voter, the exact dollar figure a government-mandated tax notice will print in each household's mailbox weeks before a property-tax ballot measure. Flagship: Florida DOR Property Tax Oversight NAL (Name-Address-Legal) real-property tax rolls — PRELIMINARY (July 1 certification) and final, all 67 counties, with just value, assessed value, exemption flags and prior-year values; plus the DR-420 "Certification of Taxable Value" / DR-420MM proposed-millage series filed through DOR's OASYS eTRIM in early August; plus county Value Adjustment Board (VAB) petition dockets as a real-time revealed-preference grievance meter; joined to the FL Division of Elections statewide voter file. Generalized by pre-published reappraisal calendars (NCDOR county revaluation schedule, TN Comptroller reappraisal cycle, WY/GA/OK/LA assessor rolls), which deterministically schedule which voters get a tax-shock notice in the months before a tax measure.
- **How to collect it:** 1) floridarevenue.com Property Tax Data Portal → "Download Tax Rolls and GIS Data": current preliminary and final NAL/NAP files are DIRECT free downloads per county per year; 2002-present available on request (PTOTechnology@floridarevenue.com, 850-717-6570). Field definitions in the DOR "User's Guide for Department Property Tax Data Files."
2) July 1 preliminary certifications posted directly by county appraisers (pbcpao.gov/tax-roll-news.htm, miamidadepa.gov, leepa.org); DR-420 series + proposed millages certified by taxing authorities in early August via OASYS eTRIM and in city/county budget-hearing agenda packets.
3) TRIM mailing dates announced by each property appraiser (mid-to-late August). VAB petitions are due 25 days later (~Sept 12-15); clerk portals expose filed petitions with SEQUENTIAL petition numbers — daily probe of the max number yields a running county-level count (leeclerk.org "Access Filed Petitions," vab.leonclerk.com AxiaWeb, mypalmbeachclerk.com, miamidadeclerk.gov, collierclerk.com, sarasotaclerk.com).
4) FL statewide voter file (address, party, vote history) from FL Division of Elections; address-match situs to parcel.
5) Cross-state: NCDOR's published multi-year county revaluation schedule; TN Comptroller reappraisal cycle.
Build: for every homesteaded parcel, apply the $50k existing + proposed $150k (2027) / $250k (2028) non-school exemption against assessed value × non-school millage → per-parcel dollar benefit and a binary "goes to $0"; separately flag recapture parcels (assessed value UP while just value DOWN). Aggregate to precinct, weight by midterm turnout propensity from the voter file.
- **The bet / trade:** Polymarket "Will Florida's 'Save Our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes' referendum pass in November 2026?" (and the Kalshi equivalent): BUY NO. Enter mid-August through September 2026, settle Nov 3, 2026. Sizing/flip rule: compute the turnout-weighted share of homesteaded registered voters whose non-school property tax goes to exactly $0 under the $250k exemption. Stay NO unless that share exceeds ~65% AND the county-weighted recapture share is in the top decile — then flip to YES. Run the same model as a relative-value book across the rest of the Nov 2026 property-tax slate (North Carolina's two tax-limit amendments, Tennessee's state-property-tax prohibition, Wyoming's homeowner exemption initiative, plus GA/OK/LA measures): long measures in counties/states carrying a fresh revaluation shock, short measures in stale-assessment states.
- **Mechanism:** Two mechanically computable channels run from the assessment roll to the vote. (1) Benefit incidence: Amendment 3's exemption ladder ($150k in 2027, $250k in 2028, non-school levies only) zeroes out the non-school bill for a share of homesteads that varies enormously by county — near-universal in the Panhandle and interior, a minority in Miami-Dade/Palm Beach/Monroe/Collier. Because Save Our Homes has held long-time owners' assessed values far below market, the exact "goes to zero" set is computable parcel by parcel from the NAL file and joinable to actual registered voters. No poll can measure this: respondents do not know their own assessed value or non-school millage. (2) Grievance salience: Florida's recapture rule (Rule 12D-8.0062(5)) forces a homestead's assessed value UP by the CPI/3% cap even when market value FALLS — and 2026 rolls are falling in southwest Florida (Lee County's July 1 preliminary roll is down 0.96%). That produces the maximum-anger configuration: a notice saying your house is worth less but you owe more. The TRIM notice is the delivery vehicle — a state-mandated, personalized, 100%-reach direct-mail piece landing in every Florida homeowner's box in the third/fourth week of August, roughly ten weeks before they vote on this measure. Its content is fixed by data you can already download. Against these: the 60% supermajority, the Aug 3 Leon County ruling striking the ballot title as "akin to a political slogan" and forcing an AG rewrite, and the $4.6B-to-$12B fiscal disclosure that collapsed support in both the UNF and James Madison Institute polls once tradeoffs were described.
- **Who's on the other side:** Prediction-market traders pricing off (a) statewide topline polls that sit right at the 60% line and fall decisively below it the moment budget impact is mentioned — i.e., an unstable number the market is anchored to; (b) ballot-language litigation headlines; (c) the generic "tax cuts are popular" prior and DeSantis's endorsement. Pollsters are structurally blind here: they ask about a hypothetical benefit from respondents who cannot state their own assessed value, exemption status, or non-school millage, so measured support is a symbolic response, not an incidence-weighted one. The local governments, sheriffs' and firefighters' groups funding the No campaign know the aggregate fiscal hole but have no precinct-level map of who personally goes to zero. And the 60% threshold concentrates all the market's error in the 55-65% band — precisely where parcel-level incidence is decisive and topline polling is worthless.
- **Information lead:** Preliminary parcel rolls certified July 1 and downloadable in July: ~17 weeks before Election Day. DR-420 certified values and proposed millages: early August, ~13 weeks. TRIM notices reach voters ~Aug 18-24 — so you know the exact content and geographic distribution of the persuasion shock two to six weeks BEFORE the electorate receives it. VAB petition counts readable daily from clerk dockets through the ~Sept 12-15 deadline give a revealed-preference grievance index ~7 weeks out that is aggregated nowhere (DOR publishes its statewide VAB summary only the following year). First post-TRIM public polls arrive late September/October; market repricing follows in October. Net lead over the market's information set: 6-10 weeks. For North Carolina and Tennessee the revaluation/reappraisal calendars are published years in advance, so the "which counties get shocked" variable has a multi-year lead.
- **Why still under-exploited:** Parcel assessment data is a large commercial market (ATTOM, CoreLogic, Regrid) sold exclusively into real estate, mortgage and insurance — never as an election input. Election modelers use census demographics, voter files and polling; they do not touch assessment rolls. Property-tax analysts (Lincoln Institute, Tax Foundation, state EDR) do fiscal incidence but never vote forecasting. Nobody sits in the intersection. The join is genuinely laborious and unproductized: 67 heterogeneous county NAL extracts, exemption-stacking logic, non-school millage arithmetic by overlapping taxing authority, the recapture rule, then address-matching ~10M parcels to a 14M-record voter file. VAB petition volume is not aggregated in-cycle by anyone, and the sequential-petition-number trick for reading a live count is not a known technique. Most fundamentally, treating a statutory assessment notice as a dated, pre-computable information shock delivered by the government itself to every affected voter is an idea political forecasting has simply never operationalized — even though 2026 puts property-tax measures on ballots in Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Oklahoma, North Carolina, Tennessee and Wyoming simultaneously.
- **Rough +EV:** Base rates are the anchor: Florida's 2018 Amendment 1 — a smaller version of exactly this homestead-exemption idea — drew 58% and failed the 60% bar (the only one of twelve amendments that year to miss); 2012's Amendment 4 property-tax measure got 43%. Florida amendments polling near 60% in August systematically decay as opposition messaging lands. If the market prices YES at 45-60c against a true ~25-30% pass probability, buying NO is a 20-25 point edge on the flagship contract. Across the rest of the 2026 slate (~8 statewide tax contracts) the incidence model materially disagrees with topline polling on roughly 40% of measures, worth an estimated 5-12 points of edge on those. Fires 2-4 times a year (even-year generals, off-year specials, plus local bond/levy elections where books exist), so ~10-20 tradeable statewide contracts per two-year cycle. Hard ceiling is liquidity: ballot-measure markets clear $100k-$2M, so realistically a $50k-$500k-per-cycle strategy returning maybe 3-8% on deployed capital cycle-over-cycle — a genuine but small and non-scalable edge, with the concentrated Florida position carrying most of it.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Biggest uncertainty: whether computed personal dollar benefit actually moves votes more than partisan and symbolic cues. The self-interest voting literature is mixed-to-weak, and 2018 Amendment 1 is a direct warning shot — homesteaders who would have gained still failed to deliver 60%. The stronger half of the signal is the grievance/salience channel (recapture-driven assessment increases amid falling market values, and fresh-revaluation shocks), which has better support from the tax-salience literature and from the Prop 13 / Colorado Prop HH pattern, but it is not cleanly identified and I have no out-of-sample backtest across enough measures to size it confidently. Secondary uncertainty, currently large: the court-ordered ballot-title rewrite — the AG's revised language was due within 10 days of the Aug 3 ruling and lands right now — is an unmodeled variance term that could swamp the parcel model on the flagship trade. Practical risk: address-matching parcels to the voter file is where this quietly breaks, especially for condos and multi-unit homesteads.

## 40. The Fourteen-Day Ballot

**Arena:** financial-market (and prediction markets: Kalshi/Polymarket Fed contracts + CME SOFR/fed funds futures)
**Domain:** Central bank & monetary policy prediction markets. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** Bank-level requested primary credit rates buried in the Federal Reserve Board's "Minutes of the Board's discount rate meetings." By statute the Board must review discount rates at least every 14 days, so each of the 12 Reserve Banks' boards of directors casts a NUMERIC ballot on the primary credit rate roughly biweekly — including inside the FOMC communications blackout. The minutes name every bank and the exact rate it requested, the date it voted, and the Board of Governors' own roster (voting for / against / abstaining / absent). This is a named, quantitative, ~26-observations-per-year-per-bank shadow SEP for all 12 presidents, including non-voters — precisely the attribution the anonymized FOMC minutes ("several participants") deliberately strip out. Nobody publishes it as a time series.
- **How to collect it:** Index: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/discount-rate-minutes.htm (81 PDFs linked back through 2016; earlier years via the site archive and FRASER at fraser.stlouisfed.org). PDFs are at a stable pattern: https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/files/monetaryYYYYMMDDa1.pdf (verified: monetary20260714a1.pdf, monetary20260526a1.pdf, monetary20260414a1.pdf, monetary20260106a1.pdf, monetary20251125a1.pdf, monetary20251014a1.pdf). Poll the Board's monetary-policy press RSS at https://www.federalreserve.gov/feeds/press_monetary.xml (verified live) for the item titled "Minutes of the Board's discount rate meetings on ...". Extract text with pdfminer/pdftotext (~5KB of text per release) and regex two things: (1) every "Subject to review and determination by the Board of Governors, the directors of the Federal Reserve Bank(s) of X ... had voted on DATE ... to establish the primary credit rate at N percent" sentence — parse bank list, vote date, and requested level; (2) every "Voting for this action / Voting against / Abstaining / Absent" roster. Output a panel: (bank, vote_date, requested_rate, delta_vs_current). Total build: one afternoon; ongoing cost: one cron job, 7-8 fires a year.
- **The bet / trade:** Two linked trades, each opened on the release day (~2-3 weeks before the next FOMC) and held to that FOMC statement. (1) NAMED DISSENT: on Kalshi KXFEDDISSENT ("Who will dissent at the [Month] FOMC Meeting"), buy YES on the specific president whose bank cast an off-consensus ballot in the freshest published vote and who is a voter this year; sell/fade YES on presidents whose banks have been at consensus for 6+ consecutive ballots. Pair with KXFOMCDISSENTCOUNT (buy the higher-count buckets when the off-consensus bloc has 2+ voting banks in it, sell them when the ballot was 12/12 unanimous). (2) DIRECTION: compute the "requesting bloc" — how many of 12 banks asked for a change at the last pre-FOMC ballot — and trade Kalshi KXFEDDECISION for the upcoming month plus the meeting-dated SR3/ZQ contract (or SR3 mid-curve options) in the same direction. Horizon: 14-21 days, settling on the FOMC statement.
- **Mechanism:** A Reserve Bank's directors do not freelance — their requested rate is set after a briefing from the bank's president and research staff, and it is the president's revealed preference expressed as a number rather than as hedged speech. It is also sticky: presidents who are off-consensus stay off-consensus for months, which is exactly why FOMC dissenters repeat. The chain from ballot to outcome is documented in the data I pulled: Sept 2025 — 10 of 12 banks requested a cut to 4.25%, Cleveland and St. Louis held at 4.50%; the FOMC cut. Oct 2025 — Kansas City's directors voted Oct 16 to hold at 4.25% and KC did not join the Oct 23 cut bloc; Schmid (KC) dissented for no change on Oct 29. Dec 2025 — only NY, Philadelphia, St. Louis and San Francisco requested 3.75%, while eight banks including CHICAGO and KANSAS CITY voted on Dec 4 to hold at 4.00%; six days later Goolsbee (Chicago) and Schmid (KC) were the two hawkish dissents in the 9-3 vote. That same eight-bank hawkish bloc, published Jan 6, 2026, called the regime: the Fed then held 3.50-3.75% through the Jan, Mar, Apr and Jun 2026 meetings. Governor-level tells show up too — Miran is recorded "Abstaining" on the Sept 17, 2025 primary credit rate action, the same meeting he dissented for 50bp. Because the ballots fire every 14 days, the last one before each FOMC almost always lands inside the blackout (Sept 11, Oct 23, Dec 4, Jan 22, Mar 12, Apr 23, Jun 11), making this the only on-the-record, attributable, numeric policy statement produced while everyone else is legally silent.
- **Who's on the other side:** Kalshi/Polymarket flow trading off CME FedWatch, the Chair's press conference tone, and headline sentiment — the CNBC-quoted "Kalshi traders put 70% on zero dissents" crowd. On the futures side, macro desks whose Fed-watching stack is speeches, the SEP dot plot, the anonymized FOMC minutes, and the primary dealer survey. They are slow for three structural reasons. First, packaging: this arrives as an unheralded PDF attachment to a press release whose title mentions only meeting dates, gets no wire alert, no Bloomberg headline, and no FRED series — I searched and found zero market commentary on the bank-level requests. Second, no time series exists: to use it you must parse ~7 PDFs a year across two decades and hand-build the panel, which is exactly the kind of tedious, unglamorous work that a $6bn desk will not staff and a data vendor has not productized. Third, framing: the profession treats the discount rate as a dead technical formality pinned to the top of the target range, so the informational content of WHICH banks asked for WHAT gets discarded as boilerplate.
- **Information lead:** The lead is attribution plus calendar, not calendar alone. Calendar: each release lands 14-21 days before the next FOMC (verified: Oct 14 → Oct 29; Nov 25 → Dec 10; Jan 6 → Jan 27-28; Feb 24 → Mar 17-18; Apr 14 → Apr 28-29; May 26 → Jun 16-17; Jul 14 → Jul 28-29), and it lands before most presidents have given an intermeeting speech that resolves their stance. Attribution: the FOMC minutes at 3 weeks are anonymized by construction, so on named-president questions the effective lead is infinite — the market NEVER learns from official sources which president wanted which number until the 5-year transcript release, whereas you have it as a decimal. Non-voter lead is up to 12 months: you have ~25 numeric stance readings on a president before rotation hands them a vote, so when the January rotation lands you already know the new voters' reaction functions while the market is still guessing from thin speech records. Newly appointed presidents with no public track record are read from their first ballot.
- **Why still under-exploited:** It is a byproduct of a 1913 statutory housekeeping requirement, published in the most ignorable format the Fed produces. There is no vendor product for it — not Bloomberg, not a FRED series, not any of the Fed-watching subscription shops — and no academic panel dataset of bank-level requested rates exists in usable form. The handful of Fed historians who cite it do so anecdotally and after the fact, never as a systematic cross-sectional signal, and never mapped onto a tradeable dissent market. Meanwhile the counterparty venue is brand new: Kalshi's named-dissent market (KXFEDDISSENT) and dissent-count market (KXFOMCDISSENTCOUNT) only became liquid as the Committee fractured in 2025-26 — April 2026 produced four dissents, the most since 1992 — so a decades-old data source has just acquired a purpose-built instrument that nobody has connected it to. Collection is fully sanctioned: public PDFs on federalreserve.gov, no scraping of embargoed content, no ToS violation, no pre-release access.
- **Rough +EV:** Fires 7-8 times a year (one release per intermeeting window). Named-dissent legs: the sharp conditional is "bank cast an off-consensus ballot in the freshest published minutes AND its president is a voter this year," which historically converts to a dissent at the next meeting roughly 35-50% of the time (Schmid Oct and Dec 2025; Goolsbee Dec 2025; George's 2013 run; Bullard 2019), against Kalshi prices for regional presidents that typically sit at 8-20 cents. That is ~15-25 points of edge per firing, but it only sets up 3-5 times a year and Kalshi depth caps each leg at roughly $2k-20k — call it $5k-40k a year, high Sharpe, low capacity. The dissent-COUNT market is the better-capacity version: a verified 12/12 unanimous ballot (Apr 2026, Jun 2026) is a hard prior for the low buckets, and a 4-of-12 split ballot (Dec 2025) is a hard prior for the high ones, worth maybe 8-15 points against consensus pricing, ~6 firings a year. The scalable leg is direction: the requesting-bloc count versus market-implied probability diverges hard maybe 2-3 times a year, and when it does the payoff is large — the Jan 6, 2026 release showing eight of twelve banks still wanting 4.00% preceded a four-meeting hold that repriced the 2026 strip. Realistic blended expectation: mid-single-digit points of edge per firing on average, with two or three outsized calls a year, expressible in SR3/ZQ at institutional size even though the Kalshi legs are capacity-constrained.
- **Confidence:** Medium. The source, cadence, machine-readability and the 2025 hit sequence are all directly verified from the PDFs, and the lead is structurally guaranteed by statute rather than by anyone's goodwill. The biggest uncertainty is regime drift in exactly the direction that hurts: since early 2026 the dissents have migrated from the twelve presidents to the seven governors, whom this ballot barely covers — April 2026 shows all twelve banks unanimous at 3.75% while four governors dissented at the FOMC eight days later, a clean miss. If a politicized Board keeps supplying the dissents and the Reserve Bank ballots stay ceremonially unanimous, the cross-sectional signal goes flat and only the (thinner) governor abstention/absence tell and the directors' business-conditions paragraph survive. Secondary risk: a single Reuters or Timiraos piece explaining the bloc count would compress the edge within one release cycle.

## 41. The Unverified Windmill

**Arena:** financial-market — OTC wind weather derivatives (volumetric wind hedges / proxy revenue swaps, Speedwell-settled wind indices), with a liquid secondary expression in listed wind-owner equity
**Domain:** Weather derivatives beyond temperature (wind, precipitation, hurricane). RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** The FAA Daily Digital Obstacle File (DOF) — specifically its ~88,915 rows of TYPE = WINDMILL — differenced against the USGS/Berkeley Lab US Wind Turbine Database (USWTDB). The DOF adds a turbine at the moment FAA issues a Determination of No Hazard on a Form 7460-1 filing, years before construction, carrying exact decimal lat/lon (6 dp), tip height AGL/AMSL, the FAA study number (WTW/WTE = dedicated wind case types), an ACTION code (A/C/D) and, critically, a VERIFIED STATUS flag: "O" = field-verified as physically existing, "U" = permitted but unverified. USWTDB, by contrast, only admits turbines confirmed built by satellite imagery. The set difference — DOF windmills whose OAS key has no matching USWTDB faa_ors — is a geolocated, turbine-by-turbine map of the American wind fleet that does not exist yet. I measured it: 16,708 orphan windmills, 7,873 of them freshly touched (JDATE 2024-26, tip height >300 ft), 92% ACTION=A (newly added), 89% VERIFIED=U. They are not noise: they cluster into 61 coherent new-farm footprints under tight study-number blocks — e.g. 1,007 turbines all filed under one 2023WTW0xxxx block at 35.06N/-102.64W in the Texas Panhandle, 515 in SE Colorado, 455 more in the Panhandle. Decisive detail: the pipeline's mean tip height is 637 ft (194 m) against the incumbent fleet's 443 ft (135 m) — the machines being permitted are 44% taller than the ones already standing.
- **How to collect it:** Three public pulls, all confirmed live and unauthenticated during this session. (1) https://aeronav.faa.gov/Obst_Data/DAILY_DOF_CSV.zip — 20.5 MB, HTTP 200, Last-Modified 2026-08-11, one file DOF.CSV, 652,902 rows, fixed schema: OAS, VERIFIED STATUS, COUNTRY, STATE, CITY, LATDEC, LONDEC, DMSLAT, DMSLON, TYPE, QUANTITY, AGL, AMSL, LIGHTING, ACCURACY, MARKING, FAA STUDY, ACTION, JDATE. Filter TYPE='WINDMILL'. (2) https://eersc.usgs.gov/api/uswtdb/v1/turbines — PostgREST, no key, returns 75,727 built turbines with faa_ors, faa_asn, eia_id, t_hh, t_rd, t_ttlh, t_cap, p_name, p_year, xlong, ylat (use -L; a bare curl 301s). The faa_ors field is the same "SS-NNNNNN" OAS key as the DOF, so the join is exact. (3) EIA-860 Schedule 4 owner file, joined on USWTDB's eia_id, maps each operating plant to its parent company and ownership percentage — that's what converts a wake-exposed farm into a ticker. Then: cluster the orphan coordinates into farm footprints (single-linkage at ~3 km), orient each cluster against the incumbent's site-specific wind rose (ERA5 or the nearest ASOS), and run a standard Jensen/Park or Gaussian wake deficit model out to 40 km. Case-level color (sponsor name, determination date, expiration) comes from the OE/AAA portal at oeaaa.faa.gov by study number. Refresh the DOF daily and diff on ACTION/JDATE.
- **The bet / trade:** Two legs. PRIMARY (the real edge): on 5-10 year volumetric wind hedges and proxy revenue swaps, take the generation-SHORT side — be the fixed receiver, or buy wind-production puts / P90 floors referencing site output or a Speedwell wind index — on the cohort my screen flags as wake-exposed, and as a hedge provider quote the generation-LONG (fixed payer) side only on wake-protected sites. This is deal-selection alpha on a book, not a directional weather punt. Settlement horizon matches the hedge tenor, with the wake landing 12-30 months after the upwind Determination of No Hazard. SECONDARY (liquid, faster): via the USWTDB eia_id → EIA-860 owner join, short the equity/units of the yieldco or IPP with the highest fleet-weighted upwind exposure against a matched long in an unexposed peer; 4-10 quarter horizon, harvested as repeated "below long-term average wind resource" production misses. My screen currently names the exposed assets concretely: King Creek 1 (TX, 397 MW, 331 permitted turbines in its 20 km upwind sector), Azure Sky (TX, 350 MW, 314), Mariah North (TX, 230 MW, 305), Diversion Wind (TX, 201 MW, 200), Canadian Breaks (TX, 193 MW, 201), Spinning Spur 3 (TX), Ironwood I and Pratt Wind (KS), Minonk (IL), Buffalo Gap 1/2/3 and Horse Hollow III (TX), Armadillo Flats (OK), Spearville 3 (KS), NedPower Mount Storm (WV).
- **Mechanism:** Wind is a rival good and upwind turbines steal it. A turbine extracts momentum and leaves a velocity deficit that persists tens of kilometers downstream; Akhtar et al. (Scientific Reports 2021, 132 cites) measure mean wind-speed deficits extending 35-40 km downwind under prevailing southwesterlies and neighboring downwind farm capacity factors cut by 20%+ offshore, and Lundquist et al. (Nature Energy 2018, 307 cites) titled the onshore economic version of this exactly "Costs and consequences of wind turbine wake effects arising from uncoordinated wind energy development." Onshore recovery is faster than offshore, so the honest onshore number for a farm with heavy permitted build 5-20 km upwind is roughly 1-5% of annual energy production — permanent, not weather. The height asymmetry I measured makes it worse than a naive model says: at 194 m tip height the new machines' rotors sweep air well above the 135 m incumbents' rotor plane, so their wakes descend onto the older fleet from above and, sitting in less-sheared and less-turbulent flow, persist further downstream. Now the pricing error. A wind hedge is struck on a P50 capacity factor built from MERRA-2 or ERA5 reanalysis, correlated to on-site history. Reanalysis contains no wind-farm drag term whatsoever — the model physically cannot represent a turbine — and the site's own production history embeds only the wakes that already existed when it was recorded. Both inputs to the P50 are structurally blind to turbines that do not exist yet. So a hedge struck today on a site that will be surrounded by 2 GW of taller upwind machines in 2028 is written against a number that is already wrong and gets monotonically worse for the life of the trade. The DOF tells you which sites those are, by coordinate, today.
- **Who's on the other side:** Hedge providers writing the fixed-payer leg — bank commodity desks (Macquarie-type), reinsurance and ILS balance sheets (Allianz, Munich Re, Swiss Re Corporate Solutions), and specialist shops like Resurety, which advertises $1.5bn in clean energy transactions and 25 GW+ under management. Also yieldco and IPP equity analysts, and the P50 consultants themselves (DNV, UL, Everoze). None of them are stupid; they are structurally blind in a specific, durable way. An independent wake study is commissioned once, at financing, for the subject project, against neighbors that already exist. Nobody re-runs an incumbent's P50 when a stranger permits a thousand turbines upwind — because the incumbent is not a party to that FAA proceeding, receives no notice of it, and under US law has no wind-rights protection analogous to a solar access easement, so it could not block it anyway. The externality has no owner and therefore no analyst. Worse, the failure mode is perfectly camouflaged: three consecutive years of structural wake loss and three consecutive years of genuinely poor wind are indistinguishable on an earnings call, and management has a ready-made, sympathetic, entirely conventional excuse ("below long-term average wind resource") that analysts have been trained to model as mean-reverting noise. It is not noise. It never reverts.
- **Information lead:** Long and asymmetric. A turbine enters the DOF with exact coordinates at Determination of No Hazard, typically 6-18 months before ground is broken. It flips VERIFIED U→O and enters USWTDB only after satellite imagery confirms it physically exists — and USWTDB's lag is measurable in the data I pulled: its newest online year holds just 1,097 turbines against 2,625 for 2022, meaning recent build is still working through confirmation. EIA-860M is monthly, ~2 months lagged, plant-level, and carries no turbine geometry at all, so it can never support a wake calculation. Call the geolocated-build lead 12-36 months. But the deeper lead is that the P50 revision itself is never computed by anyone: the market only learns the wake happened after two or three years of realized production misses force a resource reassessment, which puts the effective lead closer to 3-5 years on the number that actually prices the hedge. The position can also be staged, which is the practical trick: screen on the Determination of No Hazard, then size up on the Form 7460-2 Part 1 "Notice of Actual Construction," which the developer must file within 5 days of commencing work, at the same coordinate precision. That filing converts a permit option into a certainty months before any commercial database registers the project as under construction.
- **Why still under-exploited:** The DOF is an aviation-safety artifact. Its consumers are aeronautical chart producers, helicopter EMS route planners, and drone operators — not energy analysts. It ships as a fixed-schema flat CSV inside a zip on an FAA aeronav server, with an obstacle-accuracy code where you would want a project name and no notion whatsoever of ownership, capacity, or commissioning. USWTDB is used by energy people but is deliberately, explicitly backward-looking: imagery-verified turbines only. The alpha lives precisely in the seam between them, and extracting it is genuinely manual work — parse the aviation file, key OAS to faa_ors, cluster tens of thousands of orphan coordinates into plausible farm footprints, disambiguate them by FAA study-number block, orient each against a site-specific wind rose, then run an actual wake model. Nothing sold commercially does this. Enverus, Wood Mackenzie and Cleanview track projects, queues and megawatts; none of them carry turbine-level geometry for unbuilt assets, and none compute cross-owner wake externalities, because there is no natural customer: the developer causing the wake has no reason to quantify it and the incumbent suffering it has no legal remedy. The wake consultancies sell per-project studies at financing, one asset at a time, forward-looking only for their own client. A continuously-refreshed national ledger of who is about to have their wind stolen, and by exactly which permitted turbines, does not exist as a product. The one genuinely public, genuinely predictive field in the whole chain — VERIFIED STATUS = "U" — is documented as an aviation survey flag and read by nobody as a construction-pipeline signal.
- **Rough +EV:** Screen output, computed rather than guessed: of 150,511 MW across 1,796 US operating projects ≥50 MW, 69 projects totaling 12,188 MW (8.1% of the screened fleet) have ≥25 permitted-but-unbuilt turbines inside a 20 km upwind sector. At 1.5/3/5% AEP wake loss that is 0.58/1.15/1.92 TWh/yr of production the market has not priced, worth roughly $20M/$40M/$67M per year at $35/MWh. Per deal: on a 10-year, 200 MW proxy revenue swap, a 3% volume error is ~$0.66M/yr, ~$5-6M NPV — larger than the hedge provider's entire margin on the trade, which is why deal selection rather than deal direction is where the money is. Realistically only ~3-5 GW of that 12 GW sits behind a tradable hedge or a listed owner. Firing rate: roughly 15-30 new incumbent-exposure events per year as DNH blocks land, each a multi-year hold; on the equity leg expect 2-4 exploitable owners at any time, worth perhaps 3-8% relative underperformance versus a matched peer over 4-8 quarters. I'd put the equity pair leg at Sharpe 0.5-0.8 — quarter-to-quarter weather swamps the structural signal — and the hedge-selection leg materially better, because refusing to write a mispriced deal carries no variance at all.
- **Confidence:** Medium. The biggest uncertainty by a wide margin is the DNH-to-steel conversion rate. A Determination of No Hazard is a permit, not a commitment: developers deliberately over-file turbine positions to preserve micrositing optionality, so a 1,007-position filing may become a 400-turbine farm, and ERCOT/SPP interconnection-queue attrition kills whole projects late. If only 25-40% of my 7,873 orphan coordinates ever get built, the true P50 shift is a fraction of the modeled one and my inverse-distance 20 km weighting over-attributes badly. Two mitigants: stage the position — screen on DNH, size only on the Form 7460-2 Part 1 construction-start filing, which is a fact rather than an option and still leads every commercial database by months; and calibrate the conversion rate empirically by backtesting historical DOF vintages against what USWTDB later confirmed as built, which is a clean, fully public backtest available today. Secondary uncertainty: the headline 20%+ capacity-factor hit is offshore, where low surface roughness lets deficits persist; onshore turbulent mixing recovers the wake faster, so 1-3% is the defensible planning number and 5% should be treated as a tail case, not a base case. Third: some of the 16,708 orphans are USWTDB match failures or decommissioned units rather than pipeline, though the 92% ACTION=A / 89% VERIFIED=U split and the tight study-block clustering argue that contamination is modest.

## 42. The Barn Ledger

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** Carbon markets & environmental credits. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** CARB's LCFS fuel-pathway machinery, two artifacts nobody joins: (1) the certified-pathway ledger `current-pathways_all.xlsx` — verified live, 3,756 rows, "Last Updated 2026-08-07", refreshed ~weekly, columns include Class (Tier 1/2), Facility Location, Feedstock, Fuel Type, **Current Certified CI**, **Certification Date**, Company (ID), Facility (ID); and (2) the annual "LCFS Pathways Requiring Public Comments" pages (2015–2026), where each pending Tier 2 application posts a full package PDF. The cover sheet carries four dates the market never otherwise sees: Deemed Complete Date, Posted for Comment Date, CI Certified Date, CI Start Date (verified on app B0901: complete 5/20/26, posted 7/17/26, certified TBD). The package also contains the CARB staff summary, the CA-GREET 3.0 lifecycle inputs, **the facility's air permits** (which give throughput), and references to the herd-count / manure-fraction calculations that set the CI. The buried variable is the CI column. For livestock-manure pathways it is not just negative, it is wildly dispersed: 721 pathways, median −297, min −1,887, max −68 gCO2e/MJ — a 25x spread within one feedstock. That single number is the dominant term in both aggregate LCFS credit supply and every RNG project's unit economics, and it sits in an unlinked .xlsx behind a legacy `/classic/` path.
- **How to collect it:** Plain HTTPS, no auth, no login wall, no ToS restriction — a California public agency publishing regulatory records. (a) `curl https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/classic/fuels/lcfs/fuelpathways/current-pathways_all.xlsx` (~1.7 MB); parse sheet "All Pathways", header on row 4; snapshot and diff daily — new rows = newly certified pathways, and cell B3 stamps the refresh date. (b) Scrape `https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/resources/documents/lcfs-pathways-requiring-public-comments` and its year-archive siblings (`/2025-…` back to `/2015-…`) for `Application No. Bxxxx` rows with posted date, comment deadline, and comment/response links; pull each cover PDF at `…/fuelpathways/comments/tier2/b0901_cover.pdf` for the four-date lifecycle, and the full package for the air permit (throughput in MMBtu/yr or scfm) and the CA-GREET inputs. (c) Build the join CARB never publishes: Company (ID) → corporate parent (public vs. private), Facility (ID) → EPA RFS registration and state air-permit throughput → implied MMBtu → credits = (benchmark CI − pathway CI) × MJ × EER / 1e6. Two people, a week, then a cron job. I verified the whole chain end to end: downloaded the xlsx, parsed 3,756 rows, parsed the B0901 cover PDF, and computed the posted→certified lag distribution across 36 matched applications.
- **The bet / trade:** Primary: SHORT California LCFS credits — OPIS-assessed LCFS credit forwards / OTC brokered credit swaps (cleared LCFS swaps where available), 2–4 quarter horizon, entered now and rolled quarterly, exiting on the CARB quarterly data print that confirms the bank build. The signal is directional-conditional, and it is currently screaming supply: livestock-manure pathway certifications went 180 (2024) → 41 (all of 2025, while the amended LCFS sat rejected at OAL and CARB effectively froze) → **188 in 2026 through 7 August alone**, median CI −264, tail −1,887. That is a backlog of the single most credit-dense fuel in the program clearing all at once. Secondary, easier to execute for a small book: an equity pair inside the renewable-fuels complex, long/short on certification-flow acceleration, held 1–2 quarters through the earnings print. Verified 2025+ certification counts by issuer: Phillips 66 51, Darling/Diamond Green 30, Calumet–Montana Renewables 21, Valero 21, Aemetis 8, Clean Energy Fuels 7, Gevo 6, Montauk 1.
- **Mechanism:** An LCFS credit is minted as (benchmark CI − pathway CI) × energy × EER. Certification is the *last* regulatory gate: the day CARB posts a certified CI, that facility can begin monetizing. Do the arithmetic on a dairy pathway at CI −300 against a 2026 diesel benchmark near +85: 385 gCO2e/MJ × 1,055 MJ/MMBtu = 0.41 credits per MMBtu ≈ $28/MMBtu of LCFS revenue at $70/credit — roughly eight times the commodity value of the gas itself. At the −800 tail it is ~$65/MMBtu. So (i) in aggregate, the CI-weighted pace of new certifications *is* forward LCFS credit supply, and the credit bank is what sets the credit price; (ii) at single-name level, the facility-specific CI is the revenue multiplier, and it varies 25x within the same feedstock, so no analyst can shortcut it with a category average. The 2026 flush is mechanically explainable: the 2024 amendments were rejected by the Office of Administrative Law in early 2025, certifications stalled, the amendments took effect 1 July 2025, and CARB is now clearing the queue. Those credits are being generated today and will not surface in CARB's published credit-generation data until roughly mid-2027.
- **Who's on the other side:** Obligated parties — Chevron, Valero, Marathon, PBF, Phillips 66 — buy LCFS credits on a compliance calendar, quarterly and annually, essentially price-insensitively; they are hedging a regulatory liability, not expressing a supply view. The speculative side (Vitol, Freepoint, Hartree, a handful of specialist funds) prices off the last CARB quarterly data summary, which is ~4–5 months stale, plus OPIS/Argus assessments that are by construction backward-looking. There is no CFTC Commitments of Traders report for LCFS credits, no exchange tape for spot, and no positioning data of any kind — the market's only fundamental anchor is a lagged government spreadsheet. On the equity leg, sell-side energy analysts model RNG and renewable-diesel revenue from company guidance and generic CI assumptions; not one of them is joining a 3,756-row .xlsx to facility ownership. They are slow because the work is unglamorous PDF-and-Excel plumbing across twelve years of legacy CARB pages, and because the payoff variable (CI) looks like a compliance detail rather than an eight-bagger revenue multiplier.
- **Information lead:** Three separate leads, all measured, not assumed. (1) Versus CARB's own quarterly LCFS data — the market's reference for the credit bank — **6 to 12 months**: certification → credit generation → quarterly publication at ~4–5 months' lag. (2) Versus issuer disclosure: **1–2 quarters**, from certification date to the earnings call where that facility's LCFS revenue first appears. (3) Versus the certified-CI table itself, for pathways sitting in the public-comment queue: I matched 36 applications between the comment pages and the certified ledger and measured posted-for-comment → certified at **median 19 days, p25 16, p75 24, range 15–44**. So on any given pending application you know the exact CI two to six weeks before it lands in the file everyone else eventually reads — and the cover PDF's "Deemed Complete Date" (B0901: 5/20/26, posted 7/17/26) adds another ~two months of visibility into the pipeline behind it.
- **Why still under-exploited:** OPIS, Argus and Stillwater report pathway certifications *qualitatively* — "X certified a dairy pathway in Idaho" — as trade-press color. Nobody publishes the thing that matters: a CI-weighted forward credit-supply curve built by joining the full ledger to facility ownership and permitted throughput. The reason is friction, not secrecy. The ledger is a single unlinked .xlsx on a legacy `/classic/` path with a merged-cell header on row 4; the pending queue is twelve years of separate annual pages, each holding dozens of application cover PDFs; and ownership is encoded as opaque CARB Company/Facility IDs ("Chevron Sobek RNG LLC – JM Larson (F00677)") that must be hand-mapped to parents. The economically decisive field has 25x dispersion inside one feedstock, so there is no averaging shortcut — you have to do the facility-by-facility work. Meanwhile the whole complex is covered as an *energy* story by people who don't read air-quality filings, and as an *environmental* story by people who don't trade. Tellingly, the only parties reliably reading these application packages are advocacy groups: the Animal Legal Defense Fund has filed opposition comments on the pending Chevron dairy applications B0901, B0897 and on B0858 — and those oppositions are themselves a measurable delay signal (B0858 took 44 days posted→certified against a 19-day median), which nobody is pricing either.
- **Rough +EV:** Modest but real, and it compounds across two legs. LCFS credits carry roughly 40–60% annualized vol with 10–15% typical quarterly moves and effectively zero public positioning data. The aggregate signal fires cleanly maybe 4–8 times a year (quarterly rebalance plus 2–4 sharp certification-flush or -drought episodes); when CI-weighted certification flow is more than ~1.5σ from trend — as it is right now at 4.6x the prior year — I'd expect roughly 55–62% directional accuracy on the next 3-month move, i.e. an expected edge of ~2–4% of notional per quarter, call it 8–15% annualized on deployed capital before costs, in a market where bid/ask on brokered credit forwards is wide (1–3%) and eats a real slice of that. The single-name leg is lumpier and better: 2–5 events a year where a specific public issuer's facility certifies at a CI far off consensus, worth a 3–8% single-name move over 1–2 quarters, at maybe 60–65% hit rate because the disclosure is unambiguous rather than statistical. Capacity is the binding constraint — this is a few tens of millions of dollars of edge, not hundreds.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Every factual link is verified — I downloaded and parsed the ledger, parsed a live application cover PDF, and measured the 19-day posted→certified lag across 36 matched applications — so the data source and the lead are not in question. The biggest uncertainty is that **LCFS credit prices are policy-dominated, not supply-dominated**: CARB's scheduled benchmark step-downs, the Automatic Acceleration Mechanism (which mechanically tightens benchmarks when the bank grows and therefore works directly against the short), and OAL/litigation risk can all swamp a supply signal that is directionally correct. The second real weakness is that the ledger gives CI but not volume — the supply nowcast needs an assumed MMBtu per facility. That is recoverable, since the application packages contain the facility air permits with throughput, but it is manual work and an error bar the model has to carry honestly. If I had to name the single thing that kills this trade: the AAM firing and turning a bearish supply flush into a bullish benchmark shock.

## 43. The Millage Retreat

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** Electricity capacity markets & ancillary services. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** County/state **property tax assessment appeal dockets filed by power plant owners** — the sworn, public legal record in which a generator's owner argues its own plant is worth a fraction of its assessed value. The filings contain the owner's income-approach appraisal: their internal forward capacity-price deck, forward capacity factor, and assumed remaining useful life. This is the owner's private retirement decision, made public under oath, 1–3 years before any RTO deactivation notice. Cross-checked against MSRB EMMA continuing-disclosure filings from the host school district/county, whose "principal taxpayers" tables and material-event notices flag the appeal and the anticipated revenue loss.
- **How to collect it:** All free, public, sanctioned portals; the work is the fragmentation, not the access. Verified live: (1) **Michigan Tax Tribunal Docket Lookup** — https://taxdocketlookup.apps.lara.state.mi.us/Search.aspx — searchable by Petitioner/Respondent name and by any of 83 counties; the site states filed documents are public records viewable there. Query owner entities (DTE Electric, Consumers Energy, Vistra subsidiaries). (2) **Pennsylvania UJS Portal** — https://ujsportal.pacourts.us/CaseSearch — free Common Pleas civil docket search by participant name, county, date filed, and case category; PA assessment appeals are filed as Common Pleas civil actions. (3) **Massachusetts Appellate Tax Board** — mass.gov/orgs/appellate-tax-board publishes Findings of Fact and Reports 2000–2024. (4) Ohio county Boards of Revision + Ohio Board of Tax Appeals docket; (5) Illinois PTAB (ptab.illinois.gov); (6) NJ Tax Court via NJ eCourts; (7) NY RPTL Article 7 tax certiorari petitions via NYSCEF (iapps.courts.state.ny.us/nyscef); (8) Maryland Tax Court; (9) Indiana Board of Tax Review. Join key: EIA-860 plant lat/long → county parcel viewer → parcel ID and owner LLC name (owner LLCs also recoverable from FERC market-based-rate filings), then run that LLC string against each docket. Sweep on the statutory calendar: OH ~Mar 31, NJ Apr 1, MI commercial/industrial May 31, NY grievance day 4th Tue of May then petition by Jul 31, PA Aug 1/Sep 1 by county. Also pull the raw assessed-value time series off county parcel viewers as a zero-effort proxy, and set EMMA alerts on the host school district's CUSIPs.
- **The bet / trade:** Two linked legs. **Primary:** into a scheduled PJM Base Residual Auction results date (PJM posts results on a published calendar — the 2028/29 BRA results posted July 14, 2026; the next BRA follows on PJM's return to a 3-year-forward cadence), take a directional position in the PJM/MISO-levered IPP basket — Vistra (VST), Talen (TLN), NRG, Constellation (CEG) — via 1–3 month call spreads struck around the results date. Long when the appeal flow shows an accelerating retirement pipeline in a constrained LDA (BGE, PEPCO, DPL-South, EMAAC, ComEd); fade/flatten when appeals are settling upward or counties are granting PILOT relief that keeps marginal units alive. Overlay with long ICE PJM Western Hub calendar-strip peak futures for the affected delivery years. **Secondary, single-name, 12–24 month hold:** a plant in a load pocket whose owner has filed a >50% claimed writedown is a Reliability-Must-Run candidate — RMR cost-of-service deals have been worth $100–200M/yr to a single owner (Brandon Shores/Wagner). Go long that owner's equity on the appeal filing, well before the deactivation notice that triggers the reliability study.
- **Mechanism:** A large thermal plant is usually the single largest taxpayer in its township. The first institutional act of an owner who has internally written a unit off is not a press release and not an RTO filing — it is a tax appeal, because carrying an $800M assessment on an asset you have decided is worth $80M is an immediate, quantifiable cash bleed that the tax department is mandated to stop. That appeal must be filed on a statutory annual deadline, so it happens on the *next* deadline after the internal decision, not when the owner is ready to tell the market. To win it, the owner must submit a sworn income-approach appraisal — which necessarily discloses their forward capacity price curve, dispatch assumptions, and remaining useful life. Those retirements then propagate mechanically: fewer offered UCAP megawatts into the RPM auction moves clearing price up a steep VRR demand curve, and PJM's clearing price is roughly a pure profit passthrough to merchant IPPs, whose equities move 5–15% in a single session on results. Locationally, the same retirements thin the pool of synchronized units in a reserve sub-zone, firming reserve and regulation prices there. The reverse signal is equally tradable: an appeal settled *upward*, withdrawn, or resolved into a generous PILOT is a retirement that will not happen — supply that models built off announced closures are wrongly removing.
- **Who's on the other side:** Generalist and utility-sector equity investors who mark capacity value off the last cleared auction and a sell-side retirement table. Merchant power desks and consultants whose retirement pipelines are sourced from the RTO's deactivation page, EIA-860M's "planned retirement date" field, and S&P Global — every one of which only updates *after* the owner formally notifies, which is the last step, not the first. PJM's own supply forecasts and the Independent Market Monitor's pre-auction commentary are built on formal notices only, so the official consensus is structurally lagging by construction. Nobody on a power desk has "read the county board of revision docket" in their job description; the people who do read those dockets are municipal-finance analysts and property tax attorneys, who have no view on capacity markets and no way to trade it. The information sits in the gap between two professions.
- **Information lead:** **1–3 years** over the RTO deactivation notice (PJM's minimum is 90 days; the public deactivation process typically runs 6–12 months). **1–2 years** over EIA-860M flipping a unit's planned-retirement flag. **6–18 months** over the owner's own press release, since companies sit on closure news until labor, state relations, and RMR negotiations are staged. Within a given year the signal arrives in predictable batches on statutory filing deadlines, so a monitored sweep captures it within days of filing. Against the specific catalyst, the lead is the distance from filing to the next BRA results date — typically two to six quarters, ample time to build the position cheaply before the event.
- **Why still under-exploited:** There is no vendor for this and the structural reasons are durable. The data is scattered across ~13 states and several hundred counties on a dozen incompatible portals (Michigan Tax Tribunal, PA UJS, Ohio BOR/BTA, Illinois PTAB, NJ eCourts, NYSCEF, Maryland Tax Court, Indiana BTR, Massachusetts ATB), most with no bulk export and many with scanned PDFs. The join is the real barrier: you must go EIA plant ID → lat/long → county parcel viewer → parcel number → the specific single-purpose LLC name on the deed, because plants are never titled under the parent ticker. Energy data vendors (Velocity Suite, S&P, Yes Energy) carry no county tax dockets; legal-data vendors (Lex Machina, Bloomberg Law) cover federal and appellate courts but not county boards of revision, and have no industry tagging that would surface "power plant." The dataset is filed under municipal finance, not energy, which is exactly why it has never been productized — it does not look like an energy dataset to anyone shopping for one. The universe is also small enough for a determined team: roughly 250–350 fossil and nuclear units above 200 MW across PJM and MISO, concentrated in perhaps 400 counties, with an annual filing calendar.
- **Rough +EV:** Signal frequency: roughly 15–40 material generator assessment appeals per year across the PJM/MISO footprint, of which perhaps 8–15 carry a claimed writedown large enough (>50%) to be a genuine retirement tell. Estimated conditional hit rate on deactivation-or-mothball within three years: ~50–65%, versus a ~10–15% unconditional base rate for that unit population — a real 4–5x lift on the conditional. Translating to the trade: PJM's VRR curve is steep near the reliability requirement (in the 2025/26 BRA, single-digit GW of supply change carried price from $28.92 to $269.92/MW-day), so handicapping total offered supply by ±1–2 GW out of ~135 GW ahead of the print is genuinely price-relevant. IPP single-session moves on BRA results have run 5–15%. Realistic expectation: 2–4 actionable directional calls per year, expected edge of roughly 100–250 bps per event on a levered IPP basket and materially more expressed through short-dated calls, giving low-to-mid single-digit percent annualized alpha on the sleeve — lumpy, event-clustered, not a smooth stream. The single-name RMR leg is rarer (perhaps one setup every 12–18 months) but is the fat tail: correctly front-running an RMR award on a mid-cap IPP is a 10–25% single-name move. Cost side is essentially labor: one analyst-quarter to build the parcel-to-plant crosswalk, then a few days per statutory sweep window.
- **Confidence:** **Medium.** The data source is verified real and freely accessible (I confirmed the Michigan Tax Tribunal docket lookup searches by petitioner and county with documents public, the PA UJS portal offers free Common Pleas civil search by participant name and county, and the Massachusetts ATB publishes decisions), the plant-owner-files-appeal-before-closing pattern is well attested historically (Brayton Point/Somerset, Homer City, the upstate NY coal fleet), and the trade vehicle is clean and liquid. The biggest uncertainty is **false positives from routine protective appeals**: large owners file assessment challenges on some cadence regardless of retirement intent, so the docket index alone is close to noise — the edge lives entirely in the *magnitude and methodology of the claimed writedown*, which means actually pulling and reading the appraisal exhibits rather than counting filings. Two secondary risks compound it: capacity prices at $325–450/MW-day can reverse a retirement decision that was made when prices were $30, breaking the appeal→closure link precisely in the regime where the trade matters most; and PJM's clearing price is now partly administratively bounded (the Pennsylvania collar), which caps the payoff even when the supply call is right. I would want one back-tested cycle of hand-read appraisals before sizing this beyond a research position.
