## 63. The Captive Stack

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** Semiconductors & fab equipment. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** Real-time smokestack tele-monitoring (TMS) telemetry published by Korea Environment Corporation's CleanSYS for the CAPTIVE 585 MW LNG cogeneration plants that SK hynix built INSIDE its Icheon and Cheongju fab campuses (~KRW 1.7tn program, operating from 2023), plus the equivalent utility/cogen stacks at Samsung's Pyeongtaek and Giheung–Hwaseong campuses. Korea mandates TMS on large combustion sources and has published the readings publicly in real time since 3 April 2020, covering ~965 large facilities nationwide. Because SK hynix's power and process steam are generated on-campus rather than bought from the grid, these stacks are effectively a public, free, real-time load meter bolted to the world's largest HBM/DRAM production base — Icheon (M14/M16) and Cheongju (M11/M15/M15X).
- **How to collect it:** 1) Free open API, no cost: GET https://apis.data.go.kr/B552584/cleansys/rltmMesureResult (data.go.kr dataset 15074658). Params: serviceKey, areaNm (region, LIKE), factManageNm (facility name, LIKE), stackCode (outlet ID), type=json|xml. Register on data.go.kr for a serviceKey (free, auto-approved for dev). Returns per-stack measured concentrations vs. permitted limits for dust, SOx, NOx, HCl, HF, NH3, CO. 2) Build the mapping table ONCE via the web UI at cleansys.or.kr (ptsList.do = real-time list, statAnnual.do = annual totals): search factManageNm for 하이닉스 / 삼성전자 and filter areaNm to 경기 이천, 충북 청주, 경기 평택, 경기 화성, 경기 용인, recording each 사업장 → stackCode set → fab campus. 3) Poll every 5–30 min per stack; persist concentration series plus the online/offline state of each outlet. Construct a per-campus composite: NOx level x number of reporting outlets, weather- and LNG-spread-normalized. 4) Calibrate and cross-check against KEPCO's free monthly open API 계약종별별 전력사용현황 (data.go.kr 15059135, endpoints incl. 시군구별 계약종별 전력사용현황) for 이천시 / 청주시 흥덕구 / 평택시 industrial kWh, and against KEPCO's 산업분류별 법정동별 전력사용량 (dataset 15104908) for legal-dong x KSIC ground truth.
- **The bet / trade:** Two legs on the same feed. (1) DISRUPTION LEG: on a sustained multi-hour collapse in campus composite firing rate / mass offline-state across a memory campus's stacks, outside logged maintenance windows — buy MU equity or 1–2 week MU calls, plus long SNDK/WDC for NAND-side events. Hold 3–10 trading days; exit on wire confirmation plus the first DRAM/NAND spot print. (2) SUPPLY-RAMP LEG: on a sustained step-UP in the Cheongju composite (M15X energization, HBM3E 1b DRAM) or the Pyeongtaek composite (P4/P5), fade memory beta over the following 1–2 quarters — short MU against long SOX, or cut memory length; sized into MU's quarterly print roughly one quarter after the step. A flat composite through a period of record DRAM pricing is the inverse signal: supply discipline is holding, stay long.
- **Mechanism:** SK hynix built captive cogeneration because fabs need uninterrupted 24/7 power and process steam. Cogen firing rate therefore tracks campus utility demand, which tracks how many cleanroom modules are actually energized and loaded — not how many are announced. Chain up: a new fab phase is powered up → steam/electric demand steps → cogen fires harder → stack NOx and flow rise → visible publicly within minutes. Chain down: a fab trip or utility incident → process steam demand collapses → cogen throttles or outlets drop offline within an hour or two, while WIP in the fab is destroyed instantly. The two legs then diverge in timing because DRAM cycle time is ~10–13 weeks: a wafer-start step in month M becomes market supply around M+3 (tradeable as a supply inflection a quarter out), whereas a disruption vaporizes in-process wafers immediately and moves spot within days. Korea's two campuses are the swing factor in global DRAM and the majority of HBM, so campus-level load is close to a global supply state variable.
- **Who's on the other side:** Memory is traded off DRAM/NAND spot and contract prints (TrendForce/DXI), sell-side channel checks, and quarterly earnings — every one of which is an OUTPUT observed after the fact, not the input. Korean environmental compliance telemetry is invisible to that crowd: CleanSYS is a Korean-only citizen environmental-oversight portal, needs a data.go.kr key, and is useless without a hand-built 사업장명/stackCode → fab-campus mapping. The people who do read CleanSYS are ESG analysts, air-quality academics and local activists, who aggregate to annual tonnage for compliance and have no reason to look at intraday firing rate. Companies confirm outages only after Korean media force the issue, and confirm phase ramps only on the earnings call. Short-vol and short-memory books take the other side of the disruption leg; consensus long-memory positioning takes the other side of the supply-ramp leg.
- **Information lead:** Disruption: hours to ~2 days ahead of Reuters/Korean wire confirmation, and ~3–10 days ahead of the spot-price reaction (historic analogues — the 2018 Samsung Pyeongtaek outage, the 2019 Kioxia Yokkaichi outage — moved NAND spot mid-single-digits days later). Capacity step: 1–3 months ahead of any company acknowledgment that a phase is loaded, and ~3 months ahead of the resulting bits reaching the market — i.e. roughly a full quarter ahead of the earnings call where it gets discussed. Versus the obvious substitutes, this is 6–10 weeks faster: KEPCO regional electricity and Korean customs data both publish with roughly a two-month lag, and satellite construction imagery shows a completed shell but cannot distinguish "built" from "energized and loaded."
- **Why still under-exploited:** CleanSYS was built in 2020 for public environmental oversight, not finance — no English interface, no financial-vendor packaging, no facility-to-fab crosswalk, and no alt-data vendor sells it (this is not Kpler/Yipit/M Science territory; it is a K-eco compliance portal). The structural fact that makes it work is recent and postdates most analysts' mental model: Korean fabs were historically pure KEPCO grid customers, and it is only since ~2023 that SK hynix's two 585 MW on-campus captive cogens turned an environmental stack into a single-customer fab meter. Meanwhile the well-worn Korean alt-data — KCS 20-day export data, DART 공시, TrendForce spot — is completely saturated, so attention has never drifted toward the environmental regulator. Collection is genuinely manual and fragmented: the hard part is the one-time mapping of Korean facility names and stack codes to specific fab campuses.
- **Rough +EV:** Modest but real; an overlay on a memory sleeve, not a standalone book. Disruption leg: ~2–4 genuine memory-campus disruptions per year across the Korean campuses; assume ~60–65% precision after filtering scheduled maintenance and cogen economic dispatch, ~3–6% move in MU over the following week, capturing ~1.5–3% net per true positive on a sized position → roughly 4–8% annual gross on the tactical sleeve, concentrated in a handful of days. Supply-ramp leg: 2–4 step-change signals per year; value is mostly in not being wrong-way long memory into a supply wave (worth several hundred bps on a memory-heavy book) rather than a cleanly attributable P&L. Blended, call it a few hundred bps per year of alpha on a memory sleeve. Setup cost is a few days of work and effectively zero data spend.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Biggest uncertainty by far: whether the SK hynix Icheon/Cheongju captive cogens and Samsung's Pyeongtaek/Hwaseong utility plants actually appear in the CleanSYS TMS registry under resolvable facility names, AND whether the public API exposes enough to reconstruct firing rate — the documented response fields are per-pollutant concentrations against permitted limits, and I could NOT confirm that stack gas flow (유량) is published. Concentration-only data is a substantially noisier load proxy than mass flow, though outlet online/offline state alone still detects hard shutdowns. This is cheap to settle definitively: pull the full facility list from the API and match 사업장명/areaNm against 경기 이천 / 충북 청주 / 경기 평택 in an afternoon — do that before committing capital. Secondary risks: cogen dispatch responds partly to LNG-vs-grid spark spread and to seasonal HVAC load, so the series needs weather and fuel-spread normalization before step changes are trustworthy; and a large fixed cleanroom base load compresses sensitivity to marginal utilization changes, meaning the signal is far stronger for discrete phase energizations and outages than for gentle wafer-start trimming.

## 64. The Clearing Yard Blind Spot

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** Rail & intermodal freight. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** The Surface Transportation Board's brand-new weekly data collection from The Belt Railway Company of Chicago (BRC) on Clearing Yard — opened by STB letter on August 3, 2026, first submission filed August 11, 2026 (three days ago). It is a machine-readable weekly xlsx reporting, PER CLASS I RAILROAD: on-time departure percentage, inbound/outbound train annulments, extras requested and extras DENIED, BRC's allocated daily car quota per carrier, average cars received, and haulbacks — plus yard-level average daily dwell, inventory, cars humped, and cars RE-humped.

Why this specific feed is structurally special: Clearing Yard is owned by BRC, a terminal railroad jointly owned by BNSF, CN, CPKC, CSX, NS and UP. Cars plugged in Clearing are therefore NOT on any Class I's books, so they are structurally invisible in the Class I's own mandated STB EP 724 weekly filings (Item 2 terminal dwell covers only the carrier's own terminals; cars interchanged to BRC drop out of "cars online"). Six large-cap railroads can each report clean system dwell and velocity while their Chicago interchange is choking inside a yard none of them individually reports. This BRC feed is the only public window into that hole, and it is 3 days old.

Actual week-31 values I pulled from the first filing (week ending Aug 6, 2026): average daily dwell 28.61 hrs (BRC's own comment: "Realistically, dwell numbers below 24 hours denote fluidity"; BRC's 2026 plan was 21.30); average daily inventory 5,056 cars; 2,955 cars humped/day against 387 RE-humped/day (a 13% rework rate); on-time departure by carrier — BNSF 27%, CPKC 42%, UP 18%, CSX 11%, NS 5%, CN 0%, BRC itself 18% (only 26 of 146 outbound trains left within 2 hrs of slot); haulbacks — CSX 31, BNSF 17, UP 16, CN 4, NS 3, CPKC 1; outbound annulments — CSX 8, CPKC 2, BNSF 2, NS 1, UP 0; daily quota — CSX 920 (largest), BNSF 588, UP 549, NS 424, CPKC 226, CN 163. STB's letter cites inventory 5,048 in week 30 vs 3,212 a year earlier and dwell up from ~18 to ~31 hrs, with inventory +26% and dwell +63% since April 2026.

Second, complementary feed (also underused, also freshly restarted): the STB-1145 CSVs carrying weekly "Percentage of Successful Local Planned Service Windows" (industry spot and pull) and "% of manifest shipments delivered within 24 hrs of OETA" broken out BY OPERATING DIVISION for all six Class I's — I confirmed ~54 division-level series (UP "02-CHICAGO", "09-HOUSTON", "20-LOS ANGELES"; CSXT "Midwest - North"; NS "GREAT LAKES"; BNSF "Chicago"; etc.). This collection ran Sept 2024–Aug 2025, went dark when the 7th Circuit vacated the reciprocal switching rule (Grand Trunk Corp. v. STB, July 2025), and was revived permanently by the STB's EP 787 final rule with an initial reporting date of July 8, 2026 — five weeks ago. It gives the divisional confirmation that the Chicago plug is propagating into customer-facing local service.
- **How to collect it:** Fully sanctioned, plain public HTTP — no login, no scraping of anything gated.

1) BRC weekly feed. Poll https://www.stb.gov/reports-data/rail-service-data/belt-railway-of-chicago-data-reporting/ daily and diff for new .xlsx links. Files follow the pattern https://www.stb.gov/wp-content/uploads/BRC-Submission-M-D-YYYY.xlsx (the live one is BRC-Submission-8-11-2026.xlsx). Single worksheet named "Machine Readable Template" with columns Measure | Sub-Measure | Week Start Date | Week End Date | Week Number | Value, plus a free-text "BRC Comments" column that contains the raw numerator/denominator behind each on-time percentage (e.g. CSX "(5/46)", NS "(1/20)") — parse those, they give you train counts the percentage alone hides. Reading is a 20-line zipfile+regex parse of xl/sharedStrings.xml and xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml; no Excel needed. Cadence: BRC has shifted to a Wednesday reporting date; the next file is due Aug 19, 2026 and covers THREE weeks at once (Jul 27–Aug 2, Aug 3–9, Aug 10–16). Also grab the two context PDFs on that page: 8-3-26-Letter-from-STB-to-BRC.pdf and BRC_Response_to_STB_2026-08-10.pdf.

2) Divisional ISP/OETA. Direct CSV downloads, no parsing gymnastics: https://www.stb.gov/wp-content/uploads/STB-1145-ALL-CARRIERS.csv and per-carrier STB-1145-{BNSF,CPKC,CSXT,GTC,NS,UP}.csv. Long format; filter measure_name_full on "Percentage of Successful Local Planned Service Windows" and "Percentage of Shipments in Manifest Service, Delivered within 24 hrs of OETA", key on sub_measure (division) and report_period_end_date. These carry Sept 2024–Aug 2025 history today; watch for the EP 787 refresh appending July 2026 forward.

3) Baseline/denominator. Weekly Class I EP 724 files at https://www.stb.gov/wp-content/uploads/files/rsir/{BNSF,CSX,NS,UP,CPKC,CN}/{CARRIER}%20Data%20YYYY-MM-DD.xlsx and the roll-up "EP724 Consolidated Data through YYYY-MM-DD.xlsx" in the "All Class 1 Railroads" folder. Railroads file Wednesday COB, STB posts Thursday COB. Note the EP 724 (Sub-No. 5) final rule that just added chemicals/plastics as a distinct "cars-held" reporting category — useful for the Gulf Coast read-through.

Total build: one cron job, a few hundred lines of Python, zero cost.
- **The bet / trade:** Short CSX (CSX) against a beta-matched long in Union Pacific (UNP) — or outright CSX puts, Oct/Nov 2026 expiry — entered now and held through CSX's Q3 2026 print in late October 2026. Roughly 10 weeks.

Sizing and re-underwriting rule: hold full size while BRC-reported Clearing Yard average daily dwell prints above 26 hours; cut to half on the first sub-24-hour print (BRC's own stated fluidity threshold); exit entirely on two consecutive sub-24-hour prints or if CSX's weekly haulbacks and outbound annulments fall to the CPKC/BNSF range. The Aug 19 filing is the first hard checkpoint and delivers three weeks of data at once.

Why CSX is the leg rather than the worse on-time performers: NS (5%) and CN (0%) look worse on the departure metric, but NSC's equity is pinned to the UP merger arb spread and will not respond to operating fundamentals, and CN's Chicago exposure through Clearing is tiny (163-car quota). CSX is the largest user of the yard (920-car daily quota, 815 cars/day received), owns the worst rework signature (31 haulbacks, 8 outbound annulments), and is the carrier that structurally changed behavior by shifting Chicago classification off its own Barr Yard onto Clearing — so it has both the most exposure and the least optionality to unwind.

Secondary expression for a smaller, longer-dated sleeve: the persistence of a visibly degrading Chicago gateway during the STB's UP–NS review (application accepted May 28, 2026 but held in abeyance; supplemental information completed late July 2026; close targeted mid-2027) raises conditions/denial risk on the deal. Buy downside protection on the NSC deal spread — the merger's core public-benefit claim is seamless single-line service through Chicago, and BRC's weekly per-carrier data is exactly the evidentiary ammunition opponents will file into the record.
- **Mechanism:** Clearing Yard is the largest classification yard in the United States and the physical junction where western railroads hand cars to eastern railroads. The causal chain is short and mechanical.

Step 1 — the plug is real and worsening. Inventory is 5,056 cars/day against 3,212 a year ago (+57%); dwell is 28.6 hrs against ~18 hrs a year ago and against BRC's own 21.3-hr operating plan. A 13% re-hump rate means roughly one car in eight is being classified twice, which is pure capacity destruction: every re-hump consumes a hump slot that a fresh car needed.

Step 2 — the failure is on the pull side, not the push side. Only 26 of 146 outbound trains left within two hours of their scheduled slot. BRC prepared the trains; the Class I road crews did not show up to take them. That is a crew-and-power availability failure at the receiving railroads, which is exactly the condition that does not self-heal in weeks — you cannot conjure qualified Chicago-district crews on demand.

Step 3 — it lands on CSX's income statement. Cars sitting 30 hours at Clearing are cars not delivered to CSX customers east of Chicago. That produces: (a) merchandise trip-plan compliance deterioration and cycle-time extension, which forces more cars and more locomotives online to move the same volume; (b) recrews, deadheading and taxi/lodging expense on the Chicago district as crews expire on Hours of Service waiting on the yard, hitting comp-and-benefits and purchased services; (c) haulbacks — 31 in one week for CSX — which are trains that ran, burned a crew start and fuel, and produced zero revenue movement; (d) suppressed demurrage and accessorial revenue, because a railroad cannot bill storage on cars it failed to deliver, and will owe service credits under contract; (e) volume leakage as time-sensitive merchandise and domestic intermodal shippers divert to truck, which shows up in the following quarter's carloads.

Step 4 — the disclosure asymmetry is the whole trade. Because Clearing is BRC's yard, none of this appears in CSX's own STB EP 724 weekly filing. CSX's reported terminal dwell covers CSX terminals; cars interchanged to BRC leave CSX's cars-online count. So the sell-side dashboard everyone actually uses — AAR weekly carloads plus EP 724 velocity and dwell — will show CSX looking normal right up until the Q3 operating ratio arrives with the bill attached. The damage accumulates in a place the standard data structurally cannot see.

Step 5 — the divisional ISP feed is the corroborating instrument. When the Chicago plug starts starving local service, it appears in the STB-1145 "Percentage of Successful Local Planned Service Windows" for CSXT "Midwest - North" and UP "02-CHICAGO" before it appears in any volume statistic, because a missed spot at a customer's door is the first-order consequence of a car stuck in a classification yard.
- **Who's on the other side:** Long-only rail holders, index and dividend funds, and the sell-side transport analysts whose weekly rail models are built on two inputs: AAR/Rail Time Indicators carload and intermodal counts, and the STB EP 724 velocity/dwell series. Both of those inputs are blind to this by construction — EP 724 excludes yards the carrier does not own, and AAR carloads are a coincident count of what moved, not a leading measure of what is stuck. An analyst can run their full weekly process and see nothing wrong.

Railroad management is the second counterparty and is actively incentivized to be slow. On the Q3 call CSX will report system dwell and velocity — metrics that exclude Clearing — and characterize Chicago as a transitory industry-wide issue. CSX has already publicly maintained that the volume it sends to Clearing has remained steady, which is a claim BRC's own quota and cars-received data (920 quota, 815 received, 31 haulbacks) lets you test independently for the first time. Nobody has been able to audit that statement before this week.

The trade press is the third group, and they are directionally right but quantitatively useless for a model. Trains.com, The Loadstar, Progressive Railroading and Railway Supply all covered the August 3 STB letter within days, so the narrative "Chicago is congested and CSX is implicated" is public. What is not public in any usable form is a weekly, per-carrier, machine-readable time series of who is annulling trains, who is being denied extras, whose quota is being cut, and whose crews are failing to pull prepared trains. That series began three days ago on a subpage of a subpage of stb.gov. There is no vendor product, no Bloomberg field, and no Substack tracking it, because it did not exist until August 11, 2026.

The final group is the merger-arb book long NSC, which is pricing the UP–NS spread off procedural docket milestones and political read-through, not off weekly operating evidence that the Chicago gateway is deteriorating while the STB holds the application in abeyance.
- **Information lead:** Layered, and the innermost layer is unbounded.

Versus EP 724, the dataset the market actually watches: permanent. Clearing Yard dwell will never appear in CSX's, NS's, UP's or BNSF's weekly STB filing, because Clearing is not their terminal. This is not a timing lead, it is a coverage gap — the market's primary rail instrument cannot ever print this number.

Versus CSX's Q3 2026 earnings (late October 2026): about 10 weeks, refreshed weekly. You get roughly ten independent observations of the plug's trajectory before management speaks.

Versus AAR weekly carloads: 2–6 weeks. A yard plug precedes the volume loss it causes; carload defection to truck is a decision shippers make after two or three missed weeks.

Versus the STB-1145 divisional ISP feed: 1–3 weeks. Yard congestion propagates to missed customer spots with a lag, so BRC's Wednesday file front-runs the divisional service data that confirms it.

Versus the trade press: days on the raw numbers, but effectively months on anything quantitative. The press reported the STB letter's two headline figures (5,048 cars, 31 hours) as a snapshot. Nobody is publishing per-carrier on-time departure, haulbacks, annulments, extras-denied, or quota allocation as a series, and those are the fields that let you assign the damage to a specific ticker.

Versus the merger record: the BRC data will eventually be filed into the UP–NS docket by opponents, which is when the arb community sees it. You are reading it at the source weeks-to-months before it becomes a litigated exhibit.

Concretely: the Aug 19, 2026 filing drops three weeks of data at once and is the single highest-information event in this trade. Have the parser running before it posts.
- **Why still under-exploited:** It is eleven days old as a regulatory obligation and three days old as a dataset. The STB sent the letter on August 3, 2026; BRC filed the first submission on August 11, 2026. There is no history, no vendor, no ticker mapping, and no analyst has a model input for it. Kpler, Vortexa, YipitData and M Science cover vessels, cards and web traffic; none of them cover a jointly-owned Chicago terminal railroad's hump-yard quota sheet.

The location is genuinely obscure. It is not on stb.gov's main Rail Service Data table alongside the EP 724 files that everyone downloads. It sits behind a single sentence of link text — "Click here for data collected from the Belt Railway of Chicago related to the Board's August 3, 2026 letter" — on a page whose file listing runs to thousands of links, and it resolves to a separate subpage with three attachments. You have to already know to look.

The format fights casual use. It is an .xlsx labelled "Machine Readable Template" with a long-format Measure/Sub-Measure/Value layout, Excel serial dates, a week-number field containing the literal string "31 (partly 32)", trailing spaces in measure names ("Average Cars Received "), a typo'd field ("Extras Outbound  Denied" with a double space), and — critically — the actual numerators and denominators buried inside a free-text comments column rather than in numeric cells. That is exactly the kind of friction that keeps a dataset out of institutional pipelines and available to someone willing to write a parser.

The institutional framing is wrong for finance. This is a service-quality inquiry aimed at shippers, unions and regulators. SMART-TD wrote it up as a labor story. The trade press wrote it up as an operations story. Nobody framed it as an equity input, so the natural audience for the file has no position to express and the audience with positions is not reading regulatory subpages.

The companion divisional ISP/OETA feed is under-exploited for a different and even better reason: it was created to administer a rule that no longer exists. Part 1145 was vacated by the 7th Circuit in July 2025, the collection went dormant in August 2025, and anyone who had built against it walked away. The STB then quietly revived the same metrics permanently under EP 787 effective July 8, 2026. So there is a live, machine-readable, division-level service dataset covering all six Class I railroads — roughly 54 geographic series including UP "02-CHICAGO" and CSXT "Midwest - North" — sitting behind seven unlabelled CSV links, orphaned by a court decision and re-adopted under a different docket number that the people who abandoned it are not watching.

Finally, the structural blind spot itself has never been exploitable before. Cars hidden inside a jointly-owned terminal railroad have always been invisible in Class I reporting; what is new is that a regulator just forced the terminal railroad to publish who is hiding what. That window may close as soon as the STB is satisfied.
- **Rough +EV:** Event-driven and rare, not a repeating factor. A special STB data collection aimed at a specific terminal is roughly a once-per-several-years occurrence (the 2014 polar-vortex CTCO reporting, the 2022 EP 770 service crisis, now this). So the setup fires maybe once every 3–5 years — but it is firing right now, and within this instance you get roughly 10 weekly re-underwriting points between now and the Q3 print.

Rough sizing of the current instance. A sustained Chicago-gateway plug of this magnitude historically costs an eastern carrier on the order of 50–150 bps of quarterly operating ratio through recrews, extended cycle times, added cars and power online, haulback waste, and lost demurrage/accessorial revenue, plus 1–3% of merchandise volume as shippers divert. CSX equity typically moves 4–8% on an OR miss in that band. Weight that by roughly a 55–65% probability the plug persists into September — the base rate for yards unplugging quickly is poor when the failure is on the crew-availability side, inventory is +57% year over year, the re-hump rate is 13%, and Q4 peak volumes are arriving — and net out the portion already discounted by the public trade-press narrative, which I would put at maybe a third of the move.

That leaves an expected edge of roughly 2–4% on a beta-neutral CSX-versus-UNP pair over about a 10-week hold, with a realistic distribution running from about −3% (fast unplug, CSX rerouting back to Barr Yard, relief rally) to about +10% (plug persists through peak season and lands in the Q3 OR). Expressed in Oct/Nov puts the payoff is more convex but you are paying elevated pre-earnings implied volatility, so the pair is the cleaner risk-adjusted expression and the options only make sense if you can buy them before the Aug 19 three-week data drop.

The weekly exit rule matters more than the entry: BRC published its own fluidity threshold (24 hours), which gives you an unusually crisp, counterparty-defined stop that does not depend on your own judgment.
- **Confidence:** Medium.

What I am confident about, because I pulled and parsed the primary files rather than relying on summaries: the dataset exists, is public, is machine-readable, is weekly, is broken out per Class I, and is three days old. The specific values are real — 28.61 hrs dwell, 5,056 cars inventory, 387 of 2,955 cars re-humped, 26 of 146 outbound trains on time, CSX at 11% on-time with 31 haulbacks, 8 outbound annulments and the largest quota at 920 cars/day. I also confirmed the divisional ISP/OETA CSVs and their ~54 division series, and the EP 787 revival with a July 8, 2026 initial reporting date. And I confirmed the structural point that makes this worth trading: Clearing is BRC's yard, so this congestion cannot appear in any Class I's own EP 724 filing.

The single biggest uncertainty is attribution-to-P&L magnitude. I can prove the yard is plugged and I can prove CSX is the largest and most rework-heavy user of it, but Clearing Yard is one node in a ~20,000-route-mile network, and I cannot yet prove from public data how many basis points of CSX's consolidated Q3 operating ratio flow from this specific chokepoint. It is entirely possible the plug is real, visible, and still too small relative to CSX's total cost base to move the print — in which case the signal is correct and the trade is noise. Compounding this, the "who is to blame" question is genuinely contested: BRC's own filing pointedly disclaims that its on-time departure metric denotes cause or responsibility by any carrier, CSX maintains its Clearing volumes have been steady, and the low on-time departure numbers could reflect BRC's own crew and hump constraints rather than the road carriers'. If BRC is the bottleneck rather than CSX, the damage spreads thinly across six railroads instead of concentrating in one ticker, and the pair trade loses its edge.

Secondary risks: with only one week of the new feed published, I have no way to know whether week 31 is representative or an outlier, so the Aug 19 three-week drop could materially revise the picture in either direction; the STB could be satisfied and close the collection, removing the data source entirely; and the plug could drain fast once BRC rations quotas and carriers embargo traffic into Chicago, which is precisely what regulatory pressure of this kind is designed to produce.

## 65. The 250-Point Deed

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** Hotels, lodging & travel demand. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** County recorder "official records" indexes for timeshare **consumer deeds, developer mortgages, claims of lien, and trustee-foreclosure instruments** filed by the vacation-ownership developers. The non-obvious fact that makes this work: modern *points-based* timeshare products are still conveyed by a recorded real-property deed. Marriott Vacations' entire MVC Trust points business conveys each purchase (unitized in 250-point "Beneficial Interest" tranches) via an "MVC Trust Consumer Deed" **recorded in Orange County, Florida** — documented in the Lennen v. Marriott Ownership Resorts litigation record, which describes "thousands" of such deeds. Hilton Grand Vacations is likewise almost entirely deeded ("virtually all HGVC memberships are deeded," conveyed by warranty deed at the county level). So every North American sale by VAC and HGV drops a timestamped public instrument into a small, known set of recorder systems. The mirror-image leg: F.S. 721.855/721.856 require a **recorded claim of lien**, a **recorded notice of appointment of trustee**, and a recorded trustee's deed before a non-judicial timeshare foreclosure completes — i.e., the default pipeline is also a public recording stream.
- **How to collect it:** Five to eight jurisdictions cover the overwhelming majority of VAC/HGV North American volume:
1. **Orange County, FL Comptroller** — or.occompt.com (EagleRecorder) + selfservice.or.occompt.com. Free party-name + document-type + date-range search. This single county captures essentially all MVC Trust points sales and much of HGV Orlando. Query grantor strings: "MARRIOTT OWNERSHIP RESORTS", "MVC TRUST OWNERS ASSOCIATION", "HILTON RESORTS CORPORATION", "HILTON GRAND VACATIONS".
2. **NYC ACRIS via NYC Open Data / Socrata API** — fully programmatic, no scraping: `Real Property Master` (bnx9-e6tj), `Real Property Parties` (636b-3b5g), `Real Property Legals` (8h5j-fqxa), `Master Deeds` (asrm-u43g). Captures HGV's highest-price-per-contract product (Hilton Club NY, The Residences, The Central at 5th).
3. **Hawaii Bureau of Conveyances** — single statewide system; captures HGV's highest-VPG market (Grand Waikikian, Kalia, Maui Bay Villas).
4. **Clark County, NV Recorder** — free grantor search + Declaration of Value (states price). Captures Elara, Boulevard, Flamingo, Trump Intl.
5. **Horry County, SC Register of Deeds** — HGV/Bluegreen Myrtle Beach. Plus Osceola/Volusia/St. Johns FL and Beaufort SC for the tail.
Build: nightly index pull by grantor + document type + recording date; parse the instrument face for number of Beneficial Interests / points conveyed and for documentary-stamp notation (FL doc stamp $0.70 per $100 of consideration) to derive dollars, not just counts. Critically, read the **execution/closing date printed on the instrument**, not the recording date, which requires pulling document images and OCR'ing them — this is the step that de-noises the monthly series. Precedent that the method works: DVCNews.com has counted Disney Vacation Club deeds monthly out of Orange County FL, Indian River County FL, and Beaufort County SC for years — nobody has generalized it to the public timeshare issuers.
- **The bet / trade:** **Primary:** directional equity/short-dated options position in **Marriott Vacations Worldwide (VAC)** and **Hilton Grand Vacations (HGV)**, entered ~T-25 to T-15 days before the quarterly print and held through the earnings release (+1 day). Direction and size set by the gap between the deed-derived contract-sales nowcast and sell-side consensus contract sales — long when the nowcast beats by >1 standard error, short when it misses. ~8-12 events/year across VAC, HGV, and (partially) TNL. VAC Q1'26 printed $411M contract sales (-2% y/y) on Apr 30; Q2'26 on Aug 6 — a ~30-37 day post-quarter reporting lag defines the window.
**Secondary, longer horizon:** a 1-3 quarter outright short in HGV or TNL when the recorded **claim-of-lien / notice-of-appointment-of-trustee / trustee's-deed** count inflects upward by >20% y/y for two consecutive months — a position on the loan-loss provision rate, held into two earnings cycles.
**Tertiary:** developer-as-*grantee* deeds (deed-backs and ROFR exercises) as an inventory-spend and owner-attrition read.
- **Mechanism:** Contract sales is *the* number for these stocks — it drives revenue recognition, the deferral, financing revenue, and the whole EBITDA bridge; guidance is issued in contract-sales dollars (VAC's 2026 guide: $1,815-1,885M). Every North American contract sale mechanically produces one recorded instrument, because the product is legally structured as a real-property conveyance for state timeshare-law compliance. The chain is: sale closes → statutory rescission period runs (FL 10 days, NV 5, HI 7, SC 5) → down payment clears → title company records the deed, typically 2-6 weeks after contract. Counting deeds by grantor therefore reconstructs unit volume; parsing Beneficial Interests/points per deed reconstructs volume in points; doc-stamp consideration reconstructs dollars and average price per contract (a direct VPG proxy). On the credit side: a timeshare receivable that goes bad eventually forces the managing entity/lienholder to record a claim of lien and appoint a foreclosure trustee. That physical filing happens when the servicer has actually given up, whereas the P&L provision is set by a static-pool model plus management discretion — so the recordings lead the reported provision rate. HGV's provision rate migration from the low-teens to ~20%+ over 2024-25 is exactly the kind of move this leg would have flagged early.
- **Who's on the other side:** Long-only small/mid-cap value funds and retail holders who own VAC/HGV on the "cheap FCF, buyback" thesis and find out about contract sales on the press release, plus the thin sell-side bench (these are $2-5B caps with modest coverage) whose contract-sales estimates are largely last-quarter-plus-a-trend. They are slow for structural reasons: (1) card-panel alt data badly under-measures this sector because 55-70% of purchases are developer-financed at the sales gallery rather than card-swiped, so the panels see the down payment at best; (2) web-traffic data measures tour flow, not closing rate, and closing rate is where the volatility lives; (3) national deed aggregators (ATTOM, CoreLogic, PropertyRadar) *do* ingest these counties, but they systematically filter timeshare instruments out as junk non-arms-length records that pollute AVMs — the raw rows exist commercially and are thrown away; (4) the sector-specific knowledge that points sales are deeded at all is counterintuitive and mostly buried in consumer litigation, so most analysts assume trust/points products leave no public footprint.
- **Information lead:** Honest accounting: recording lags the sale by ~2-6 weeks, and VAC/HGV report ~30-40 days after quarter end. So you do **not** get a clean full-quarter read before the print — you get roughly **65-80% of the quarter's contract sales locked in 3-5 weeks ahead of the release**, with the trailing weeks extrapolated from a stable lag distribution. More valuable than the point-in-time lead is the *continuous* nowcast: you know months one and two of a quarter while the Street is still working off the prior quarter, which front-runs guidance raises/cuts, pre-announcements, and the intra-quarter narrative (e.g., you would have seen VAC's 2026 contract-sales strength before the guidance raise). The credit leg has a much bigger lead: lien and trustee-appointment recordings run **one to three quarters ahead** of the reported loan-loss provision, because the provision is model- and discretion-driven while the recording is a hard operational act.
- **Why still under-exploited:** Timeshare is an unglamorous, under-covered mid-cap corner that alt-data vendors have skipped. Nobody sells a "Marriott Vacations monthly contract sales" index. The three barriers that keep it underexploited are all real and all surmountable by a small determined team: (a) the *belief* that points/trust products are non-deeded and therefore invisible — false for MVC Trust and HGV, and only disprovable by reading the Lennen docket or actually pulling the Orange County index; (b) no common schema — each county uses a different recorder platform, different document-type codes, and different grantor-name spellings, and the useful field (execution date, number of Beneficial Interests, doc-stamp consideration) lives on the *document image*, not in the index, so it needs OCR rather than an API call; (c) the big commercial deed aggregators actively exclude timeshare instruments as data pollution. The existence of DVCNews doing exactly this by hand for Disney Vacation Club — and only for Disney, a rounding error inside DIS — is the strongest evidence that the technique works and that no one has pointed it at the names where it would actually pay.
- **Rough +EV:** VAC and HGV move roughly 6-12% absolute on earnings day; TNL 5-10%. Assume the deed nowcast produces a >1-standard-error signal on ~5-7 of the ~12 annual events (it will be silent or ambiguous the rest of the time) and is directionally right on contract-sales-vs-consensus ~65-70% of the time on those. At a 65% hit rate into an ~8% average move, that is roughly a +2.5 to +4% expected return per signaled event on notional, before costs; ~6 signaled events a year gives a ~15-25% gross annual return on a dedicated sleeve, call it 10-18% net of borrow, slippage, and options premium decay. The credit-inflection leg is lower frequency (perhaps one or two setups per cycle) but larger: provision-driven de-ratings in this sector have been 20-40% moves. Capacity is genuinely small — think a $10-50M sleeve given the market caps and ADV — which is precisely why no vendor has bothered to productize it.
- **Confidence:** **Medium.** The data source is verified to exist and be freely, lawfully collectible: MVC Trust Consumer Deeds are confirmed recorded in Orange County FL, HGV memberships are confirmed deeded, NYC ACRIS is a public Socrata API, and the F.S. 721.855 lien-recording requirement is statutory. The biggest uncertainty is **recording-lag stability**, and it is the thing that would kill the trade rather than merely dull it: if a developer batches recordings — title-company backlogs, quarter-end or year-end pushes, or a change in conveyance format (plausible for VAC given the Lennen ruling that the Consumer Deeds' legal descriptions were defective) — the month-to-month mapping from recordings to sales breaks and generates confident false signals. Mitigation is OCR'ing execution dates off document images rather than trusting index recording dates, but that must be validated against several years of reported contract sales before sizing anything. Secondary uncertainty is coverage leakage: Travel + Leisure's Club Wyndham Access is explicitly *non-deeded* (fee title sits with First American Trust for the PTVO Owners Association, nothing recorded per buyer), so TNL is only partially observable through its UDI deeded products; and HGV Japan plus VAC's Asia-Pacific/Europe segments are invisible. Any drift toward non-deeded trust structures across the industry would erode this signal over time.

## 66. The Zero-SNP Handshake

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** Restaurant & food service. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** NCBI Pathogen Detection — the public, daily-recomputed whole-genome-sequencing clustering system where CDC PulseNet, FDA GenomeTrakr, USDA-FSIS and ~50 state public health labs deposit every sequenced Salmonella, Listeria, STEC/E. coli and Campylobacter isolate. The specific signal is NOT the clinical cluster itself but the moment a NON-clinical isolate (epi_type = environmental/other: a food sample, a plant floor drain swab, a production-facility surface) lands at ~0–10 SNPs inside an already-growing clinical SNP cluster (a "PDS" accession). That handshake is the regulator's smoking gun, and it appears in an open NIH FTP directory days-to-weeks before the recall or public advisory that actually moves the stock. Two cross-reference layers turn the genomics into a ticker: (1) the FDA CORE Outbreak Investigation Table, which publicly lists open investigations INCLUDING ones with no product named and no advisory issued, with per-investigation checkmarks for traceback initiated / on-site inspection / sample collection / recall initiated; (2) the FSIS Meat, Poultry and Egg Product Inspection Directory, which maps an establishment number to a named firm.
- **How to collect it:** All free, all sanctioned federal open data, no scraping of anything gated. (a) Daily rsync/wget of https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogen/Results/{Salmonella,Listeria,Escherichia_coli_Shigella,Campylobacter}/latest_snps/ — the *.metadata.tsv gives PDT accession, PDS_acc (SNP cluster ID), collection_date, target_creation_date (upload date), geo_loc_name (state), isolation_source (free text: "diced onion", "floor drain", "ground beef"), epi_type (clinical vs environmental/other), bioproject_center (CDC / FDA-GenomeTrakr / USDA-FSIS / state PHL), and computed_types (serovar); the SNP-distance and cluster-list files give membership and pairwise distances. Diff it every morning. Verified live: directories timestamped August 2026. (b) Weekly scrape of fda.gov/food/outbreaks-foodborne-illness/investigations-foodborne-illness-outbreaks (the CORE table) — parse the "What's New" block plus the status/checkmark columns. (c) Weekly pull of the FSIS MPI Directory CSVs (by establishment number and by name) from fsis.usda.gov, plus the Establishment Demographic Data supplement — verified current, dated Aug 10, 2026. (d) County/state health-inspection open data (NYC DOHMH, LA County, Clark County SNHD, Chicago, Dallas, King County) for chain-brand emergency closures in the cluster's counties. (e) Hand-built crosswalk: establishment number → firm → public parent ticker; and commodity → known chain supply relationships. Alert logic: fire when a PDS cluster gains ≥5 clinical isolates across ≥3 states in 14 days, AND a new epi_type≠clinical isolate joins that cluster at ≤10 SNPs. One person with a laptop and a cron job can run the whole pipeline; the hard part is the biology, not the engineering.
- **The bet / trade:** Buy 2–4 week out-of-the-money put spreads (or short the stock outright with a 3–15 trading-day hold) on the specific US-listed name the handshake resolves to. Two legs: (1) the WORKHORSE leg — protein/prepared-food/produce suppliers where the FSIS establishment number makes attribution mechanical (TSN, PPC, HRL, CAG, POST, SFD, JBS, LW, DOLE, FDP, LANC, THS, JJSF, UTZ); (2) the PAYDAY leg — restaurant chains (MCD, CMG, WEN, YUM, JACK, QSR, CAVA, SG, DRI, TXRH) when the cluster's state footprint plus a same-window emergency closure in a county health-inspection feed plus the commodity identify the brand. Enter on the handshake; exit into the CDC/FDA/FSIS press release or recall, or let it decay if nothing lands in 21 days. Because these are unscheduled catalysts with no earnings or FDA PDUFA date attached, the 2–4 week implied vol you are buying is at its structural cheapest. Add an optional post-announcement continuation short on chains only (comps damage runs 2–3 quarters), 1–3 month horizon.
- **Mechanism:** WGS is now the primary US foodborne-outbreak detection method. State labs sequence essentially every clinical isolate and upload continuously; NCBI re-clusters daily and assigns PDS accessions automatically, so a growing clinical cluster mathematically means an outbreak exists — regardless of whether any human has announced one. But regulators cannot act publicly until they can name a food, which requires traceback plus on-site sampling. When an FDA/FSIS/state investigator swabs a plant or tests a lot and that isolate lands at ~0 SNPs from the clinical cluster, the investigation is effectively over internally: a Class I recall or Public Health Alert follows near-mechanically. The lab uploads that isolate to NCBI as routine open-data practice, on the lab's own schedule — before the press office writes the release. Meanwhile the equity market's clock does not start until the press release. Restaurant equities gap violently on that release (MCD fell ~7% intraday and ~10% after-hours on Oct 22, 2024 when FDA/CDC named Quarter Pounder slivered onions; Chipotle lost roughly 40% over the 2015–16 episode) because the market instantly reprices 2–3 quarters of traffic damage plus headline risk. So the trade monetizes the gap between "the genome says a recall is coming" (public, free, ignored) and "a press release says a recall is here" (public, free, priced instantly).
- **Who's on the other side:** Long-only holders and sell-side analysts of restaurant and packaged-food equities whose information clock starts at the CNBC headline. More importantly, the options market makers writing 2–4 week wings at baseline vol: with no scheduled catalyst on the calendar, they carry zero idiosyncratic event premium, so you are buying a known-forthcoming binary at unconditional pricing. The incumbent food-safety data industry is not competing here — Sedgwick/Stericycle Recall Index, FoodChain ID, HorizonScan and similar sell post-hoc recall ARCHIVES to corporate compliance and QA departments, a completely different product for a completely different buyer. Food-safety journalists (Food Safety News, Food Poisoning Bulletin, Marler Clark) do watch the CORE table, but they publish to a legal/public-health audience on a weekly cadence and never map anything to a ticker. The structural reason nobody arbitrages it: reading PDS accessions, serovar calls, epi_type and SNP distances is applied microbiology and genomic epidemiology, which is not the skill set alt-data desks staff for — they hire people who parse credit-card panels and geolocation pings.
- **Information lead:** Three nested leads. (1) Clinical cluster growth is visible in NCBI typically 1–4 weeks before the investigation even appears on the FDA CORE table. (2) A CORE table listing with no product named runs a median ~3–5 weeks (observed range 2–10+ weeks; the table in August 2026 had entries posted as far back as June 3 still with no food identified) ahead of any public advisory. (3) The decisive non-clinical handshake isolate typically posts 3–20 days before the recall/PHA press release — that is the tradeable window and the trade trigger. Versus the market the effective lead is ~100% of that window, because market participants price nothing until the press release; there is no partial discounting to fade. For context on how much runway exists: in the McDonald's case, illness onsets ran Sept 12 – Oct 21, 2024, meaning the clinical cluster was accumulating in the public database for roughly five weeks before the October 22 announcement that took the stock down ~7–10%.
- **Why still under-exploited:** The database contains no company name, no ticker, no CUSIP, no brand — anywhere. It is built for epidemiologists and the only bridge to an investable entity is a hand-constructed crosswalk (PDS accession → isolation_source / submitting center → FSIS establishment number → firm → public parent). The raw data lives on a bare NIH FTP as multi-gigabyte tab-delimited genomics files with fields like PDS_acc, epi_type, minsame/mindiff SNP distances and computed_types; there is no API, no vendor, no packaged feed, and NCBI explicitly warns the accessions are non-archival so you must snapshot daily or lose history. It also got materially better only recently: the CORE table's practice of routinely listing product-UNIDENTIFIED investigations with stage checkmarks is a relatively new disclosure, and GenomeTrakr/FSIS non-clinical coverage has expanded a lot — so the raw material is fresher than the analytical infrastructure around it. Searching the alt-data landscape turns up geolocation, card panels, web-scrape sentiment and satellite as the standard menu; nothing sells foodborne-genomic surveillance as an equity signal. It is a real dataset sitting in the wrong professional community.
- **Rough +EV:** Expect ~10–20 handshake alerts per year that resolve to a named US-listed parent. Of those, roughly 6–12 produce a public recall or advisory within 21 days, and 3–6 produce an adverse single-day move greater than 2.5%. Restaurant-chain fires are rare (roughly 1–2/yr) but are the payday: a 2-week 5%-OTM put on a mega-cap chain trading ~18–20 vol costs roughly 30–50bp of notional and pays 5–15x into a -7% gap. Supplier fires are more frequent but smaller (-2% to -6%, and diversified names absorb it). Blended across all fires including the duds where nothing is ever announced, I'd estimate roughly +40–70% average return on premium risked per fire at a ~35–45% hit rate. Realistic capacity is $1–3M of annual premium before you start pushing illiquid put strikes around — call it a $0.5–1.5M/yr expected P&L sleeve for a small team. Uncorrelated to everything else in a book, but lumpy, capacity-capped, and unattractive as a standalone business.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Biggest uncertainty by far is the ATTRIBUTION step: the genomics tells you reliably THAT a recall is coming and usually WHAT commodity, but rarely WHOSE brand. FSIS establishment numbers make protein and prepared-food attribution nearly mechanical, which is why that leg is the workhorse; restaurant-chain attribution rests on a fragile triangulation of cluster state footprint, commodity, known supplier relationships and health-department emergency closures, and it will produce false brand calls. In the McDonald's case specifically, the implicated onions never tested positive, so a pure handshake trigger would have missed it — the clinical cluster growth was visible but the brand was not derivable from genomics alone. Secondary risks: clinical-isolate upload latency varies materially by state lab (some batch monthly), which can collapse the lead precisely in the fast-moving E. coli events where the payoff is biggest; and federal open-data publication practices could tighten or degrade, as CDC/FDA data granularity has already proven politically contingent. Everything here is public federal open data with no duty breached and no MNPI — the legal posture is the same as buying satellite imagery — but the strategy dies quietly if NCBI ever delays non-clinical isolate release to match press-release timing.

## 67. The VIN Coordinator's Inbox

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** Auto industry & EV supply chain. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** NHTSA's raw 49 CFR Part 565 "VIN deciphering information" correspondence stream — the actual PDF letters automakers mail to the NHTSA VIN Coordinator, published verbatim and unredacted through the vPIC `GetParts` endpoint. This is NOT the well-known decoded vPIC database; it is the upstream filing queue that feeds it. Each letter is a pre-production product bible: full trim ladder with marketing names, plant-of-manufacture codes mapped to city/country, motor count and per-motor kW, EPA test-group codes, and — critically for EV work — exact battery pack energy per VIN character. Verified live: Rivian's 5/28/2026 MY2027 letter enumerates position-6 codes as "Electric, Dual-motor, AWD, 108 kWh / Tri-motor 140 kWh / Quad-motor 140 kWh," plant N = Normal IL, plus an amendment for the unlaunched R2. Hyundai's Metaplant letter (dated 4/30/2026, published 5/4/2026) gives Ioniq 5 packs as 697V x 120.6Ah and 523V x 120.6Ah — i.e. 84.0 kWh and 63.1 kWh — with plant Y = HMGMA/Georgia. Audi's 8/10/2026 MY2027 letter lists "Audi SQ9 4.0 TFSI quattro," a nameplate Audi has not launched. The 120.6Ah figure is a cell fingerprint: it changes only when the cell itself changes. Volume measured: 1,164 filings between 8/1/2025 and 8/14/2026 from 705 distinct filers, ~21/week, with 142 already covering MY2027. Delicious detail: VW's cover letter formally requests CBI treatment under 49 CFR Part 512 and Hyundai stamps every page "protected... confidentiality agreements" — and NHTSA publishes the whole PDF to the open internet anyway. The filers believe this is secret. It is not.
- **How to collect it:** Poll `https://vpic.nhtsa.dot.gov/api/vehicles/GetParts?type=565&fromDate=M/D/YYYY&toDate=M/D/YYYY&page=N&format=json` daily; paginate until empty. Each row returns LetterDate, ManufacturerName, ModelYearFrom/To, and a `URL` of form `http://vpic.nhtsa.dot.gov/mid/home/displayfile/<uuid>` that serves the PDF with no auth, no key, no rate limit (confirmed: 705KB `27-NHTSA-Audi7.pdf`, content-type application/pdf). Also poll `type=566` for Manufacturer Identification filings — the tell for a brand-new entrant beginning manufacture — and `GetWMIsForManufacturer/<name>`, which returns each World Manufacturer Identifier with `CreatedOn` and `DateAvailableToPublic` timestamps; a new WMI is a new plant or new vehicle class and is legally filed >=60 days before the first VIN is stamped. Build: (1) a ~60-name manufacturer whitelist, since 77% of filings are trailer, RV, boat and welding-shop noise that nobody will ever bother to filter; (2) per-OEM PDF parsers with pypdf/pdfplumber — Audi ships a graphics-heavy Visio export, Hyundai a spreadsheet print, Rivian a clean table, so roughly 40 templates cover the entire tradeable universe; (3) a differ that keys on (manufacturer, nameplate, model year, VIN position) and emits deltas: pack kWh or V*Ah changed, plant code changed, trim added/deleted, nameplate first-seen, motor count changed. Maintain a side table mapping cell Ah/voltage fingerprints to cell makers (LGES, SK On, Samsung SDI, Panasonic, CATL) from teardowns and datasheets. Total build: a few weeks for one competent person; ongoing cost ~zero.
- **The bet / trade:** Event-driven single-name equity and short-dated options in US-listed EV OEMs and their dedicated battery/powertrain suppliers, with three triggers. (A) LAUNCH-SLIP SHORT — the highest-conviction leg: if a company has publicly guided to start selling a nameplate in a given quarter and no Part 565 letter for that nameplate/model-year exists by 60 days before the guided start-of-sales date, the launch cannot legally happen on time. Buy puts or short the equity spanning the delivery/earnings print; hold 4-10 weeks through the catalyst. (B) SPEC-DELTA PAIR — when a filing changes a pack's Ah or voltage fingerprint for a high-volume nameplate, trade the implicated cell supplier against its peer (e.g. LG Energy Solution 373220.KS vs Samsung SDI 006400.KS, or SK Innovation 096770.KS), one to two quarters. (C) PLANT REASSIGNMENT — when position 11 or the WMI moves a nameplate's assembly between countries, trade the OEM against a peer on the Section 232 tariff/USMCA-content margin swing, one to three quarters. Primary instrument for a small team: leg (A) via 1-3 month puts on the guided-launch OEM, plus leg (C) via long/short OEM pairs.
- **Mechanism:** 49 CFR 565.16 forces the disclosure. Subsection (d) requires VIN deciphering information be submitted "at least 60 days prior to offering for sale the first vehicle identified by a VIN containing that information," and subsection (b) requires a new manufacturer identifier "at least 60 days before affixing the first VIN using the identifier." A vehicle physically cannot be sold in the US without a VIN, and the VIN cannot be decoded without this filing. So the letter is a hard, calendar-anchored precondition for revenue. That gives a rare two-sided causal chain. Positive: the letter enumerates exactly which trims, which pack sizes, and which plant will produce the thing that generates next quarter's revenue — the trim ladder is the mix assumption, the pack kWh is the per-unit cell demand, the plant code is the tariff and labor-cost basis. Multiply pack kWh by expected volume per trim and you have a bottom-up GWh forecast for a named cell plant before the OEM has said anything. Negative and cleaner: absence of a filing is a legally binding statement that no sale can occur within 60 days. When a company guides to a Q4 launch and the VIN Coordinator's inbox is empty in mid-Q3, the guidance is already dead — the company just hasn't said so. That is a falsifiable delay detector with a statutory floor under it, which is vanishingly rare in equity research. Secondary channel: pack voltage and amp-hours are a cell fingerprint. Hyundai's 120.6Ah is a specific cell; when that number moves, a cell has been requalified, which means a supplier or generation switch at a named JV plant, months before it shows up in anyone's shipment data.
- **Who's on the other side:** Sell-side auto analysts and the systematic funds trading EV names. They monitor dealer inventory scrapes, EPA and CARB certification postings, monthly registration data, press releases and supplier channel checks. None of them read a NHTSA correspondence queue. The professional forecasters who would care — S&P Global Mobility/AutoForecast Solutions, Wards, LMC — build production forecasts from plant interviews and supplier chatter, then publish to subscribers on a slow, curated cadence; they do not run a nightly differ against a government PDF inbox. The VIN-data industry (DataOne, VinAudit, Vehicle Databases) consumes the *processed* vPIC decode tables for VIN lookup, which is a downstream, later, and structurally different artifact from the letters. They are slow for four structural reasons. First, the endpoint is named `GetParts`, which sounds like it returns auto components, and it is buried in an API everyone uses only for `DecodeVin`. Second, 77% of the flow is trailer manufacturers, RV builders and welding shops — the signal-to-noise is genuinely awful unless you whitelist, and nobody builds infrastructure to filter garbage they do not know contains gold. Third, there is no schema: every OEM invents its own PDF layout, so this is unglamorous per-filer parsing work that no vendor has bothered to industrialize. Fourth, and most tellingly, the filers themselves believe the documents are confidential — VW formally requests CBI treatment, Hyundai stamps every page — so the OEMs are not managing this as a disclosure channel and have no incentive to point anyone at it.
- **Information lead:** Statutory floor of 60 days before the first vehicle can be offered for sale; empirically much longer. Measured on live filings: Audi filed MY2027 on 8/10/2026 for a model year that starts retailing late 2026 into 2027 (3-6 months). Rivian filed MY2027 R1S/R1T/commercial van on 5/28/2026 (2-5 months), having filed the MY2027 R2 initial release back on 2/3/2026 — roughly a year before that volume model reaches customers. Slate Auto filed for MY2026 on 9/26/2025, more than a year before start of production. NHTSA publishes within days of receipt: Hyundai's Metaplant letter is dated 4/30/2026 and appeared in the API with LetterDate 5/4/2026, a 4-day pipe. Against the alternatives, the lead compounds: unannounced nameplates like the Audi SQ9 appear here before the OEM's own press embargo; plant assignment appears months before it is visible in monthly production or import statistics and 1-3 quarters before it flows through reported gross margin; per-trim pack energy appears before Monroney labels exist at dealers and before EPA publishes model-year certification data — and Part 565 carries plant, trim ladder and pack size, which EPA's data does not carry at all. The letters even hand you the EPA test-group codes, letting you join to certification before EPA itself publishes the model year.
- **Why still under-exploited:** This is a government inbox, not a product. No vendor sells it: the commercial ecosystem around vPIC sells VIN *decoding*, which consumes the cleaned downstream database, whereas the edge here is treating the upstream letters as a timestamped corporate-event stream and differencing them. Four moats keep it that way, and they are the good kind — boring rather than technical. (1) Discovery: the endpoint is misleadingly named `GetParts` and sits unremarked inside an API whose users came for `DecodeVin`. (2) Noise: 705 distinct filers over twelve months, 77% of them trailer, RV, boat and metal-fabrication shops, so anyone who glances at the raw feed sees junk and leaves. (3) Unstructured heterogeneity: no two OEMs use the same PDF layout — Audi exports Visio graphics, Hyundai prints spreadsheets, Rivian ships tables — so extraction is ~40 bespoke parsers of genuinely tedious work with no reusable schema, exactly the kind of labor that fails a vendor's build-versus-buy test. (4) Nobody is advertising it: the filers actively believe the documents are confidential business information and stamp them accordingly, so there is no OEM investor-relations pointer, no analyst convention, and no incumbent product to displace. The material is hiding behind tedium rather than behind a paywall or a legal barrier, which is the most durable kind of obscurity — it does not get arbitraged away by someone writing a check.
- **Rough +EV:** Fire rate: ~1,160 filings/yr, ~270 from real OEMs (23%). Of those, realistically 30-50/yr carry a genuinely new tradeable fact — first-seen nameplate, plant reassignment, pack-spec delta, trim deletion, or a guided-launch absence — of which perhaps 12-20/yr are clean enough to be single-name catalysts. Expected edge is asymmetric across the three legs. Leg (A), the launch-slip short, is the money: it fires maybe 3-6 times a year, but the statutory floor makes it near-deterministic when it is clean, and EV names routinely move 8-20% on a delivery miss or a guidance cut, so short-dated puts bought 6-10 weeks ahead can return multiples on the premium. Legs (B) and (C) are thesis-weight rather than standalone — call it a 2-4% move on the underlying captured over 4-10 weeks at a 58-63% hit rate, which is real but modest. Blended, I'd put this at roughly 150-400bps/yr of alpha on a dedicated auto/EV sleeve, with fat right-tail contribution from two or three leg-(A) events and the occasional unannounced-nameplate surprise. Costs are trivial: no data fees, no licensing, a few weeks of build, and near-zero marginal running cost. The honest deflator is that most filings are routine amendments, and the largest-cap name in the space (Tesla) files sparsely and writes vaguely, so the highest-liquidity ticker is the one where this works least well — the edge concentrates in Rivian, Lucid, Hyundai/Kia, and the Korean cell makers.
- **Confidence:** Medium-high on the data (fully verified live: the API returns filings, the PDFs download unauthenticated, and 49 CFR 565.16(b) and (d) confirm the 60-day statutory lead) and medium on the trade. Biggest uncertainty by a distance: 565.16(d) contains an escape hatch that guts the negative signal. If "information concerning vehicle characteristics sufficient to specify the VIN code is unavailable to the manufacturer by that date," the manufacturer may instead file "within one week after that information first becomes available." An OEM that is genuinely late on specs can therefore file legally at T-7 days rather than T-60, which means absence of a filing does not strictly prove a slip. The leg-(A) short must be sized for that: it needs a base-rate study of how often each specific manufacturer actually invokes the late path before the signal can be traded with size, and the answer will differ by filer — a disciplined homologation department like Rivian's or Hyundai's files early and predictably, while a chaotic one may live in the exception. Second-order uncertainties: spec is not volume, so a pack-size change tells you cell content per vehicle but nothing about units; an Ah change could be a relabeling or a measurement-convention change rather than a supplier switch, so fingerprint-to-supplier attribution carries real false-positive risk; and NHTSA could restrict public access if an OEM ever presses the CBI request that VW already puts in writing on every cover letter — which is the tail risk that eventually kills this source.
