## 88. The Curie Ceiling

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** LICENSING AND REGISTRY CHANGES as corporate tells. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** Per-site, per-isotope MAXIMUM POSSESSION LIMITS on NRC Form 374/374A radioactive materials licenses (and their Agreement-State equivalents), plus the amendment stream that changes them. Column 8 of every materials license states "Maximum amount that licensee may possess at any one time," in curies/millicuries, per radionuclide, and Column 9 states the authorized use — critically, whether it is "research and development... commercial distribution is NOT authorized" or distribution of radioactive drugs to medical-use licensees under 10 CFR 32.72. For a radiopharmaceutical plant this number IS the legal ceiling on production. Verified live examples: PharmaLogic Idaho LLC, NRC License 11-35774-01 (Docket 030-39401), Amendment No. 1 (ADAMS ML25336A246): Lu-177 30 Ci, F-18 5 Ci, Mo-99 2 Ci, Ac-225 25 mCi, At-211 100 mCi, Tb-161 500 mCi, Pb-212 100 mCi, Ra-224 50 mCi, Cu-64 1 Ci — all flagged R&D only, no commercial distribution. A separate license (ML26056A169) carries Ac-225 at 200 mCi WITH 32.72 commercial distribution authority. The second, orthogonal feed is the NRC's monthly "Licensing Actions Received or Taken" log (e.g., ML26006A020 for Dec 2025), which lists every application RECEIVED — state, city, licensee, license number, date received, action type — months before the license is granted. Example rows from that file: "IN Noblesville Curium US LLC 13-35179-02 12/4/2025 Amendment" and three simultaneous Curium Maryland Heights MO amendments (24-04206-01/-02/-05MD) received 12/18/2025.
- **How to collect it:** Three sanctioned public channels, all free. (1) NRC ADAMS (adams.nrc.gov/wba, Publicly Available Records System): full-text search for "MATERIALS LICENSE" / NRC Form 374 by licensee name or docket; documents resolve to https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML{YYnn}/{accession}.pdf. Direct curl from a datacenter IP gets 403 — use a normal browser UA / residential egress or headless browser; the PDFs then parse cleanly with pypdf (I extracted the full possession-limit tables above this way). Pull the monthly "Licensing Actions Received or Taken" accession each month for the application-receipt tape, and pull the same dockets' inspection reports and Notices of Violation for disruption signals. (2) The crown jewel of coverage: INDIANA, MISSOURI, MICHIGAN, IDAHO, DELAWARE, ALASKA, HAWAII, MONTANA, SOUTH DAKOTA, WEST VIRGINIA and CONNECTICUT are NOT Agreement States, so the NRC licenses them directly and the complete license document is public in ADAMS. Indiana and Missouri happen to be the US radiopharma manufacturing capital — Novartis/Advanced Accelerator Applications Indianapolis (the Pluvicto plant), Curium Noblesville IN and Maryland Heights MO, Telix Fishers IN, SpectronRx South Bend IN, Niowave in Michigan, PharmaLogic in Idaho Falls. (3) For the 39 Agreement States, scrape the state notices and registries: the Texas Register publishes "Licensing Actions for Radioactive Materials" SEMIMONTHLY as a free PDF at sos.texas.gov/texreg/archive/{Month}/In Addition/ — tables of NEW LICENSES ISSUED / AMENDMENTS ISSUED / RENEWALS / TERMINATIONS with licensee name, license number, city, amendment number and exact date of action (verified: "HOUSTON CARDINAL HEALTH 414 LLC DBA CARDINAL HEALTH NUCLEAR PHARMACY SERVICES L05536 amendment 69 02/12/26"; RLS (USA) Inc took amendments in Dallas, Houston and San Antonio in the same fortnight). TX DSHS, CA RHB, IL IEMA, NJ, MA and NY run their own RAM license search portals; the license document itself (with the limits) comes via routine state public-records request, typically 10-30 days and under $50. Build: a per-site time series of curies-authorized by isotope, plus an authorized-use state machine (R&D → 32.72 commercial), plus a pending-application queue keyed on the NRC monthly log.
- **The bet / trade:** Long/short single names in radiopharmaceuticals and nuclear-medicine supply, held through one to two quarterly reports (3-6 months), expressed in equity plus 3-6 month options. Universe: Lantheus (LNTH), Telix (TLX on ASX/NASDAQ), Perspective Therapeutics (CATX), Actinium (ATNM), BWX Technologies (BWXT), Cardinal Health (CAH, Nuclear & Precision Health), Novartis (NVS) as the low-beta readthrough leg. THE PRIMARY BET IS THE NEGATIVE ONE: when management guides to a launch, capacity ramp or dose-volume inflection at a named site, and no granted license amendment authorizing the required isotope, quantity and commercial distribution exists at that site 90+ days before the guided start, short the stock or buy puts into that quarter's print. You cannot legally possess the material without the license, so the ramp is arithmetically impossible on the guided timeline. SECONDARY LONG: when a site's license flips Column 9 from "commercial distribution is not authorized" to 10 CFR 32.72 distribution, or a key isotope's possession limit rises 3x or more, go long into the next two prints. THIRD, a partnership tell: when a radiopharma CDMO adds an exotic isotope to its license (Pb-212, At-211, Tb-161, Ra-224), that isotope maps to a very short list of sponsors — a CDMO does not pay for a license amendment without a signed customer — so buy the small-cap whose isotope it is before the partnership is announced.
- **Mechanism:** Possession limit is a hard legal ceiling on how much activity may sit on the site at any instant, and therapeutic/diagnostic isotopes decay too fast to stockpile: Ga-68 has a 68-minute half-life, F-18 110 minutes, Lu-177 6.6 days, Ac-225 9.9 days. Because you cannot bank inventory, steady-state on-site activity is nearly proportional to throughput, so curies-on-license is a direct upper bound on doses per week, which is a direct upper bound on revenue. The regulatory chain runs strictly ahead of the commercial one: the company files an amendment application (appears in the NRC monthly received log), NRC or the state grants it and issues an updated Form 374 (appears in ADAMS or in the Texas Register table), only then can material be received, only then can FDA inspect and approve the site for commercial manufacture, only then does the company issue a press release, and only then does a dose reach a patient and revenue reach the P&L. Every one of those steps is dated and public at step two or three, while the market reacts at step five. This sector's single defining event — the Pluvicto supply crisis of 2022-23, when Novartis had approved demand it could not physically make and burned billions in deferred revenue — was a possession-and-capacity problem, not a demand problem, and the entire sector still trades on the question "can they actually make it?" The license answers that question in curies, with a date, for free.
- **Who's on the other side:** Healthcare sell-side analysts and long-only specialists who model radiopharma capacity entirely from management slides, investor-day plant maps and ribbon-cutting press releases — i.e., from the company's own narrative about a physical constraint the company has every incentive to sound confident about. Generalist biotech funds model demand (prescriptions, label breadth, competitive trials) and treat manufacturing as an execution footnote. Index and passive flows are wholly indifferent. The people who actually read Form 374 — radiation safety officers, health physicists, regulatory affairs staff, the ERP vendors selling RAM-limit tracking software — have no position and no reason to publish. There is no analyst on the Street whose job description includes reading ADAMS accession numbers. They are slow because the information sits behind an accession-number retrieval system with a hostile UI, in scanned-quality PDFs, in a document type nobody in finance knows exists, and wrong because they substitute a guided date for a granted license.
- **Information lead:** Three tiers. The application-received log gives 3-12 months over the grant and 6-18 months over any corporate announcement — I can see Curium filed three simultaneous amendments on its main Maryland Heights site on 12/18/2025 with zero press coverage. The granted license in ADAMS typically posts weeks to a few months before the company's own announcement — the standard pattern is exactly the SpectronRx headline "Receives U.S. NRC Materials License for New Indiana Facility," where the ADAMS document predates the wire. Against the number actually mattering — the quarter where capacity shows up in revenue or forces a guidance revision — the lead is one to three quarters. Even the slowest channel, the semimonthly Texas Register, runs 2-6 weeks behind the action and still lands well ahead of any 10-Q or earnings call. The negative signal has the longest lead of all: if a company guides in January to a Q3 ramp and no application has even been RECEIVED by March, you know in March that the Q3 guide is dead, because NRC materials amendments do not clear in under a quarter.
- **Why still under-exploited:** No alternative-data vendor sells it — I searched specifically and found only compliance-software marketing and NRC guidance documents, nothing pointed at investors. It fails every screen a data company uses: it is not a single API, it is 1 federal system plus 39 heterogeneous state programs; it is not bulk-downloadable, ADAMS serves individual accession numbers and blocks naive scrapers with 403s; it is not structured, the payload is a two-column table inside a PDF form; and the entities are a mix of public companies, private CDMOs (Curium, PharmaLogic, SpectronRx, NorthStar, SHINE, Nusano) and hospitals, so there is no clean ticker join. The financial world's mental model of "regulatory catalyst" in this sector is FDA-shaped — everyone watches PDUFA dates and nobody watches the agency that controls whether the molecule can physically be in the building. The fragmentation and the PDF-parsing tax are exactly the moat: a two-person team with pypdf, a browser-UA fetcher and a records-request template can build the entire national capacity census in a few months, and that census does not exist anywhere else. Bonus timing: NRC's May 2026 proposed rule "Modernizing NRC Regulations for Byproduct Material Use," with a November 2026 final-rule deadline, is about to reshuffle which radiopharmaceutical activities need specific licenses — a window where the licensing tape gets noisier and more informative at once.
- **Rough +EV:** Roughly 15-30 actionable events per year across ~7 directly tradable tickers plus readthroughs from private CDMO licensing into public customers and suppliers. These are 40-70% implied-vol names where supply and capacity news routinely moves the stock 5-15% in a day. Realistic capture is 3-6% of move per event at a 55-65% hit rate, netting roughly 1.5-3% edge per event before costs. Concentrated in a dedicated sleeve that is maybe 300-700bps of annual alpha on $20-60M, with the sleeve capacity-capped by CATX/ATNM/TLX liquidity rather than by signal supply. The negative leg carries most of the expected value and most of the convexity: a guided ramp with no granted license is a high-probability guidance cut, and 3-6 month puts on a mid-cap radiopharma into a missed capacity quarter are a 2-5x payoff, so a 30-40% hit rate on that leg alone clears cost of carry. Setup cost is one engineer-quarter plus a few hundred dollars of records-request fees; ongoing marginal cost is near zero.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Biggest uncertainty by far: possession limits are requested with deliberate headroom. Amending a license is slow and expensive, so licensees routinely ask for 5-10x the activity they intend to run, which means a limit INCREASE is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a capacity increase and the positive long leg will produce false positives. The clean, near-deterministic side is the absence signal — no license, no material, no doses, no revenue — and I would size the short/put leg 2-3x the long leg for that reason. Secondary risks: ADAMS posting latency is policy-driven and variable (documents typically go public within days of issuance but not on a guaranteed clock); NRC withholds security details for IAEA Category 1/2 quantities, though the therapeutic medical isotopes that matter here (Lu-177, Ac-225, Pb-212, At-211) are not in those categories while Co-60 and Cs-137 are; and Agreement-State disclosure quality varies wildly, partly mitigated by the fortunate accident that Indiana and Missouri, the two states holding the most important radiopharma plants in the country, are non-Agreement and therefore fully public in ADAMS. Indiana filed a letter of intent in 2021 to become an Agreement State — if that completes, the single best window in this dataset narrows and the edge degrades toward records-request latency.

## 89. The NoBo Ladder

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** TESTING, CERTIFICATION AND INSPECTION THROUGHPUT. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** The EU rail homologation paper-trail, as a two-register panel: (1) ERADIS — the European Union Agency for Railways' Database of Interoperability and Safety — specifically its Notified Body (NoBo) EC Certificates, NoBo Intermediate Statements of Verification (ISVs), EC declarations of verification of subsystems, and EC declarations of conformity of interoperability constituents; and (2) ERATV — the European Register of Authorised Types of Vehicles — which publishes every authorised rail vehicle type with Date of Authorisation, authorising entity (ERA or a named national safety authority), authorisation holder, manufacturer, area of use, and status (Active/Suspended/Withdrawn), plus every new variant and version. Cross-referenced against NANDO (the EU notified-body register) to resolve NoBo names/numbers. Together these form a per-program state machine of where every European train build sits in its certification queue, and a per-authoriser and per-NoBo throughput meter.
- **How to collect it:** All public, no login, sanctioned. ERADIS: https://eradis.era.europa.eu/interop_docs/NoBoCert/search.aspx is an advanced search with filters for certificate number, certificate type (EC Certificate of Conformity / Suitability for Use / ISV), NoBo name and NANDO number, applicant name+country, manufacturer name+country, subsystem, object of assessment, and — critically — a Date of Issue range, so you can pull rolling monthly windows. EC declarations list at https://eradis.era.europa.eu/interop_docs/ecDecl/default.aspx?DocumentType=ECDeclVer (subsystems) and ...?DocumentType=ECDeclCnf (constituents); individual records render at .../ecDecl/view.aspx?id=<N>&DocumentType=ECDeclCnf with sequential integer IDs, so a determined team can enumerate ids 1..N nightly and get a complete, timestamped census rather than relying on search. Records expose Applicant Name/Country, Notified Body + NANDO number, interoperability constituent, EC certificate ID number, Date of issue, Date of validity. ERATV: https://eratv.era.europa.eu/eratv/ — browse/search published types, per-type detail pages, and native export to Excel/XML/PDF; also mirrored as a dataset on data.europa.eu. Both are ASP.NET WebForms apps (VIEWSTATE postbacks), so the scraper needs a session-cookie/headless-browser harness — about a week of work, then a nightly cron that diffs new certificate IDs, new ERATV type numbers, new versions/variants, area-of-use additions, and status flips. Build a per-OEM, per-program monthly "clearance count" index.
- **The bet / trade:** Primary: directional equity/options position in Alstom (Euronext Paris: ALO; ADR ALSMY), entered 3-6 weeks before each results print and held through it — Q1 sales/orders (mid-July), H1 (mid-November), Q3 (mid-January), FY preliminary/full (April/May). Long (or call spreads) when the trailing 6-month NoBo Ladder clearance index for Alstom programs is above its 2-year trend; short (or put spreads) when it is decaying, which is the higher-conviction leg because rail delivery misses are violently repriced. Holding horizon 4-13 weeks. Secondary: single-name event trades on the smaller, single-program-levered builders — Stadler Rail (SIX: SRAIL), CAF (BME: CAF), Talgo (BME: TLGO), Vossloh (XETRA: VOS) — bought on a program's ladder completing (final EC certificate posted, then ERATV type/variant published) and sold into the eventual company announcement. Third leg: a market-neutral pair, long the OEM whose ladder is clearing against short the one whose ladder has stalled, to strip out sector beta. Credit variant: Alstom bonds/CDS, since the FCF-and-leverage narrative is the same variable.
- **Mechanism:** A European train cannot be delivered, accepted, or paid its final milestone until its vehicle type is authorised. The chain is strict and each rung is publicly filed: NoBo issues design-review and type-test ISVs, then the EC certificate; the applicant files the EC declaration of verification for the subsystem; only then can the authorising entity (ERA via the One-Stop Shop, or a national safety authority such as Germany's EBA) issue the vehicle type authorisation, which is then registered in ERATV. ERA's own guidance is explicit that authorising entities must ensure ERADIS is adequately populated *before* delivering an authorisation — so the ERADIS entries are a hard precondition, not a coincident report. Trains built but not yet authorised sit as inventory and contract working capital. Therefore the rate at which certificates and ISVs post per program is a direct, physical meter of how fast a builder's revenue and cash will convert. When the ladder stalls — NoBo capacity, ETCS/ERTMS baseline changes, TSI revision cutovers, an NSA backlog — deliveries slip, working capital balloons, and free cash flow misses. This is not theoretical: in April 2026 Alstom withdrew its three-year FCF target, flagged a ~EUR 1.5bn H1 cash outflow versus roughly EUR 560m expected, reported cars manufactured down to 4,284 on "rolling stock projects moving at a slower-than-anticipated pace," and the stock fell ~28-30% in a day. The same registers also let you measure the authoriser side — authorisations issued per month by ERA versus each NSA, and certificates issued per month by each NoBo — which is a sector-wide supply constraint that hits every builder delivering into that country simultaneously.
- **Who's on the other side:** Sell-side capital-goods and rail analysts (Kepler, ODDO, Barclays, JPM, Bernstein) and long-only European industrials funds, who model deliveries almost entirely from company guidance, backlog conversion assumptions, and press releases. They are slow for four structural reasons. First, the issuers themselves are late: Alstom's own incoming CEO was publicly warning of "further fallout from delayed projects" only *after* the April 2026 collapse, meaning management's internal program visibility was already worse than a register-based view. Second, program-level homologation status is essentially never disclosed — companies press-release flagship authorisations (Talgo's Talgo 230/ICE L, authorised jointly by ERA and EBA on 11 August 2025) and stay silent on the long tail of variants, versions, and country-by-country area-of-use extensions that actually gate deliveries. Third, the sector has zero data-vendor coverage: there is no Kpler or YipitData for rail, and no broker runs a homologation tracker. Fourth, the raw material is genuinely unpleasant — two clunky ASP.NET registers with no bulk API, plus NANDO, plus the domain knowledge to map a certificate for a "traction subsystem, applicant Alstom Transport SA" onto a specific customer contract and revenue line. That mapping cost is the moat.
- **Information lead:** Three different leads, stacked. (1) Against the authorisation itself: ERADIS must be populated before an authorisation is delivered, and NoBo ISVs/EC certificates typically post 2-9 months ahead of the authorisation decision — so the ladder tells you a program is about to clear, or has silently stopped moving, well before the decision exists. (2) Against the company: builders disclose delivery pace only at quarterly results and never by program, so a rolling ERADIS/ERATV clearance index gives roughly one to two quarters of lead on the delivery-pace surprise that moves the stock. (3) Against the tape on discrete events: Commission Implementing Decision 2011/665/EU obliges the authorising entity to register a type authorisation or variant in ERATV within 20 working days of issue, with ERA validating within a further 20 working days. For flagship trains the company's press release may beat the register by days, so there is little edge there — the edge is the unpublicised long tail of variants, versions, area-of-use extensions and, importantly, Suspended/Withdrawn status flips, which appear in ERATV and are never announced by anyone.
- **Why still under-exploited:** It is not a product; it is two EU compliance registers built for safety transparency, not for analysis. There is no API, no bulk feed, no CSV endpoint — ERATV offers a per-type Excel/XML export and ERADIS offers a form-based search behind VIEWSTATE postbacks, which is precisely why no one has industrialised it. Rail is a small, unloved, capex-cycle sector that alternative-data vendors have skipped entirely; the commercial alt-data industry is built around shipping, cards, web traffic, satellites and app data. The domain also demands genuine expertise: you need to understand TSIs, subsystems, interoperability constituents, ISVs versus EC certificates, and the ERA One-Stop Shop versus NSA split before the records mean anything. And the clean panel is new — ERA only became the EU authorising authority under the 4th Railway Package in June 2019, and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/250 standardised the EC declaration and certificate templates, so a consistent, comparable multi-year time series really only starts around 2020-21. By quant standards that is a brand-new dataset that has never been mined.
- **Rough +EV:** Alstom prints are high-variance: the April 2026 FY preliminary was -28% to -30% in a session, and ordinary FCF/delivery prints routinely move the stock 5-12%. Assume ~4 tradeable Alstom prints per year plus ~8-12 across Stadler/CAF/Talgo/Vossloh, so 12-16 print-trades annually, plus roughly 10-20 long-tail authorisation or status-flip events on the small caps. If the clearance index calls the direction of the delivery-pace surprise 58-62% of the time against an ~8% average absolute move, that is roughly 1.3-2.0% expected return per print-trade gross; at 20-30% notional per trade and 12-16 trades, plausibly 8-15% annualised on deployed capital, heavily skewed — most of it earned in the one or two quarters a year when a ladder stall precedes a guidance withdrawal. Options express it better than stock: buying 1-3 month put spreads into a decaying ladder is cheap because implied vol does not price a delivery-miss tail, and a single correct call on an Alstom-style event pays multiples of a year's premium spend. Small-cap event trades add a handful of 5-15% single-day moves per year but liquidity in TLGO/CAF caps size at low single-digit millions. Setup cost is roughly one engineer-month plus a rail-domain consultant to build the certificate-to-contract mapping; ongoing cost is trivial.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Biggest uncertainty: register population discipline. ERADIS and ERATV are legally mandated (20-working-day ERATV deadline; ERADIS must be populated before authorisation) but historically patchily and unevenly filled, and some notified bodies and applicants batch-upload records in bursts. If uploads are lumpy rather than prompt, the "throughput" signal degrades into a measure of upload behaviour and the timing edge collapses — this must be validated first by reconstructing 2021-2026 monthly per-OEM clearance counts and checking them against reported cars manufactured and FCF surprises before risking capital. Second-order uncertainty: homologation clearance is necessary but not sufficient for delivery — customer acceptance, supplier failures (Stadler's 2024 Valencia flooding and supplier destruction), software/ETCS commissioning and project management can still gate deliveries, so the ladder explains part, not all, of the delivery-pace surprise; expect it to be a strong negative signal (a stalled ladder reliably means trouble) and a weaker positive one (a clearing ladder does not guarantee delivery).

## 90. Premium Per Stamp

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** INSURANCE AND ACTUARIAL FILINGS as forward indicators. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** Monthly per-insurer surplus-lines (E&S) premium AND policy-item counts published free by the 15 state surplus-lines stamping offices — the compliance/tax utilities every E&S broker must file each policy with. The two biggest E&S states publish this at INSURER-NAME granularity, monthly: (a) Florida Surplus Lines Service Office "Surplus Lines Premium Report" — premium and policy count by individual insurer, by coverage code, by county, filterable to specific months; plus the "FL Monthly Premium Report" PDF which adds new-business-vs-renewal split and an explicit Average Cost Per Policy line with YoY %; (b) Surplus Line Association of California "California Premium By Insurer" report + archive, monthly, on registered date. Texas (SLTX) adds fast monthly aggregates plus per-insurer PDFs at sltx.org/Insurers/Summaries/{NAIC}_{Name}.pdf and "Company Totals by Name," "Coverage Totals by Company," "Company Totals by Lines of Business" YTD PDFs that can be month-differenced. The derived signal nobody computes: per-carrier, per-coverage premium ÷ item count = a carrier-specific realized RATE index, and the new-business vs renewal spread within it. Stamping-office states = 63% of all US surplus lines premium ($90.3B in 2025).
- **How to collect it:** All public, no login, no scraping of gated systems. (1) FSLSO interactive tool: https://www.fslso.com/header-utility-items/market-data-reports/surplus-lines-premium-report — pivot by insurer × coverage × county × month; monthly PDF at https://www.fslso.com/docs/default-source/uploadedfiles/reports/fl-monthly-premium-report/monthly-fl-premium-report.pdf (verified 2026-08-14: already carries JULY 2026 data with premium, policy count, average cost per policy, YoY — a ~2-week lag). (2) SLA California: https://www.slacal.com/industry-reports/california-premium and the archive at /industry-reports/industry-reports-archive/california-premium. (3) SLTX: https://www.sltx.org/forms-reports/policy-and-premium-reports/ (July 2026 posted: $1.859B, 305,074 filings) and https://www.sltx.org/forms-reports/market-data-reports/. (4) Confirmation tier: AZ, NV, UT, ID, OR, WA, MN, MS, NC, PA, IL stamping offices + ELANY (NY), mostly quarterly/annual — list at wsia.org/wcm/Legislative_Advocacy___PAC/Stamping_Offices___SLAs.aspx. Build: weekly cron pulling the dashboards and PDFs (pdfplumber for the PDFs, headless browser for the two JS dashboards), hand-map each state's coverage-code taxonomy to a common schema (the genuinely tedious part — each office has its own codes and its own date convention: submitted vs. registered vs. processed), and map NAIC company codes to public-company tickers using each issuer's 10-K subsidiary list (e.g. Kinsale Insurance Company = NAIC 38920). Store as a carrier × coverage × state × month panel; compute YoY premium, YoY item count, premium-per-item YoY, and (FL only) the new-vs-renewal premium-per-item spread on trailing-3-month sums.
- **The bet / trade:** Two legs off one panel. LEG 1 (event, primary): directional trade on E&S pure-play equities into their quarterly GWP print. Universe: KNSL (Kinsale), SKWD (Skyward), BOW (Bowhead), PLMR, HCI, plus RYAN/BWIN on the broker side using FSLSO's Top Brokerages report. Signal = stacked FL+CA+TX carrier-level YoY premium growth and premium-per-item, z-scored against that carrier's own 8-quarter history, compared to consensus GWP growth. Enter T-10 to T-5 business days before the earnings date, exit T+2. Express as dollar-neutral pair vs. a specialty-P&C basket (WRB/RLI/AXS) to strip sector beta; use short-dated single-name options only when |z| > 1.5. LEG 2 (regime, higher capacity): when FL+CA commercial-property premium-per-item goes negative YoY for 3 consecutive months, go underweight the E&S property-levered complex (KNSL/PLMR/HCI/SKWD) against casualty-levered specialty, 2-quarter holding period; reverse on 3 consecutive positive months.
- **Mechanism:** Every E&S policy bound in these states must be stamped and filed with the state's stamping office within roughly 30 days, because that is how the premium tax and stamping fee get assessed. So the stamping office mechanically accumulates a near-complete census of the carrier's written premium and policy count in that state, with a short and stable lag — months before the carrier reports and months before any statutory filing. Premium alone is ambiguous (fewer, bigger policies vs. more, cheaper ones), but premium ÷ item count separates them, and that ratio is a direct read on realized rate. Rate is the variable that drives E&S carrier valuation: these stocks trade on GWP growth, not on current earnings — Kinsale is down ~37% over the past year purely on growth deceleration while beating on EPS ($5.54 vs $5.11 consensus in Q2 2026), with commercial property GWP -32.7%. Critically, carriers cut price on NEW business before they cut renewals, so the FL new-business premium-per-item series turns before the renewal series, which turns before reported GWP, which turns before combined ratio. That gives a stacked lead chain. Industry commentary already validates the mechanic without exploiting it at carrier level: the H1 2026 read was explicitly "the gap between falling property premium and rising transaction volume points to rate compression rather than a loss of demand" — that is exactly the premium-per-item divergence, but computed only once, semiannually, for the whole market.
- **Who's on the other side:** Sell-side E&S analysts (KBW, JMP, Truist, Wells) and the long-only specialty-insurance funds who set consensus GWP. They model growth from three inputs, all of which are strictly worse: (1) management's commentary from the PRIOR quarter's call, which is stale by construction; (2) aggregate rate surveys — Ivans Index, CIAB Market Index, MarketScout — every one of which publishes only line-of-business aggregates and explicitly does not disclose carrier-level data; (3) statutory Schedule T / state pages, which are the only other public source of a carrier's state-by-state premium and are filed roughly 45-60 days AFTER quarter end, i.e. AFTER the earnings release. So on the day of the print, essentially nobody in the market has seen state-level or coverage-level carrier data for that quarter. Also on the other side: options market makers pricing E&S earnings straddles off realized-move history rather than a fundamental nowcast, and index/passive flow. The reason they're slow is not stupidity — it's that assembling this requires harmonizing 15 separate nonprofit compliance utilities, each with its own website, coverage-code taxonomy, and date convention, with zero APIs. It is unglamorous plumbing across a sector that receives a small fraction of alt-data budgets.
- **Information lead:** Verified empirically on 2026-08-14: FSLSO's monthly report already carries JULY 2026 — a ~10-15 day lag. SLTX likewise had July 2026 posted. So for a quarter ending June 30, you hold April data by ~mid-May, May by ~mid-June, June by ~mid-July. Kinsale reported Q2 2026 on July 23. That is a ~6-week lead on two-thirds of the quarter and a ~1-week lead on the complete Florida quarter, at carrier × coverage granularity, versus a market that has nothing. Against the only comparable public source — statutory state-page/Schedule T detail — the lead is 3-4 months, and that source arrives after the stock has already repriced. Against WSIA's semiannual stamping-office aggregate press release (H1 2026 released Aug 5), the lead is up to 6 months, and WSIA never publishes carrier or coverage splits at all. Against Ivans/CIAB/MarketScout, the lead on the aggregate is small but the granularity gap is total: they have no carrier-level series to lead you on.
- **Why still under-exploited:** It is not sold by anyone. Searching the alt-data ecosystem (vendor catalogs, hedge-fund alt-data guides, AlternativeData.org) surfaces zero stamping-office products — the recognized categories are card transactions, geolocation, web traffic, satellite. Insurance is an under-served alt-data sector generally. The data is published as a regulatory/tax byproduct for member brokers, state DOIs, and trade-press headlines, not for investors: WSIA aggregates it twice a year for a press release, and each office puts out marketing-flavored PDFs. Nobody has built the carrier × coverage × month panel because the work is deliberately unrewarding — 15 independent nonprofits, each a different stack (FSLSO an ASP.NET dashboard, SLTX static PDFs where per-insurer detail is annual-only and must be recovered by differencing YTD files, SLA-CAL a JS dashboard, ELANY annual PDFs), each with a bespoke coverage taxonomy needing hand-mapping, and each using a different timestamp semantic (submitted vs. registered vs. processed date) that must be reconciled or the months don't line up. The commercially available substitutes (Ivans, CIAB, MarketScout, AM Best, Conning) all stop at aggregate and are therefore useless for single-name work. It is fragmented, manual, boring, and public — the ideal profile.
- **Rough +EV:** Leg 1: ~25-35 tradeable earnings events per year across 6-9 E&S-levered names. KNSL's average absolute one-day earnings move runs ~8-10%; the smaller names ~5-8%. Realistic chain: the stacked-state signal calls the sign of the GWP growth surprise ~60-65% of the time, and the GWP surprise sign explains the move sign ~70% of the time, netting ~57-62% directional accuracy. On an ~8% average move that is ~+1.0 to +1.9% gross expected per event outright, less slippage; the pair-hedged version has similar raw EV but roughly half the variance, so the Sharpe is where the value sits. Sized at ~15% notional per event, that is a low-single-digit annual contribution on total capital as a standalone sleeve, but genuinely uncorrelated with everything else in a book. Leg 2 carries the larger dollars: a 3-month-negative premium-per-item trigger on FL/CA commercial property would have put you underweight the E&S property complex through Kinsale's ~37% drawdown, a multi-quarter move worth far more than any single print. Costs are trivial — the data is free; the build is roughly 2-4 weeks of engineering plus ongoing taxonomy maintenance.
- **Confidence:** Medium. The data's existence, granularity, freeness, and ~2-week lag are directly verified, and the absence of any competing carrier-level product is verified. The biggest uncertainty is BOOK COVERAGE AND CONFOUNDED INTENT: FL+CA+TX capture maybe 25-40% of a national E&S carrier's premium, and the residual can move the other way in the same quarter. Worse, a state-level property decline can be a deliberate, already-telegraphed CAT-management retrenchment rather than a demand or rate signal — which is precisely what Kinsale has been doing (property -32.7% while ex-property grew +3.7%), so raw premium would have given a false read. That is the trap. The mitigations are to work at coverage-code level so property retrenchment is separated from casualty growth, and to lean on premium-per-item (rate) rather than raw premium, since rate is the one variable management cannot simply choose. Secondary uncertainties: whether FSLSO's tool truly cross-tabs insurer × coverage × month or only offers those as separate one-dimensional views (still valuable if the latter, since insurer × month alone nowcasts state GWP); and paper-attribution noise for carriers using fronting arrangements (Bowhead) versus clean single-paper writers (Kinsale, NAIC 38920). Backtest 8-12 quarters of the panel against reported segment GWP before sizing anything.

## 91. The B-Case Roster

**Arena:** financial-market (event-driven equities: US small/mid-cap + Swiss/EU-listed CDMOs; expressed in cash equity and listed options)
**Domain:** GRANULAR TRADE AND CUSTOMS MICRODATA. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** U.S. Foreign-Trade Zones Board "Notification of Proposed Production Activity" dockets (case numbers [B-xx-YYYY]) filed under 15 CFR 400.22/400.37, plus their sibling documents: Authorization, *Limited* Authorization, scope expansion, and — the money document — Withdrawal.

The alpha is not the notice title, which is a bland parenthetical like "(Medications)" or "(Peptides)". It is the run-on list buried in the body. Because 15 CFR 400.14 limits FTZ authority to the *specific* foreign-status components and *specific* finished products described, every filer must publish an exact, legally binding bill of materials and product roster for a plant before it is allowed to make anything there. Two live examples I pulled:

- [B-86-2026], PolyPeptide Laboratories Inc., FTZ 202, Torrance CA (received 7/13/26, published 7/21/26). Finished products: "liraglutide, sodium; nectin; linaclotide; and peptides." Components include Fmoc-Lys(Mtt)-OH, Boc-His(Trt)-Ala-Glu(OtBu)-Gly-OH, 2-CTC Resin, MBH-Br Resin, Rink Amide-MBHA Resin, and "O(6)-NPE-N(2)-iBu protected G PMO Monomer." That roster is a commercial-scale solid-phase peptide line *plus* a phosphorodiamidate-morpholino (antisense oligo) line, with a GLP-1 (liraglutide) and a Linzess molecule (linaclotide) named outright. PolyPeptide Group AG is listed (SIX: PPGN) and never names customer molecules in its own reporting.
- [B-100-2026], Viatris Pharmaceuticals LLC, FTZ 61, Vega Baja PR (received 7/30/26): a complete SKU census of the plant — Ibrance, Lorbrena, Vizimpro, Xeljanz XR, Lipitor, Lyrica, Celebrex — plus the API sourcing structure (palbociclib tablets, talazoparib tablets, lorlatinib tablets as *imported inputs*).
- [B-57-2026] Withdrawal, Foxx Development, Inc., FTZ 153, San Diego (docketed 5/27/26, published 6/5/26; withdrawal requested 8/6/26, published 8/11/26). Foxx Development Holdings trades on Nasdaq as FOXX; its entire equity narrative is Made-in-USA smartphone assembly. It quietly killed the filing 10 weeks in.
- **How to collect it:** All free, all sanctioned, all public.

1. Poll the Federal Register JSON API daily, agency-filtered:
`https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/documents.json?conditions[agencies][]=foreign-trade-zones-board&order=newest&fields[]=title&fields[]=publication_date&fields[]=raw_text_url`
Volume is tiny and tractable: 102 (2023), 95 (2024), 93 (2025), 131 YTD-2026 production notifications, plus authorizations and withdrawals — roughly 200-250 documents/yr total.

2. Get an extra 1-2 calendar days by polling the public-inspection endpoint instead, which posts documents at 8:45am ET before publication:
`https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/public-inspection-documents/current.json` (verified: a doc filed 2026-08-12 carried publication_date 2026-08-14).

3. Pull the body via `raw_text_url` (`/documents/full_text/text/YYYY/MM/DD/<docnum>.txt`). The federalregister.gov HTML front end 302s to an anti-bot page; the API and raw-text endpoints do not.

4. Deepen with OFIS, the Board's Online FTZ Information System: `https://ofis.trade.gov/ManufacturingDB` (verified HTTP 200) — searchable by company name and 6-digit HTSUS, holds the actual submitted notification letters (more detail than the FR summary) and full case history per zone/subzone back to 2009. Also `trade.gov/ftz-case-processing-times` for decision-latency drift.

5. Build the two crosswalks that are the actual moat: (a) filer legal entity → listed parent ("PolyPeptide Laboratories Inc."→PPGN.SW; "Patheon Pharmaceuticals Inc."/"Patheon API, Inc."→TMO; "PPL Healthcare dba Piramal Pharma Solutions"→PPLPHARMA.NS; "Viatris Pharmaceuticals LLC"→VTRS) — no ticker appears anywhere in the document; and (b) INN/reagent → program → issuer, using the FDA Orange Book/Purple Book, ANDA filings, and a chemist's read on reagent classes (2-CTC/MBHA resin = commercial SPPS; PMO monomer = morpholino oligo; phosphoramidites = siRNA/ASO; ADC linkers; ionizable lipids = LNP).
- **The bet / trade:** Event-driven equity, signal fires at the public-inspection posting (T+0), enter T+0 to T+2.

SHORT LEG (higher conviction, fatter payoff): buy 3-9 month out-of-the-money puts on, or short, US-listed micro/small caps whose equity story is a specific onshoring plant, when a **Withdrawal of Notification of Proposed Production Activity** posts for that plant. Hold 1-6 months, through the next two earnings prints. Live instance as of this week: FOXX (Foxx Development Holdings, Nasdaq, Russell Microcap) — withdrawal published 2026-08-11 for its San Diego smartphone line. Same trigger fired 2026-08-10 for Corvus Energy USA (Bellingham WA maritime battery). A downgrade of a full authorization to "Authorization of *Limited* Production Activity" is a weaker version of the same signal — it means a domestic producer filed an objecting comment and the Board carved the scope.

LONG LEG: buy the listed parent of a CDMO/API maker when a new notification's roster reveals a won commercial program the company has not disclosed — a named on-patent or newly-genericizing molecule, or a reagent set implying a new commercial modality. Hold 3-9 months into the next results/capital markets day. Live instance: long PPGN.SW on the 2026-07-21 Torrance roster (liraglutide + linaclotide + PMO monomer at commercial resin scale).

DERIVED LEG (slowest, largest): when a US generic manufacturer's roster names a molecule still under brand exclusivity, buy long-dated puts/put-spreads on the single-product brand owner sized into the LOE window, 6-18 months.
- **Mechanism:** The causal chain is statutory, not inferential.

1. 15 CFR 400.14: production activity in a foreign-trade zone may not be conducted without prior Board authorization, and the authority granted is limited to the exact components and finished products described in the notification. Most Puerto Rico pharma, much US auto and semiconductor assembly, and most tariff-arbitraging electronics assembly sits inside FTZs because of inverted-tariff and weekly-entry MPF economics. So to make a new product at those sites, the operator is legally compelled to publish what it will make, before it makes it.

2. The roster is a bill of materials, and a BOM is a commitment. A company does not tech-transfer, validate, and file for liraglutide unless a customer has contracted. Listing kilogram-scale 2-CTC and MBHA resins is commercial solid-phase synthesis, not bench chemistry. Listing a PMO monomer means a morpholino antisense program is going to commercial supply — which back-solves to a specific biotech's Phase 3/BLA confidence. Listing brand SKUs (Ibrance, Xeljanz XR) tells you exactly which plant carries which revenue, i.e. what breaks if that product moves, and where tariff-exposed API is concentrated.

3. Timing is fixed by regulation and runs ahead of revenue. Received → docketed and published in ~7-14 days → 40-45 day comment window → Board must act within 120 days of receipt → then validation, registration, qualification → commercial output typically 6-24 months later. The roster front-runs the P&L by design.

4. The withdrawal is the cleanest fact in the dataset, because filing costs money and reputational capital with the Board. A withdrawal means the project died or the arithmetic broke. And in 2025-26 the arithmetic broke often: the notices themselves state which components fall under Section 122/232/301, and those decisions force admission in privileged foreign status (19 CFR 146.41), which destroys the inverted-tariff benefit that justified the FTZ in the first place. A reshoring microcap that files and then withdraws has run the numbers and found onshoring uneconomic — the exact thesis-breaking fact — and disclosed it in a Commerce Department notice instead of an 8-K.
- **Who's on the other side:** Index and passive funds, retail momentum holders of reshoring narrative microcaps, and pharma generalists who model loss-of-exclusivity off ANDA-approval headlines.

Why they are slow, specifically:
- No sell-side analyst reads Foreign-Trade Zones Board notices. The FTZ Board is a tiny office inside ITA; its output is dry procedural notices signed by an Executive Secretary.
- Headline-level NLP misses it completely. The title payload is a generic parenthetical — "(Medications)", "(Peptides)", "(Pharmaceutical Products)", "(Smartphones)". The tradeable content is a semicolon-delimited chemical list in the body. RavenPack-style entity/event extraction on Federal Register headlines returns nothing usable.
- No ticker appears in the document, ever. Entity resolution is manual and genuinely hostile to automation: subsidiary legal names ("PPL Healthcare dba Piramal Pharma Solutions"), FTZ numbers instead of addresses, city-level geography.
- The domain mapping needs two rare skills in one seat. Turning "O(6)-NPE-N(2)-iBu protected G PMO Monomer; 2-CTC Resin; Fmoc-Lys(Mtt)-OH" into "commercial SPPS plus morpholino oligo line" needs a synthetic chemist. Turning "liraglutide" into a dated US generic-entry thesis needs an Orange Book analyst. Almost nobody has both plus a Federal Register scraper.
- The filer actively wants it quiet. This is a duty-savings compliance filing drafted by outside trade counsel; IR typically never sees it and has no obligation to press-release a withdrawal.
- The incumbent alt-data vendors are pointed the wrong way in time. Panjiva/ImportGenius/Descartes/Datamyne sell bills of lading — what already shipped. Kpler/Vortexa sell vessels in motion. Nobody sells "what this US plant is legally about to be allowed to start making." The only published guidance on using OFIS is a NAFTZ trade-association webinar for compliance officers benchmarking their own duty savings.
- **Information lead:** Layered, and the layers are very different sizes.

- vs Federal Register publication: 1-2 calendar days, from the public-inspection API (8:45am ET prior-day filing; verified a doc filed 8/12 with pub date 8/14).
- vs the CDMO's own disclosure of a program: 2-4 quarters. Peptide/oligo CDMOs essentially never name customer molecules; they report aggregate order book at H1/FY. The FTZ roster names the molecule.
- vs consensus on a generic entry: 6-18 months ahead of the ANDA approval or launch headline that normally reprices the brand.
- vs the market understanding a withdrawal: effectively unbounded, and this is the real edge. A microcap that withdraws a production notification typically files nothing. The market learns when guidance is cut or the plant quietly disappears from the deck — commonly 2-3 quarters later. Foxx docketed 2026-05-27 and withdrew 2026-08-06; the withdrawal notice published 2026-08-11 is, as far as I can tell, the only public record.
- vs revenue actually appearing: 6-24 months, because production is legally barred until the Board acts (≤120 days from receipt) and then still needs validation and qualification.
- **Why still under-exploited:** It is a genuinely orphaned dataset sitting in plain sight, and three separate frictions keep it that way.

Structural: no vendor productizes it. The trade-microdata industry is built entirely around shipment records — what crossed a border — because that maps cleanly to revenue nowcasting and sells easily. FTZ production authority is *forward intent*, sits in a different agency, has no shipment records attached, and offers no obvious per-quarter number to regress against. It has never been packaged. There is no API, no email alert for production notifications specifically, no bulk download; you must agency-filter the Federal Register API yourself and then scrape OFIS for the underlying letters.

Cognitive: the signal survives only if someone can read organic chemistry *and* pharma capital markets *and* write a scraper. The Torrance roster is worthless to a quant who cannot tell an Fmoc-protected amino acid from a resin, and worthless to a chemist who does not know PolyPeptide Laboratories Inc. rolls up to a SIX-listed small cap.

Temporal: the dataset only recently became rich. Pre-2018 these notices were about duty arbitrage on ordinary goods. Since the Section 232/301 and then 2025 IEEPA and pharma-tariff regimes, every notice now carries an explicit component-level statement of which inputs are tariff-exposed and under which authority — turning the corpus into a live, company-by-company census of who is genuinely onshoring versus who is merely narrating it, and (via withdrawals) exactly when the onshoring math failed. Filing volume jumped to 131 YTD-2026 from ~95/yr. That specific analytical value is roughly a year old and nobody has claimed it.

Honest caveat on novelty: FTZ Board dockets are well known to trade-compliance lawyers and FTZ operators, who mine OFIS to benchmark competitors' duty savings. What is unclaimed is the securities application — nobody has built the INN/reagent → program → issuer crosswalk.
- **Rough +EV:** Shots on goal are the binding constraint, not edge size.

Universe: ~200-250 FTZ Board documents/yr. Of those, maybe 25-40/yr map to a liquid listed issuer where the roster is materially informative, and 8-15/yr are high conviction.

Long leg (CDMO/API order-book confirmation), ~8-15 trades/yr: I'd estimate a 55-60% hit rate, winners +8-15% vs sector over 3-9 months, losers around -8%. Call it +3-5% expected alpha per trade, so roughly 30-60 bps of book-level alpha per name at typical sizing.

Short leg (withdrawal on a single-plant-story microcap), only ~3-8/yr but where most of the EV lives: when a reshoring narrative breaks, these names routinely draw down 30-60%. Even at a 45-50% hit rate with adverse moves of -20% (microcap squeeze risk, expensive borrow), long-dated puts are clearly the right vehicle — the payoff is convex, the trigger is a hard dated fact, and the market has no competing catalyst pulling attention to it. Expected +15-30% per option position, but only a handful of qualifying setups a year.

Blended: plausibly 4-10% annualized alpha on a market-neutral sleeve, capacity-constrained to roughly $20-80M by microcap liquidity and Swiss small-cap borrow. Build cost is trivial — one chemist plus one developer, ~2 months, then near-zero ongoing since every source is a free government endpoint. The strategy's problem is not cost or edge, it is that it fires a few dozen times a year.

Discount for the boring majority: a large share of notices are aftermarket A/C components and engine parts with no listed read-through. The screen has to be aggressive about discarding them.
- **Confidence:** Medium.

Biggest uncertainty is the attribution problem on the long leg. The roster tells you what a plant is *authorized* to make — not the volume, not the customer, not whether the line ever ramps. Trade counsel has every incentive to file broad, defensive rosters covering everything the site might conceivably produce over the authorization's life, because amending later is slow and production outside the listed scope is a violation. That means a meaningful fraction of "new molecule appears" signals are option value being reserved, not contracts being executed, and I have no way from the document alone to separate the two. A roster naming liraglutide is consistent with both a signed commercial supply agreement and a CDMO keeping its options open.

Secondary uncertainty, and it is real: the withdrawal signal is much cleaner in mechanism but the sample is tiny — a handful per year, of which only a fraction map to listed microcaps. With 3-8 events annually, this strategy could be entirely correct about the causal mechanism and still be statistically indistinguishable from noise for three to five years. Anyone running it should size it as a conviction overlay on a small number of high-quality setups, not as a systematic sleeve, and should not expect a backtest to settle the question.

Third: FTZ policy risk cuts both ways. If the 2025-26 tariff regime is unwound or FTZ privileged-foreign-status rules change, filing volume and the informational content of withdrawals both shift, and the historical base rate stops applying.

## 92. The 240-Day Shell

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** STRUCTURAL EXCLUSIONS where a legal rule routes an entire sector's data OUTSIDE the standard institutional feed (the No-PACER archetype). RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection — no anti-bot evasion, harvested credentials, pretextual identities, side channels

- **Data source:** The per-case "Procedural Details" timeline on ICSID's public case database (icsid.worldbank.org), cross-referenced to listed nano-cap claimants. Investor-state disputes are structurally barred from national courts: the ICSID Convention (Art. 26) plus BIT/NAFTA/CAFTA/ECT arbitration clauses and sovereign immunity strip domestic courts of jurisdiction, so a multi-billion-dollar class of corporate claims NEVER appears in PACER, SEDAR litigation feeds, state courts, or any docket product. The entire docket lives on a World Bank IGO website. Crucially, each case page publishes a dated, chronological procedural log — tribunal constitution, arbitrator disqualifications, each memorial/counter-memorial/reply/rejoinder, hearing dates, post-hearing briefs, cost statements/submissions, and "the Tribunal declares the proceeding closed." Verified live: ARB/23/14 (Suntech Power International v. Italy) shows the full ladder through "July 31, 2026 - Parties file cost statements." That last entry is the alpha: under the 2022 ICSID Arbitration Rules, AR 58(1) requires the award within 240 days of the last written submission; under the 2006 Rules, AR 38(1)/46 require it within 120 days of declared closure, extendable 60. So a free public webpage yields a legally-mandated award DEADLINE, computable months ahead, for a binary event that moves nano-caps 100-200% in a day.
- **How to collect it:** (1) Enumerate cases via https://icsid.worldbank.org/cases/pending and /cases/concluded; fetch each detail page at the verified URL pattern https://icsid.worldbank.org/cases/case-database/case-detail?CaseNo=ARB/23/14 . No login, no paywall, public IGO site — poll politely (a few req/min, honor robots.txt) and diff the procedural table daily; the diff IS the signal. (2) Mirror/complement with italaw.com (free open repository of ICSID pleadings, decisions and award PDFs — verified hosting e.g. the Silver Bull v. Mexico award) and UNCTAD's ISDS Navigator for structured outcome history. (3) For UNCITRAL/treaty cases administered outside ICSID, add the PCA case pages (pca-cpa.org). (4) Map claimants to tickers manually — this is the fragmented, hand-built part: claimants are named as opaque holding entities, so you resolve them via SEDAR+/EDGAR/ASX filings and company IR pages. (5) Pull tribunal composition from the same page and build arbitrator-level and respondent-state-level claimant win-rate priors from the italaw/UNCTAD outcome corpus. (6) Timestamp company disclosure (SEDAR+, EDGAR 8-K, ASX, RNS) to measure your realized lead per event.
- **The bet / trade:** Long a basket of listed ISDS claimants (TSXV/ASX/OTC/Nasdaq nano- and micro-caps whose treaty claim exceeds their market cap), entered the day the ICSID procedural log posts the award-clock trigger — "cost statements/submissions filed" or "proceeding declared closed." Two legs. PRIMARY (drift capture, higher Sharpe): hold ~3-6 months into the statutory window and exit into the pre-award anticipation run-up, before the award prints. This deliberately avoids the binary. SECONDARY (binary, smaller sizing): hold a minority of names through the award and sell into the T+0/T+1 print. Position sizing 3-8% per name, 12-20 names. Horizon: 120+60 days (2006 Rules cases) or 240 days (2022 Rules cases) from the trigger date, which the page tells you exactly. Same calendar logic applies to annulment and enforcement events — e.g. Gabriel Resources (TSXV: GBU / OTC: GBRRF), whose ad hoc committee annulment hearing was held May 11-12, 2026, putting a decision-clock on a pure claim-shell. Skip or fade names where the tribunal bifurcated and jurisdiction is already shaky, where the president has a strong pro-state record, or where the stock has already re-rated past ~25-30% of a realistic present value of the claim.
- **Mechanism:** These claimants are typically shells: the operating asset was expropriated, blockaded, or permit-denied years ago, so the arbitration claim IS the company. Market cap is a stale, deeply discounted option on an award whose timing the market treats as indefinite ("someday"). The legal rule that created the structural exclusion also created a hard statutory clock: once the last written submission is filed, AR 58(1) (2022) / AR 38+46 (2006) force the tribunal to sign the award inside a fixed window. So the moment ICSID posts "cost statements filed," the event moves from undated to dated. Dated binaries with claim-to-market-cap ratios of 5-40x re-rate on two channels: (a) mechanical option-value expansion as time-to-resolution collapses from "unknown" to "under 240 days," and (b) leakage-driven accumulation as counsel, funders, and holders position. Then the award prints and the stock gaps: Odyssey Marine (OMEX) +157% to +186% in a single session on its NAFTA award (Sept 18, 2024); Lupaka Gold (TSXV: LPK), a nano-cap, won ~US$65M from Peru with a negotiated payment schedule. The downside is symmetric and real: Silver Bull Resources (ARB/23/24) was dismissed on jurisdiction/prescription May 29, 2026; Gabriel Resources lost on the merits 2-1 and owed Romania ~US$10M in costs.
- **Who's on the other side:** Nobody with size is on the other side, which is the point. Sell-side does not cover $10-80M shells with no revenue. Quant and index capital cannot touch sub-$1, sub-$1M-ADV TSXV/OTC tickers. The people who genuinely understand this data — litigation funders like Burford, Omni Bridgeway, and Tenor (which funded Crystallex and Rusoro) — express the view by buying the CLAIM or funding the case, not the listed equity, and they are conflicted out of trading the issuer. The specialist information vendors (Jus Mundi, IAReporter, Global Arbitration Review, italaw) are legal-research products priced and marketed to arbitration counsel, not traders; they publish analysis of awards after issuance, and none of them ships an investor-facing "award due date" calendar. There is no Bloomberg field for ICSID award deadlines. The retail junior-mining channel (Junior Mining Network, INN, "Arbitration Award Update" newswires) reacts to the COMPANY's press release, which is downstream. And the issuers themselves are the slowest link: a TSXV shell has no obligation to announce that a tribunal received cost submissions or declared a proceeding closed — it is not a material change in their view — so the ICSID page routinely runs ahead of any company disclosure.
- **Information lead:** Two distinct leads. TIMING: weeks to several months. The ICSID procedural log posts hearing dates 6-18 months before an award and posts the last-submission/closure trigger typically 4-8 months before the award drops, while the issuer often never discloses that step at all — you hold a computable award deadline the tape does not have. EXISTENCE: effectively permanent for uncovered names — because the dispute is barred from every court system anyone screens, a $400M claim against a sovereign can sit invisible on a $20M shell for years with zero coverage. The narrow lead is on award day itself (companies do PR the award within hours), which is exactly why the primary leg exits before it. Measurable: backtest by diffing archived ICSID case pages (Wayback Machine) against SEDAR+/EDGAR/ASX release timestamps across 30-50 resolved cases to quantify the realized lead per event before committing capital.
- **Why still under-exploited:** The structural exclusion is doubled. First, the legal rule: treaty arbitration plus sovereign immunity routes this entire sector's litigation outside every docket feed institutions consume — there is no PACER analogue, no state court aggregator, no Docket Alarm coverage. Second, the data's shape defeats commercialization: there is no ICSID API, no RSS, no bulk export; the pending-case list has no filter or download; procedural detail lives one page at a time behind a CaseNo query parameter and is poorly search-indexed; and claimants are named as opaque holding entities that must be hand-mapped to tickers across SEDAR+, ASX, and EDGAR. The commercial products that do exist (Jus Mundi, IAReporter, GAR, Lexis) are sold to lawyers for legal research and deliberately do not compute or publish award-deadline calendars. And the tradable universe — maybe 15-30 listed claimants where the claim exceeds market cap — is far too small and illiquid to support a data vendor, which is precisely why one has not been built. It is fragmented, manual, and free: the profile a small team can own and a large firm cannot justify.
- **Rough +EV:** Fires roughly 10-20 tradable times per year out of ~350+ pending ICSID cases (~40-70 with a listed claimant/parent; ~15-30 nano/micro-caps where the claim exceeds market cap). Primary drift-capture leg: entering 4-8 months ahead of a statutorily-deadlined binary in a $10-80M shell and exiting into anticipation; historical run-ups of 25-100%+ into award dates with maybe a 55-65% hit rate implies roughly +10-20% expected per event on a 3-6 month hold. At 12-18 events/year and 5-8% sizing, plausibly +8-20%/yr on the sleeve, with high variance and material drawdowns. Secondary binary leg is arithmetically fatter but far softer: ISDS claimant success runs ~30-40%, with another ~20-25% settling or discontinuing (often favorably); at 35% win (+180%) / 20% settle (+30%) / 45% loss (-55%) the naive per-event EV is about +44%, but I would haircut that to +10-25% because (a) a "win" is not cash — enforcement against Venezuela, Argentina, or Romania can take a decade or fail, (b) states routinely file annulment applications that stay payment, and (c) my win-rate and payoff inputs are estimates, not a backtest. Capacity is the binding constraint: probably $2-10M of total sleeve before slippage eats the edge.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Biggest uncertainty: leakage and liquidity acting together. In a $20M shell with three market makers, counsel, funders, and large holders plausibly know the award clock too, so some of the drift may already be in the price by the time ICSID posts — and even if it is not, exit slippage on a nano-cap gapping 150% is brutal and may consume much of the modeled edge. Secondary uncertainties: whether the ICSID page update consistently precedes company disclosure (testable, and the required first step — diff archived case pages against SEDAR+/EDGAR timestamps on 30-50 resolved cases before deploying), whether ICSID updates its procedural log promptly and uniformly across cases rather than in batches, and enforcement risk turning wins into paper. What I am confident about is that the data source is real, free, sanctioned, verified, and genuinely unpackaged: I confirmed the dated procedural ladder on a live case page, confirmed the AR 58(1) 240-day and AR 38/46 120+60-day clocks, and confirmed the payoff magnitude on OMEX, Lupaka, Silver Bull, and Gabriel.

## 93. The Pari-Mutuel Blind Spot

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** DEFINITIONAL EXCLUSIONS in official statistics that hide real activity. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** Monthly, facility-level Historical Horse Racing (HHR) handle and licensee-retained revenue published by three state RACING/LOTTERY regulators — not gaming commissions. HHR is legally pari-mutuel wagering, so it is definitionally excluded from every headline gaming statistic (the AGA Commercial Gaming Revenue Tracker states it excludes pari-mutuel horse racing and non-casino gaming; state gaming-board monthly revenue files never contain it; NAICS splits it into 711212 racetracks, not 7132 casinos). Roughly $10B+/yr of slot-like play is therefore invisible in "US commercial gaming revenue" — while being the single largest EBITDA line of a $5-8B Nasdaq mid-cap. Churchill Downs' Live & Historical Racing segment: $1.44B revenue and $637.0M adjusted EBITDA in FY2025 (+10.9% y/y), i.e. more than half of company EBITDA, essentially all of it KY + VA HHR plus New Hampshire.
- **How to collect it:** Three separate, fragmented, manual pulls, none of which appear in any commercial gaming dataset: (1) KENTUCKY, fastest leg — KRS 138.510 imposes a 1.5% excise on all money wagered on historical horse races, and HHR is ~82% of Kentucky pari-mutuel tax revenue. The "Pari-Mutuel" line item sits in the monthly "Kentucky State Government Revenue" memo from the Office of the State Budget Director, posted as a committee document to the LRC Interim Joint Committee on Appropriations & Revenue at apps.legislature.ky.gov/CommitteeDocuments (e.g. "CFG 121422 November Receipts.pdf"), ~10-14 days after month end. Divide the monthly pari-mutuel line by the blended effective rate to back out statewide HHR handle. Cross-check and get facility detail from KHRGC monthly commission meeting packets at khrc.ky.gov/Documents/ (e.g. "Pages from 2025-2-11 KHRGC Materials FINAL.pdf") and the archived Pari-Mutuel Wagering Reports at khrc.ky.gov/new_docs.aspx?cat=76. (2) VIRGINIA, best-quality leg — Va. Code Sec. 59.1-392 requires the Virginia Racing Commission to report MONTHLY to the Chairs of House Appropriations and Senate Finance on HHR gross gaming revenue "from any significant infrastructure limited licensee facility and each satellite facility licensee," with total prize payout, purse contributions, state/local tax by jurisdiction, amount retained by the VRC, and amount retained by licensee/operator. These land in the General Assembly's Reports to the General Assembly repository at rga.lis.virginia.gov (search "Virginia Racing Commission Monthly Pari-Mutuel Wagering Report"; e.g. RD153/2025 for the month ended 9/30/2024; RD519/2022; RD359/2022) and on vrc.virginia.gov plus monthly VRC meeting packets. Every Virginia HHR licensee is Churchill Downs (Colonial Downs / Rosie's / The Rose), so this is a clean, unmixed read on one issuer, and it reports amounts RETAINED — i.e. near-revenue, not just handle. (3) NEW HAMPSHIRE — NH Lottery Commission monthly charitable-gaming reports break out "historic horse racing" separately from VLT and games of chance (June 2026: $10,343,417 HHR vs $21,643,774 VLT vs $10,387,629 games of chance), ~2-3 weeks after month end. Build: monthly scrape of the three sources into a facility-level panel, then a handle-to-reported-revenue bridge calibrated on ~12 prior quarters of CHDN segment disclosures (KY needs a hold-rate model; VA gives retained dollars directly).
- **The bet / trade:** Churchill Downs Incorporated (NASDAQ: CHDN). Two legs. (A) Event leg: build the KY+VA+NH HHR nowcast for the quarter, take a directional position 2-3 weeks before the quarterly print, held through the release — long stock or ~1-month at-the-money calls when the nowcast implies Live & Historical Racing revenue above consensus, short stock / puts when below. Roughly 4 events per year; CHDN reported Q2 2026 on 7/29/26, so entry is early-to-mid month of the reporting month. (B) Structural leg, 1-2 quarters: when the facility-level panel shows a NEW venue cannibalizing an existing one (Owensboro/Ellis vs Louisville; The Rose Dumfries vs Rosie's Richmond) or a competing Virginia casino draining a specific Rosie's, put on the short 3-6 months ahead of management conceding it on a call, and reverse when the panel shows a genuine incremental ramp that the Street is modeling as cannibalization.
- **Mechanism:** HHR machines are slot machines in behavior and economics but pari-mutuel wagering in law. That legal classification is what creates both the blind spot and the data: because HHR is pari-mutuel, it is (a) omitted from every gaming-revenue statistic the sector's analysts consume, and (b) simultaneously subject to racing-commission and state-revenue reporting mandates that are far MORE granular than anything a gaming commission publishes — Virginia's statute compels facility-by-facility disclosure of the licensee's retained take. HHR handle mechanically drives CHDN's revenue (handle x hold), and Live & Historical Racing is >50% of CHDN adjusted EBITDA at ~44% segment margins, so segment revenue surprises pass through to EPS and to the stock with high beta. In FY2025 the entire segment EBITDA gain decomposed into Kentucky HHR venues (+$41.4M) and Virginia HHR venues (+$18.7M) — the two states you can read monthly. The chain is: monthly state pari-mutuel tax receipts and VRC retained-revenue filings -> statewide and facility HHR handle -> segment revenue -> EBITDA -> the print and the multi-quarter narrative about whether the new-build program is incremental or cannibalizing.
- **Who's on the other side:** Gaming/leisure long-onlys and hedge funds who track monthly state gaming revenue religiously — but from GAMING commissions (Nevada GCB, PA, NJ, MI, OH) and from monthly-revenue aggregators built on those same standardized feeds. HHR is structurally absent from all of them because it is not casino gaming. Sell-side models Live & Historical Racing off management guidance, unit counts, and prior-quarter run-rate, not off measured handle. Retail and quant flow have no HHR input at all. The people who DO see the data are the wrong audience: it lives in a state budget office's revenue memo circulated to a legislative appropriations committee, in a racing commission's board packet PDF, and in a state General Assembly's "Reports to the General Assembly" document repository — read by legislators, horsemen's associations, and the racing trade press (BloodHorse covers Kentucky's aggregate handle in occasional articles, months late, with no facility split and no revenue mapping). Nobody in that chain is trading CHDN, and nobody trading CHDN is reading a Virginia RD document. The Street is slow for a structural reason, not a lazy one: the data is in three states, three formats, three different agency types, all PDFs, and requires a handle-to-revenue bridge to be useful.
- **Information lead:** Against the quarterly earnings print: month 1 of a quarter is knowable ~10-14 days after it closes via the Kentucky pari-mutuel tax line, i.e. roughly 10 weeks before the release; month 2 roughly 6 weeks before; and by ~2-3 weeks before the print you hold measured (not modeled) data on 65-100% of the quarter's HHR revenue driver, including Virginia licensee-retained dollars that are close to booked revenue. Against the narrative — the more valuable lead — facility-level cannibalization and competitive-casino cannibalization show up in the VRC monthly facility panel within ~4-6 weeks of the month it happens, versus 1-3 quarters before management characterizes it on a call or a 10-Q segment discussion admits it. Against the sector's own headline statistic there is effectively infinite lead: the AGA tracker will never contain this activity at all.
- **Why still under-exploited:** This is not a product anyone sells. Every commercial monthly-gaming-revenue dataset is built by scraping state GAMING commission releases; HHR is definitionally outside that universe, so it is outside those products by construction. There is no HHR API, no consolidated file, and no vendor covering it — Kentucky data must be reverse-engineered from a tax line in a legislative committee PDF or dug out of a commission board packet, Virginia's data must be found in a state legislature's report repository rather than on any regulator's data page, and New Hampshire's sits inside a charitable-gaming report next to bingo and games of chance. The three sources use different units (handle vs. retained revenue vs. revenue), so they are not even summable without a calibrated bridge. The category is also new and growing fast enough that coverage habits have not caught up: Virginia HHR only started in 2019, New Hampshire authorized HHR in 2021, and CHDN was still opening venues through 2024-2025 (The Rose in Dumfries, Owensboro, Emporia). Meanwhile the material fact — that a segment excluded from the industry's headline statistic is now the majority of a well-covered mid-cap's EBITDA — has quietly become true without the data plumbing following.
- **Rough +EV:** Event leg: CHDN typically moves 5-10% on quarterly prints. If the nowcast captures ~70-80% of the variance in Live & Historical Racing revenue, and that segment drives roughly half the earnings surprise, expected directional edge is on the order of 2-4% per event before costs, fired ~4x/year — call it 8-15%/yr of alpha on a directional stock position, materially more if expressed in short-dated options where a correctly-signed 6-8% move against a ~5% implied is heavily convex, though option premium erodes much of the raw edge in the quarters where the nowcast is only mildly off consensus. Structural leg fires ~1-2x/year (a new-venue cannibalization inflection or a competing-casino hit to a named Rosie's) and is where the fat tail lives: those are 15-25% multi-quarter repricings that you would be sitting on 1-3 quarters early. Blended honest expectation: high-single to low-double-digit annual alpha on a concentrated single-name sleeve, capacity-limited to roughly $20-50M given CHDN liquidity, with the caveat that the win rate is well under 100% because non-HHR items can swamp the read in any single quarter.
- **Confidence:** Medium. The data unambiguously exists, is legally mandated, is free, is monthly, is facility-level in Virginia, and covers the majority of the company's EBITDA — that part is verified, not assumed. The single biggest uncertainty is the handle-to-reported-revenue bridge: Kentucky publishes handle (or a tax line proxying handle) while CHDN books handle x hold, and hold rates drift with game mix and with CHDN's push toward higher-hold products, so a correct handle call can still produce a wrong revenue call. Secondary risk is that the HHR read, however good, gets swamped in a given quarter by Derby-week economics, the separate Gaming segment, Exacta third-party revenue, one-time charges, or buyback timing — meaning the event leg needs to be sized as one input among several rather than as a standalone signal, and the structural leg is probably where the durable edge actually is. Third risk: Kentucky's pari-mutuel tax line includes non-HHR wagering and its allocation formulas have been legislatively amended, so the rate calibration needs periodic re-fitting against the KHRGC handle reports.
