## 94. The Garnishee's Confession

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** STATE AND LOCAL COURT SYSTEMS as an alternative distress feed. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned public dockets

- **Data source:** The garnishee's sworn answer in post-judgment garnishment proceedings in state trial and magistrate courts — not the underlying lawsuit, but the document the *bank* is compelled to file. In most states garnishment is a separate ancillary suit filed against the bank, and the bank must answer under oath within 20-30 days stating exactly what it holds for the judgment debtor. Maryland's form DC-CV-61 ("Garnishee's Confession of Assets") requires the bank to list account type, account number, amount held, exempt amounts, and balance subject to garnishment. Texas TRCP 665 requires the garnishee to answer under oath "what, if anything, you are indebted to the said [debtor], and were when this writ was served... and what effects, if any, of the said [debtor] you have in your possession." Georgia (OCGA ch. 18-4) makes it a standalone action with an answer due in 30 days, default at 45. Missouri Rule 90.07 / form CV110 "Interrogatories to Garnishee" compels the bank to list and describe the property subject to garnishment. Three payloads fall out of these answers: (1) the literal dollar balance in a private company's operating account on a dated day; (2) which bank it banks at, and when that changes; (3) when the bank refuses to turn over funds by asserting setoff or a perfected security interest / deposit account control agreement, the answer names the secured party and effectively date-stamps the moment cash dominion sprung. Cross-referenced against the named portfolio companies in publicly traded BDCs' 10-Q Schedules of Investments, this is a real-time solvency probe on companies whose only other disclosure is a manager-set quarterly mark.
- **How to collect it:** Two halves, both doable by a small team. SENSOR SIDE — state portals, all free or near-free: re:SearchTX at research.txcourts.gov (statewide, free registered account, civil e-filing mandatory in all 254 Texas counties since 2014; index search free, document pulls carry per-page fees), plus Harris County District Clerk (hcdistrictclerk.com) and Dallas (courtsportal.dallascounty.org) directly; Maryland Judiciary Case Search (casesearch.courts.state.md.us) — free, District Court garnishment cases, pull the DC-CV-61; PeachCourt (peachcourt.com) for Fulton/Gwinnett/Cobb/DeKalb magistrate and superior garnishments; Missouri Case.net (courts.mo.gov/casenet) — free statewide, Rule 90 garnishment filings; Florida county clerk portals (myorangeclerk, Broward, Hillsborough) for Ch. 77 "Answer of Garnishee"; then Ohio, Tennessee, Arizona and Clark County NV portals. Key scraping trick: the debtor's name is often NOT in the case caption — venue frequently follows the garnishee bank, so the case reads "Plaintiff v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., Garnishee." So build the REVERSE index: query each portal for civil cases where a party is one of ~20 banks (JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, BofA, PNC, Truist, Fifth Third, Comerica, East West, Cadence, Amegy/Zions) with case type "Garnishment," then OCR the writ and answer PDFs to extract the debtor name and the disclosed balance. UNIVERSE SIDE — pull every listed and non-traded BDC's 10-Q/10-K Schedule of Investments from SEC EDGAR (sec-api.io has a BDC Schedule-of-Investments parser, or parse the XBRL/HTML directly) to get ~3,500-4,000 named positions across ~2,000 distinct operating companies with fair values and non-accrual flags. Bridge the two with entity resolution: BDC holdco/deal names ("Project Ruby Buyer, LLC") map to operating subsidiaries via state Secretary of State registries, assumed-name/DBA filings, and UCC-1 debtor names (which conveniently also confirm the secured lender's identity for cross-checking the setoff assertion).
- **The bet / trade:** Short (or buy 2-4 month puts on) the common equity of the specific small/mid-cap BDC holding the flagged portfolio company, against a long in BIZD or an equal-dollar basket of BDCs with zero garnishment hits — a market- and rate-neutral pair. Entry trigger: the second independent garnishment writ against the same portfolio company within two quarters, OR a single answer showing near-zero balance / asserted setoff on the operating account of a company with $100M+ revenue. Size to the position's weight in NAV; only act where the flagged name is >=2% of the BDC's NAV. Hold through the next one to two 10-Q prints — 2 to 6 months — and cover on the non-accrual/markdown disclosure or after two clean quarters. Secondary expression for cluster events (3+ flagged names in one BDC): short the BDC's baby bonds/unsecured notes alongside, which reprice on leverage-coverage fear.
- **Mechanism:** Liquidity at a mid-market borrower tightens, so it stretches trade vendors past 90 days. Vendors sue for $25k-$400k in state or magistrate court and take default judgments — the company doesn't defend, because it can't pay. Collection counsel identifies the operating bank from checks it previously received and serves a writ of garnishment on that bank. The bank is now legally compelled to make a sworn public statement about the company's cash, and each possible answer is diagnostic. If it reports near-zero on the operating account of a company doing nine figures of revenue, the account is being swept daily into a lender-controlled concentration account — cash dominion is already on. If it refuses to turn over funds by asserting setoff or a perfected security interest under a control agreement, it names the secured party and dates the moment the springing DACA tripped, which means a covenant or availability trigger was breached weeks earlier. If it simply discloses a balance, you have a literal dated cash figure on a private company, and repeated writs give you a burn series. Clustering is the real signature: three writs from unrelated creditors inside two quarters means the company is triaging payables, which reliably precedes forbearance, amend-and-extend, PIK conversion, or a restructuring. The BDC that holds the loan eventually marks it down and moves it to non-accrual in a 10-Q, which cuts NAV, raises dividend-coverage doubt, and de-rates the price-to-NAV multiple. You bought the docket six months before the multiple moved.
- **Who's on the other side:** BDC common holders, who in small-cap names are 40-60% retail income buyers screening on dividend yield and price-to-NAV. Alongside them: BIZD and other mechanical market-cap-weighted vehicles that hold regardless of credit; sell-side analysts who model net investment income and dividend coverage rather than borrower-level credit; and third-party valuation firms (Houlihan Lokey, KBRA, Lincoln) that mark positions off DCF and comparable-yield inputs built from manager-supplied financials. None of these read a Georgia magistrate court garnishee answer. They are slow structurally, not lazily: the only credit disclosure that exists is quarterly, it is self-reported by a manager whose fee-earning assets and dividend coverage both shrink when a loan goes on non-accrual, and it is validated by a valuation process whose inputs the manager supplies. Honest caveat: the direct lender itself is NOT slow — it has monthly reporting and it is the party on the control agreement. The lead is over the BDC's public equity, not over the credit.
- **Information lead:** The garnishee's answer is docketed 20-30 days after service and is visible on the portal same-day or next-day. The BDC discloses non-accrual status at quarter-end plus 40-45 days in the 10-Q, and the non-accrual designation itself is manager-discretionary and typically lags actual payment distress by one to two quarters. Net lead over the public disclosure: 3 to 9 months. Lead over trade press (Octus/9fin/Bloomberg), which picks these up only once restructuring advisors are formally engaged: 1 to 4 weeks, occasionally a full quarter. Lead over a diligent credit desk monitoring PACER, UCC filings, and news: still real, because none of those sources contain the garnishment ancillary — PACER has no state-court content, UCC-1s show the lender's original perfection rather than the trip event, and vendor suits alone don't tell you whether the cash is already gone.
- **Why still under-exploited:** Structural invisibility, not obscurity. Garnishment is an ancillary proceeding with its own case number, usually in a small-dollar magistrate or justice court, and venue commonly follows the garnishee bank's county rather than the debtor's — so the interesting party name is frequently absent from the case caption entirely and appears only inside the writ and answer PDFs. Every caption-level litigation scraper (UniCourt, Trellis, Docket Alarm, Lex Machina) therefore misses it by design, not by oversight. The judgments involved are $25k-$500k, well below the relevance thresholds those vendors optimize for. The actual payload lives in a scanned or fillable state form (DC-CV-61, CV110), not in structured docket metadata, so it requires OCR plus per-state form parsing. There is no federal mirror to shortcut through. And the final link — private LLC operating entity to a specific line item in a BDC's Schedule of Investments — is manual entity resolution that no commercial vendor performs at scale. Adjacent products do exist and I want to be honest about them: trade-credit tools like Credit Pulse now score private companies on "legal escalation" using caption-level lawsuit counts, and BDC analytics shops track disclosed non-accruals. But nobody is reading the garnishee's answer specifically as a bank-balance and DACA-trip sensor, and nobody is routing that read into a listed-equity trade. The gap is the interpretation and the plumbing, both of which are tedious enough to have deterred everyone with capital to deploy.
- **Rough +EV:** Funnel: ~2,000 distinct BDC portfolio operating companies; roughly 30-40% have a garnishable footprint in a covered state with usable online dockets. Expect ~10-25 fresh garnishment hits per quarter across the universe, of which ~8-15 are on names not already disclosed as non-accrual, and ~4-8 are concentrated enough (>=2% of one BDC's NAV) to trade. Conditional probability that a flagged name suffers a >=20-point markdown, non-accrual, or restructuring within 2-3 quarters: I'd estimate 45-60%, against an unconditional base rate near 6-8% — call it a 5-7x lift, and even a pessimistic 35% conditional keeps the lift above 4x. Payoff: on the equity pair, a flagged name at 2-4% of NAV going non-accrual with a 40-point markdown is a 0.8-1.6% direct NAV hit, but the de-rate is the bigger move — small BDCs surprising on credit typically drop 4-9% over the print and the following week. Running 4-8 pairs per quarter with a ~50% hit rate and roughly 6% average gross move on the winners nets, after borrow costs and the ~1-2% of stubborn false positives that rip higher, an estimated 3-6% annualized alpha on deployed capital at a Sharpe around 0.5-0.8. Options are the higher-variance expression: maybe 30-40% of put trades pay 2-5x, implying +20-40% EV per trade, but BDC option chains are thin with 10-20% wide spreads and slippage plausibly eats half of that, so stock is the default. Real frictions to price in: several of the most attractive small BDCs are hard-to-borrow at 5-15% rebate, and document-download fees on Texas plus OCR compute run maybe $2-6k/quarter. Setup cost is roughly one engineer-quarter for the scrapers and entity-resolution layer.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Biggest uncertainty by far is entity resolution: BDC Schedules of Investments name holdcos and deal vehicles ("Project Ruby Buyer, LLC") while garnishments hit operating subsidiaries and DBAs under entirely different trade names, and if that bridge resolves at 30% rather than 70% the funnel collapses to a handful of tradeable signals per year — too few to be a strategy, though still valuable as an overlay. Second and nearly as serious: the credit read can be right while the price event never happens, because managers can smooth marks and park a deteriorating name in a "restructured, still accruing" bucket indefinitely, deferring or entirely muting the NAV print you're trading against. Third, smaller: portal coverage is uneven and several magistrate courts still gate documents behind in-person clerk requests, which caps geographic breadth. A cheap 90-day validation exists — backfill 2023-2025 garnishment filings against BDC portfolio companies that subsequently went non-accrual and measure the actual lead time and conditional hit rate before committing capital.

## 95. The Juncos Manifest

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** JURISDICTIONS OUTSIDE FEDERAL DATA COLLECTION. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** Puerto Rico's MONTHLY tariff-line file of merchandise shipments from Puerto Rico to the U.S. mainland, published by the Instituto de Estadísticas de Puerto Rico ("Comercio Externo"). Specifically the implantable-device Schedule B/HTS lines: 9021.50 (pacemakers), 9021.90 (other implants incl. ICD/CRT and leads), 9018.90 (catheters), 9021.31/9021.39 (joints, valves), plus HS 30 pharma lines as a cross-check. The structural point: 15 CFR 30.2 REQUIRES AES/EEI filing on PR-to-mainland shipments, so Census collects this monthly at 10-digit detail — but publishes it only ONCE A YEAR, in the FT895 "U.S. Trade with Puerto Rico and U.S. Possessions" report, ~12-15 months late. It is absent from the monthly FT900 release, from USA Trade Online's headline monthly product, from FRED, and from every manifest-based commercial trade dataset. The territory is the only entity publishing it monthly. Puerto Rico produces ~90% of the world's pacemakers: Medtronic's Juncos/Villalba plants build implantable pacemakers, ICDs, CRT devices and catheters; Boston Scientific's Dorado plant builds 100% of BSX's CRM and neuromodulation leads.
- **How to collect it:** estadisticas.pr → "Aplicaciones" tab → Comercio Externo interface (Firefox recommended; the site 503s intermittently, so cache aggressively). Filter: flow = exports/shipments, destination = Estados Unidos, classification = Schedule B (or HTS), frequency = monthly, back to July 2002; pull BOTH value and physical quantity, plus port and mode. Download CSV; a small scraper on a monthly cron is enough. Cross-references: jp.pr.gov/comercio-exterior (Junta de Planificación summary tables), DDEC's Puerto Rico Data Center industry profiles (docs.pr.gov — "Puerto Rico's Medical Devices Profile"), and census.gov FT895 annual reports for level/revision calibration. Critically, also pull PR→FOREIGN exports of the same HS lines from Census USA Trade Online (those ARE published monthly) and subtract, so you isolate the U.S.-bound leg — the world-bound leg is visible to everyone, the mainland leg is not.
- **The bet / trade:** Signal: 3-month moving average of PR→mainland shipped QUANTITY on the implantable-cardiac-device lines, detrended vs. trailing 12 months and net of the PR→foreign leg. On a ≥1 SD acceleration: buy puts / short Medicare-Advantage-levered payers (HUM primary; UNH, ELV, CVS secondary) and pair long MDT / BSX. Enter 2-6 weeks before the payer's quarterly report, hold through the print — 4-10 week horizon. On ≥1 SD deceleration, reverse the pair (long payers / fade med-tech). Simplest single-leg expression for smaller books: MDT or BSX call spreads bought into their quarterly print on acceleration, put spreads on deceleration.
- **Mechanism:** Physical devices leave Juncos/Villalba/Dorado weeks before they are implanted — they move into mainland distribution and hospital consignment inventory, then into a patient. So the PR→mainland flow is an upstream physical census of upcoming U.S. implant procedures. Implant recipients skew heavily 65+, i.e. Medicare Advantage members. Chain: rising PR device flow → rising U.S. implant volume → higher MA medical utilization → medical loss ratio comes in above the bid actuaries priced → payer misses and cuts guidance. The same flow simultaneously means CRM unit beats at Medtronic (Cardiac Rhythm & Heart Failure) and Boston Scientific. The 2023-25 MA blowups (Humana Jan-2024, UNH Apr-2024 and Apr-2025) were driven precisely by unexpected senior procedure volume — outpatient orthopedic and cardiac. Nobody was watching the boxes leave the island.
- **Who's on the other side:** Three slow counterparties. (1) MA actuaries: they set next-year bids each June off claims data that is 12+ months stale, and their own in-quarter claims run 1-3 months incomplete — they are structurally the last to know their own utilization. (2) Sell-side healthcare analysts: they proxy utilization from HCA/Tenet management commentary, quarterly channel checks, and claims panels that lag 60-120 days and cover commercial lives far better than Medicare. None of them pull Schedule B files. (3) The entire commercial trade-data industry — Panjiva, ImportGenius, Descartes Datamyne, S&P Global — is built on CBP AMS vessel/air manifests for FOREIGN imports. PR→mainland is domestic Jones Act cabotage: there is no import manifest, so their feeds are structurally blind, and their users assume "Puerto Rico is part of the U.S., so it's already in the trade data." It is — annually, fifteen months late.
- **Information lead:** Puerto Rico posts month M at roughly M+45 to M+60 days. Compare: the payer's quarterly print lands M+90 to M+130 for the quarter containing M; the med-tech print similar; CMS research-grade claims 6-12 months; and the identical AES-sourced numbers appear in the federal FT895 report ~12-15 months later. Net real lead: roughly 1.5-3 months ahead of the relevant earnings print, and 11-14 months ahead of the U.S. government publishing the exact same series.
- **Why still under-exploited:** The neglect is structural, not merely lazy. (a) It is a U.S. DOMESTIC goods flow that only a territorial government publishes monthly — an orphan between the "foreign trade" and "domestic economy" statistical universes. (b) It sits behind a Spanish-language interface on a small territorial statistics portal that intermittently returns 503s and has no API. (c) It is in no mainstream terminal — not FRED, not Bloomberg, not the monthly Census trade release everyone's vendor ingests. (d) No manifest-based dataset can ever carry it, because domestic cabotage generates no CBP import manifest. (e) It requires a cross-domain leap nobody's org chart rewards: trade-data quants don't model medical loss ratios, and healthcare analysts have never opened a Schedule B file. This is not a packaged product from Kpler/YipitData/M Science — it is a government PDF-and-CSV portal in San Juan.
- **Rough +EV:** Monthly observations; ≥1 SD tradable extremes fire roughly 5-9 times a year. On the paired book, expect ~2-4% gross edge per event at a ~57-62% hit rate — modest on its own. The real EV is in the fat tail: 2-3 times a decade an MA utilization surprise moves HUM/UNH 10-25% in a single session, and this signal should flag the setup one to two quarters early; a small standing put position sized to those events is where most of the return lives. Rough sleeve Sharpe 0.6-0.9. Capacity is high (mega-caps with deep options), so the binding constraint is signal quality, not liquidity. Data cost is essentially zero; build cost is a scraper plus one analyst-month of backtesting.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Biggest uncertainty by far: whether monthly PR→mainland device shipments track IMPLANT PROCEDURES or mostly CHANNEL INVENTORY. Consignment stock at hospitals is a buffer of unknown thickness, and it can be swamped by Section 232 tariff-threat pull-forwards, plant-specific shocks (hurricanes; the 2018 FDA warning letter to Medtronic Puerto Rico Operations in Juncos), and HS-line aggregation that mixes several device families into one code. Mandatory pre-trade work: regress the detrended monthly series against MDT's reported CRHF unit growth, BSX's CRM/WATCHMAN units, and payer MLR surprises over 2015-2025 — if the shipment-to-implant lag is unstable, the whole thesis collapses to noise. Secondary risk: the PR interface may not cleanly separate the mainland leg on every HS line in every month.

## 96. The Need Exhibit

**Arena:** financial-market
**Domain:** NONPROFIT AND MUTUAL ENTITY FILINGS that reveal commercial activity. RULES: institutions only; sanctioned collection

- **Data source:** State Certificate of Need (CON) administrative dockets — specifically the "need" exhibits inside applications, letters of intent, and affected-party opposition filings submitted almost entirely by nonprofit hospital systems and their for-profit JV partners in the 35 CON states + DC. Two things live in these dockets that live nowhere else: (1) a legally complete forward census of every new inpatient psych bed, rehab bed, dialysis station, ASC, hospice/home-health license, and major medical equipment unit that can enter a CON market for the next 2-3 years; and (2) the applicant's and the objector's own certified, facility-level historical utilization — trailing-12-month occupancy, average daily census, patient days, payer mix, and gross/net patient revenue — which CON rules force them to file to prove or rebut "need." That second item is confidential operating data on public companies (ACHC, UHS, EHC, SEM, SGRY, DVA), disclosed by their own lawyers into a state PDF docket, off the earnings calendar. Confirmed by CON consultancies: prior applications "often include detailed information on an established provider's historical and projected utilization, payor mix, gross and net patient revenues."
- **How to collect it:** Weekly scrape of ~15-20 state portals, each free and sanctioned, none standardized. Verified live: Washington DOH "CON Project Status" (736 projects; downloadable PDFs of letters of intent, applications, review notices, evaluations; filterable by applicant, project type, county, stage — doh.wa.gov/licenses-permits-and-certificates/facilities-z/certificate-need/project-status). Georgia DCH Office of Health Planning publishes a WEEKLY "CON Tracking Report" of every application under review plus an all-electronic submission portal (dch.georgia.gov/divisionsoffices/office-health-planning). New York DOH NYSE-CON, where a letter of intent naming sponsor, project description, and estimated cost must be filed at least 30 days BEFORE the application (health.ny.gov/facilities/cons/). North Carolina DHSR HPCON, Michigan MDHHS CON, Connecticut OHS, Tennessee HFC, and roughly a dozen more run equivalent dockets. Layer on the state-mandated annual facility utilization surveys that feed CON review (NC State Medical Facilities Plan / license-renewal data, Georgia Annual Hospital Questionnaire, Tennessee Joint Annual Report, Michigan annual surveys) for facility-level occupancy and payer mix. Pipeline: fetch PDFs weekly, OCR, LLM-extract applicant, target facility, bed/station/unit counts, modality and named equipment vendor, capital cost, JV partner, decision dates, and the historical utilization tables; join facility to parent company via the CMS Provider of Services file and NPPES. Where exhibits aren't posted, a state public-records request gets the full file. One analyst plus a scraper covers the 12 states that matter.
- **The bet / trade:** Primary: Acadia Healthcare (ACHC) — directional equity, sized off the docket-derived same-facility patient-day estimate, entered 3-6 weeks before the quarterly print and exited the day after (roughly a 1-2 month holding period, four events a year). Pair against UHS or an equal-weight healthcare-facilities basket to strip out the sector/Medicaid-policy beta, since ACHC trades almost purely on same-facility patient days and bed adds. Secondary, same machinery: Encompass Health (EHC) and Select Medical (SEM) on IRF/LTACH bed pipelines, Surgery Partners (SGRY) on ASC entry, DaVita (DVA) on dialysis-station awards. Structural overlay: a 12-24 month position (either direction) on ACHC/EHC based on CON-derived forward bed supply in their core markets — a bed physically cannot open in a CON state in year T unless an application was already filed by roughly year T-2, so today's docket hard-bounds next year's supply and next year's guided bed adds.
- **Mechanism:** Two independent chains. (1) Own-numbers leak: to win a CON, an applicant must document need with recent trailing-12-month utilization at its existing facilities, and an objecting incumbent must rebut with its own. ACHC is a serial CON applicant (it guided to 400-600 new beds in 2026 and added 82 in Q1 alone) and a serial objector, so its facility-level census and payer mix get certified into state dockets continuously through the quarter, referencing months that ended 1-3 months earlier. Aggregate enough facilities and you have a bottom-up estimate of the exact metric the stock trades on — Q1 2026 same-facility was +1.6% patient days, +5.6% revenue per day, and that spread is the whole debate. (2) Supply and pipeline: LOI to application to approval to construction to licensure runs 18-36 months. So the docket is a complete, exhaustive forward supply curve for every CON market — no other capacity can enter — and it reveals the company's own de novo/JV pipeline (nonprofit-system JV filings name the for-profit partner and bed count) 3-12 months before the company announces it. When a nonprofit system files for 60 psych beds in a metro where ACHC runs an 80%-occupancy facility, that is a dated, quantified 2028 rate and occupancy headwind sitting in a PDF today. Acadia's management has framed ramping beds as a $200M EBITDA opportunity; the docket tells you whether the beds to ramp actually exist in the queue.
- **Who's on the other side:** Sell-side healthcare-facilities analysts and long-only funds who model bed adds and same-facility growth off company guidance, management commentary, and channel checks with a handful of hospital contacts — plus event-driven shorts trading DOJ/malpractice/Medicaid-supplemental headlines. They are slow for structural reasons, not lazy ones. This is administrative-law data, not financial data: 35 non-uniform state agencies, scanned PDFs, no CIK, no ticker, no standard schema, some files only obtainable by public-records request, facility names that don't map to parent companies without a manual join. The conventional healthcare alt-data stack does not reach here either — claims panels (Komodo, Trilliant), card data, and HCA read-throughs all under-cover freestanding behavioral and inpatient rehab, which skew Medicaid, self-pay, and county-contract and sit outside commercial claims panels. The vendors that touch CON (Definitive Healthcare, RPC Consulting) sell it to hospital strategy teams as consulting input for writing applications, not as an investment feed. And critically, nobody thinks of a regulatory approval docket as a place where a public company discloses its own occupancy.
- **Information lead:** Three distinct leads. Utilization: dockets land continuously through the quarter with trailing-12-month data through a month that closed 1-3 months prior, giving a rough 3-8 week lead on the aggregate same-facility number versus the earnings print — and a permanent lead on facility-level detail the company never discloses at all. Pipeline: a nonprofit-system JV filing names the for-profit partner and bed count 3-12 months before the company announces the JV. Supply: the LOI-to-licensure clock is 18-36 months, so today's docket is a hard, mechanical bound on 2027-2029 capacity in every CON market, versus sell-side models that simply extrapolate management's bed-add guidance. New York's 30-day letter-of-intent rule adds a free month on top of the application itself.
- **Why still under-exploited:** Searches for a CON tracker aimed at investors return nothing — the ecosystem is policy trackers (NASHP's 50-state scan), consultancies that help hospitals write applications, and state agencies. No Kpler/YipitData/M Science equivalent exists, and there is no aggregated cross-state feed to buy at any price. The data is repellent by design: fragmented across 35+ agencies with wildly different thresholds (NY triggers CON above $30M, Iowa above $1.5M), inconsistent posting (Washington warns of a 2-3 week status lag; NC pre-2019 files need records requests), scanned PDFs, and no common identifier. The specific insight — that an adversarial "need" proceeding forces a public operator to certify its own facility-level occupancy and payer mix into a public record — appears to be unremarked in investing entirely. It is also decaying, which is exactly why it is still cheap: states have been narrowing CON (Tennessee no longer requires it to establish a psychiatric facility, South Carolina largely repealed in 2023, Georgia loosened in 2024, North Carolina is in litigation). A shrinking dataset attracts no vendor investment, so the window belongs to whoever builds it now.
- **Rough +EV:** Event edge: ~4 ACHC prints per year plus 8-12 more across EHC/SEM/SGRY/DVA, so roughly 12-16 firings annually. Docket coverage realistically reaches 15-30% of a company's CON-state beds with usable utilization exhibits — enough to call the sign and rough magnitude of the same-facility patient-day surprise, not the decimal. Assume 60-65% directional hit rate against a coin flip on a metric where ACHC's one-day earnings moves have run 8-20%. That is roughly +2 to +4% expected per event, or on the order of 8-15% annualized on the sleeve before costs, on a market-neutral pair. The structural supply call fires far less often — maybe one or two high-conviction multi-quarter positions per year — but is worth more per firing, since a market-by-market demonstration that guided bed adds cannot physically arrive (or that competing supply is already approved) is a thesis-level, 20-40% re-rating call on a name that ran 77%+ into early 2026 on precisely that narrative. Build cost is one analyst plus a scraper: call it 6-10 weeks to first signal, then low maintenance.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Existence and legality are solid — the portals are live, free, and explicitly public, and the presence of applicant utilization, payer mix, and net revenue in CON filings is confirmed by CON practitioners. The biggest uncertainty is redaction and comparability: I have verified that these exhibits routinely contain the data, but not what fraction survive trade-secret redaction, nor whether the reporting periods align tightly enough to fiscal quarters to aggregate cleanly. If most utilization tables come back scrubbed, chain (1) collapses and only the supply/pipeline read survives — still valuable, but a slower, lower-frequency signal rather than an earnings-event edge. The close second risk is political decay: continued CON repeal shrinks the observable universe state by state, and Tennessee's psychiatric carve-out already removed one of ACHC's most important markets from the docket.
